THE COMET. The Comet! he is on his way, And singing as he flies; The whizzing planets shrink before The spectre of the skies. Ab! well may regal orbs burn blue, And satellites turn pale; Ten million cubic miles of head. Ten million leaguos of tail! On, on, by whistling spheres of light He flAsnes and he flames; He turns not to the left nor right. He astis them not their names; One spurn from ids demoniac heel, Away, away, the...-fly, where daruness might be bottled up And sold for " Tynan dye." And what would happen to the land,

And how would look the sea, If in the bearded monster's path Our earth should chance to be? Full hot and high the sea would boil, Full red the forests gleam; Methought I saw and heard it all In a dyspeptic dream I saw a tutor take his tube The comets course to spy; I heard a scream—the gathered rays Had stewed the tutor's eye; I saw a fort—the soldiers all

Were armed with goggles green; Pop cracked the guns I whizz flew the balls! Bang went the magazine! I saw a roasted pullet sit Upon a baking egg; I saws cripple scorch his hand Extinguishing his leg; I saw nine geese upon the wing, Towards the frozen pole, And every mother's gosling fell Crispe I to a cracking coal. I saw the ox that browsed the grass WI ithe in the blistering rays, The herbage in his shrinking jaws Was all a fiery blaze; I saw huge fishes boiled to rags Bob throne. the bubbling brine; And thoughts of supper crossed my sunl— it had been rash at mine. Strange eights: Strange sounds! Oh fearful dream : Its memory haunts me still, The steaming sea, the crimson glare,,,,, That wreathed each wooded bill. Stranger if thr.,ugh thy reeling brain Such midnight visions sweep, 1. Spare, oh spare thine evening meal And sweet shall be thy sleep! a -"ri OLlVait WENDELL HOLMES.

A bright bide girl, who had successfully spelled the word "that," was asked by her teacher what would remain after the" t" had. been taken away. "The cups and saucers," was the reply. A gentleman aced an Amezican the other day what he thought of the English climate. He laughed and said, .• Why, you haven't got a climate; you'y,C only got &tul- les: ' The Tarks have a few good sayings, one of which is," The d 0,4 barks, and the caravan goes by; mere noise is nothing." Another is that " tne dog which is led out to hunt against his will takes DO game."

A girl heard her father criticised severely across a dinner table. The ctreless critic pawed for a moment to sal'," I hope be is no relation of yours, Miss L." And, as quick as thought, she reolied, with the utmost nonchalance, "Only a connection (Amy mother's by marriage." Some men peas through life without ever hearing heavenly music—they carry small bells of envy, jealousy, malice and hatred hanging about their minds, which by their discordant jingle torment themselves and other people, and drown every hi_th, sweet, and noble thought. BE JUST TO -CAILDRES.—Never accuse a child of a fault unless you are certain he committed it. Children should not be treated with suspicion. We should act towards them in this matter as we feel we onght to act towards others, only with greater tenderness—not less, as is usually done. Dr. Henniker, being in private conversation with the Earl of Chatham, his Lordshio asked him, among other ques- tions, what was wit, according to his opinion? " Wit, ' he replied, "my Lord, is what a peltion would be given by your Lordship to your bumble servant—a good thing well applied." "What a methodical fellow you are, Brown," said Fitkins, • who had stepped into Brown's office during the latter's ab- sence. "Why, what do you mean r asked Brown, who had just entered. " Mean ?" echoed Fitkina, "to think that you should lock all your drawers up when you are only going out for five minut.-3. Tisn't likely that any one would meddle with your pipers." "Of course not," replied Brown, "but how did you find out thlt the drawers were locked ?" The late celebrated Dr. Brown paid his addresses to a lady for many years, out unsucceeafatly ; during which time he had always accustomed himself to propose her health when- ever he was callal upon for a lady. Bat being observed one evening to omit it, a gentleman reminded him that he had forgotten to toast his favourite lady. "Why, indeed," said the Doctor, "I fild it all in vain; I have toasted her so many years, and cannot make her Brown, that I am deter- mined to toast her no longer." A HAPPY MARRIAGE.—Consider what this is, what it mit' be, whenever it occurs, whether in high places or in humble. It is not only the blending together of two human souls for the mutual society, comfort, and help of etch—not only a constant giving and. taking of the purest happiness, but also a new beginning of life, a new starting•point of use- fulness. It is Oa great call, one for all, to leave the past with all its errors and faults and follies far, far behind us, and to press forward` with new hopes and new courage and new strength into the future which lies before us.

CHEERFULNESS VERSUS FRETFULNESS —The moat at- tractive thing in woman is a sunny, cheerful disposition. On the other nand, the most disagreeable thing is a fretful, cornntaining temperament. In some instances, fretfulness is the exponent of an unhealthy body, and while in that case it cuu be tolerated, it is none the less unpleasant to come in contact with. No one cires to ba long in the society of a fretful person; it has an irritating effect upon one's nerves and a tendency to depress the most healthful atmosphere. On the contrary, cheerfulness, like sunshine, warms and radiates, drawing rather than repulsing. Habits grow upon us, and once formed, are very hard to get rid of. Whatever is cultivated in youth is apt to be prominent in maturer years. Cultivate cheerfulness, girls, and if there is an inclination to be fretful, pat it down, and your price will be "far above rubies."
THE APPRENTICE'S WINDOW, S. OCIEN CATHEDRAL.-

In connection with the two large rose-windows in the tran- sept, a tragic et ,ry is told. It is said that the master mason, Alexander litrneval, devoted his whole attention to the window in the south transept, and gave over the north transept window entirely to his apprentice. When the work was finished, it was obvious that "the apprentice's window" (as it is still called )—into the delicate tracery of which the combination of triangles, called the pentalpha, had been skilfully introduced—far excelled the production of the master. The latter was SO enraged at the discovery that he killed his talented Apprentice, and consequently suffered the extreme penalty of the law. But the monks bad great esteem for Berneval, who hid executed much good work in their cathedral, and they accordingly interred his body in the Chapel of St. Agnes, side by side with the apprentice, who, for bettering his master's teaching by the power of his native genius, had met with an early doom.—The Cities of the World. Ax EXTRAORDINARY Baran-E.—A curious illustration

occurred in a Wiltsisire village where I lived for some years. A swarm of bees had managed to evade their rightful owner, and had made their way Into the church roof, between the tiles and the lath and plaster ceiling with which most vil- lage churches were afflicted at that period. Being undis- turbed, the bees increased mightily, but they never sent out a swarm. As long as they restricted themselves to the roof, they were allowed to remain untouched. Bet after some years they found their way through the flimsy ceiling, and came into the church in such numbers that the congregation hardly dared to enter the building. At the beginning of winter, when all the bees were torpid, an entrance was made Into their domains, and a wonderful eight it was. The beams and rafters were hidden under the masses of cora)). The workmen thought that they had a valuable prize of wax and honey, but they were quite mistaken. In our artificial bee houses we can induce the insects to store the honey in separate portions of the hive. Bat in this instance the bees had so much space at command that they mixed up the honey cells with the bread cells and breeding cells, so that the labour Of separating them would not have been repaid by the reealte.—Good Words. EXTRAORDINARY FINGIUR NAILS.—It is In slam, In An- nam and in Cochin China that this extraordinary custom is carried to Its greatest development. The nobles of Annam, for instance, permit their nails to grow to such a length that the hands are absolutely useless for any practical pur- pose. The nails on the second, third, and fourth fingers at- tain a length of from four to nearly five inches. They are straight, with a slight inward carve, and present the appear- ance of immense claws or talons; which we could imagine might be of use to man in his most savage state for scratch- up the ground to find roots or seeds, but certainly do pted for either use or ornament under any of not appear ada the ordinary incidents of life. The nail of the thumb Is hardly so long as those of the other digits. It at first grows nearly straight, with also a tendency to curve inwards, but presently takes the form or an elongated spiral, and must almost entirely prevent the use of the thumb as an organ of prehension. On the first finger alone is the nail kept within reasonable bounds, and with this only mast be performed all those innumerable trifling acts which taken together add so greatly to our comfort and well-being. It sometime' hap. pens that the nails are allowed to grow to It great length to Indicate that the wearer leads a religions life, and has for- sworn at once the labours and frivolities of the world. The band of a Chinese ascetic, leading such an indolent and wasteful existence, presents the most extraordinary spec- tacle. The nail of the first finger is indeed, as in the case of the Annamese already described, left tufficiently short t render the finger of some practical service. The other fin- gers are, however, disfigured by immense horny growths, which can scarcely be called nails, which reach the enor- mons length of from si.eteen to eighteen inches.—" The World of Wonders."

A valuable horse was burnt to death. The fire is supposed to be the work of an incendiary. At a meeting of the East Riding Chamber of Agriculture, on Saturday, representing 1,000 tenant-farmere, it was re- solved unanimously that it would be useless to send in agri- cultural returns until a Minister of Agriculture is appointed. The meeting was also of opinion that the agricultural in- terest would never rally until there was more direct repre- sentation of farmers, and until compensation is granted for , unexhausted improvements. A cattle dealer, named Pearlrose, was charged at Colches- ter with cruelly torturing a cow, by neglecting to have it milked when urgently required. The evidence showed that the cow, which had a muzzled calf by her side, was left a great while without milking, the result being that her adders swelled terribly, the teats stood out obliquely, while her temperature, which was tested by a thermometer, rose to 103 deg. The magistrates imposed a fine of £2, and £2 14s. costa. At the annual sales of rains held in Melbourne, in Septem- ber, higher prizes were obtained than on any previous occa- sion. One ram of the merino breed, from Sir Samuel Wil- son's Mount Bate estate, eold for 650gse another of the same owner's, from the Erclldoune fleck, brought 400 gs. His four best sold for an average of £451 10s. each. His eight best brought an average of £275 12s. 6d., and his twenty best averaged £155 8s The sales continued for three days; and excellent prices were also obtained by other owners. The total amount realised by the sales was over £50,000. A New DISEASE.—At a meeting of the Southern Counties Vetecioary Medical Association, held at Red Lion-square last week, Mr. G. Fleming, Army Veterinary Inspector,read a paper on a new disease which he had discovered to prevail extensively, chiefly among cattle, in .this country, and the ;nature of e inch has until now been hidden in obscurity. It 1, manifests itself by greet enlargement and inclaration,as well las ulceration of the tongue. It also attacks the bones of I the face and jawe, appears inside and outside the throat in the form of tumours, and is very destructive, especially aetong young str,ck. Mr. Fleming, by means of enorbid specie-lees from the tongues and heeds of i;aivel, at well as by mier.ecopical preperatioos, cheerier demonstrated the affection to be due io the presence of a minute fungus, which probably obtains an entrance to the tissues either through the mucous follicles or an abrasion in the mouth. From tee peculiar manner in which the fungus grows, and the radiatieg arrangement of its branchete it has received the name of Actinomyces, and it is conseqtently proposed to deeignae the disease Actinonzykoses. It has hitherto only been noticed in Germany. and Italy, and no fewer than six- teen cases are reported in the Getman medical journals as haying been observed in man. Mr. Fleming produced some evidence to show that the fungus could be successfully im- planted from a diseased to a healthy animal; and one of the German cases, in which a man was affected, would lead to the suspicion that it may be communicated from the lower animals to our own species. Instances were given in which the misropbyte had also been found in pigs, goats, a horse, and a dog. The winter session of the Edinburgh New Veterinary College at Gayfield was opened on Wednesday week. Prin• cipal Williams occupied the chair, and there was a large attendance of students. The inaugural address was delivered by Professor Lewis, who dealt with the vast improvements made in the methods of conducting microscopical research, which, he said, was essential to the study of moroid. an- atomy. The profession had been rather tardy in recognis- ing the worth of a microscope as an auxiliary in the study of pathology, but the recent discoveries by means of the microscope in the pathology of splonic fever, tuberculosis, fowl cholera, louping•ill, and similar diseases, had mate- rially assisted in demonstrating its value. As illustrating its practical worth, he referred to the discoveries in connec- itton with tuberculosis and louping-ill. They had learned that the former disease, which occasioned one seventh of all the deaths of the human race was caused by rod-shaped bacteria of parasitic origin. Tuberculosis was not confined to mankind, but was very prevalent among the lower ani- mals, especially our beef and milk producers, and it had been recently calculated that in Landon 7,500 cattle affected with this disease were annually slaughtered for food. The danger attending tuberculosed flesh and milk was no imagin- ary one, fcr it had been proved over and over again by ex- periment that the disease can be readily communicated to the lower animals; and if so to cattle, sheep, and pigs, why not to man? In looping-ill, which annually destroyed great numbers of our sheep, we bad another disease due to the action of micro-organisms. Professor Williams had dis- covered that a jelly-like stabstance found in the spinal canals of sheep affected with the disease contained quanti- ties of a b tcterial myceliam, which gave a clue to the cause of the disease. Eeen in those sheep whose spinal canals did not contain the jelly-like substance, the bacteria could readily be detected by cultivating a little of the fluid in mutton broth, when similar results were obtained. In order ' to solve the connection between ticks and louping•ill, num- bers of ticks were collected from louping-ill sheep, and sub- jected to microscopical examination and to cultivation. It was then discovered that they also were infected with bac- teria resembling those ob!ained from the sheep, which showed that they introduced the disease into the system of the sheep. One link WAS still wanting—the production of the disease experimentally by inoculating sheep with the bacterium-infected tick, but any advance in that direction was forbidden by the Anti-Vivisection Act. Doas.—Thz IRISEt TERRIER.—Irish terriers have recently advanced very rapiply in public estimation, and though they have been well-known and highly appreciated in Ire- land for many years, it is only during the last four years that we have seen them—at anyrate, except occasionally— ' on this side of the Channel, and then only as a curiosity at our principal shows. Bat now the case is altogether differ- ent; the establishment of an Irish Terrier Club, with head- quarters in London, has conduced to make them very popu- lar. The appearance of an Irish terrier has all to do with it; a good one is very good-looking, though a bad one is— well, not good-looking. They are, however, good working and useful terriers plucky and determined workers, can go a good pace for their size, are capable of enduring fatigue and wet to an almost unlimited extent, and are, therefore, peculiarly adapted for the boggy ground and rainy climate of their native country. As we indicated before, a well- bred Irish terrier is a fine-looking animal; their faces are very intelligent and sprightly; they are excellent com- panions for walking, riding, or driving; their short wiry coats do not became matted or dirty through the storms of our variable climate; and their natural hardiness prevents that appearance of utter wretchedness and misery which so many breeds of dogs exhibit in severe and changeable weather. All the breed are very sagacious, and understand the meaning of words to a remarkable degree. Their very hardiness makes them very free from disease, such as mange, drc., but how long they will remain so is an open question, as dogs of a fashionable breed become so pampered and Petted as to be altogether different to workmen of the same breed. So far as the points are concerned, a true Irish terrier Should be as follows :—The head long, fiat, and narrow across, with strong, lean, pointed muzzle; the teeth very white and level; the ears small and oval, lying close to the head, and the colour of them darker than the rest of the hair; the hair of the ears very short, no long hairs to be seen; the neck well-proportioned, not thick or bull-necked ; the legs of medium length, so as to lift the body well out of the mud, and the hair on them shorter than on the back —which should be wiry, without any tendency to matting or entanglement, but more of a door-mat texture, and each hair, though very close, be distinct ; the eyes very bright And keen ; and the weight from 1.51b5 tj 24l Sach is the idea of a good Irish terrier.

Mr. Stanley has left London h survey work for some 500 miles of the Lower Congo, accomplished during the last weeks of his late mission, is very complete and full of geographical interest. —Atheneum. It is understood that Mr. Browning has finished enough fresh minor poems to form a thin volume like the two last that he has published; but it is probable that he will keep them back till he has completed a longer poem to come out with them. Mr. Joseph Thomson will leave England for Zanzibar at the end of the present month, to organise the expedition which the Royal Geographical Society are about to send, under his command, through the hitherto unexplored Maui country to the eastern shores of Victoria Nyanza. The ex- pedition will not start from the coast for some months; meantime Mr. Thomson will make a preliminary journey in. land to inquire as to the best and most practicable route. Of the two mountains in this region which rise above the limits of perpetual snow Ife will direct his attention pre- ferably to Mount Kenia, as the less known. There appears to be a pitch larger area above the snow-line on this than on Kilimanjaro, and a possibility of glaciers on its western side.—Atheneum. To ASCERTAIN WHETHER BUTTER IS ADULTERATED.— When butter is mixed with tallow It may be usually detected by melting a little of the butter in a spoon and smelling it, whsn the smell of the tallow may be at once perceived. Another way to learn whether this substance has been added is to melt a small piece of batter at a heat not exceeding that of boiling water, and pour it into a wine glass. Then Immediately pour over it two fluid drachms of commercial nitric acid (aqua fortis) and shake them slightly. If the batter employed is pure, it will rise to the suriace, and not i become opaque for some minutes; bat if it contains much I tallow, it will quickly become a Imre or less opaque white mass, the nature of the change and the time required depending on the amount of the fat present in the adulter- ated article. Sometimes butter is adulterated with horse. bone oil. In this case the butter is to be shaken up with hot water until melted, and allowed to collect upon the surface. Remove five drops of this, and place them on a watch glass, and immediately add ten drops of strong sulphuric acid. P the batter has been adulterated with horse-bone oil, a deeper colour will be produced than if the butter did not contain that substance —CasseE's Household Guide. DESTRUCTIVE TIDAL Ways.—An Indian named Palicua has visited Panama, and furnished Governor Borbna with some interesting particulars of a tidal or earthquake wave -which visited the coast of San Bias on the 7th of September. From the account given by the Indian it appears that the tide ran out a great distance, and on its return swept away the villages built on the beaches of the different islands of the archipelago and on the mainland. The outflow and in- flow occurred four times in the day, the greatest daniag6 being done by tbe third wave. The villages of Rio Coco, Isla Paloma, and Napactudi, on the islands of the same name, were swept away, and more than 40 persons were drowned. At Playon Grande every house was washed down, but only two persons were drowned. Playon Chico, which adjoins it, also suffered. All the produce stored at Rio Mono was swept away, but no lives were lost. The chief loss of produce, however, has taken place at Aguili Candi island, where good barbouraga led to the chief busi- ness of the district being carried on. Sixteen persons lost their lives there, and several thousand dollars worth of im- ported goods were swept into the sea. The villages at Rio Banana and Mosquito have also been flooded, the people left homeless, and their goods destroyed. Other villages must also have suffered, but particulars bad not reached San Blas when Pallcua lett there. San Bias is a district in the State of Panama, the principal town being situated on a cape which runs into the Atlantic. It is sparsely populated, and the inhabitants live iirincipally by collecting natural pro- ducts, which they dispose of to small coasters.—Panama Star and Herald, Oct. 12. NEW TELEGRAPH SOUNDERS.-Sir Charles Bright, who introduced the acoustic telegraph known as" Bright's bell instrument" some 30 years ago, has recently inventel an improved sounder, in which the metal stops of the ordinary Instrument are replaced by tubes of Muntee metal, against which the tongue or clapper strikes. These tubular bells emit a pleasant musical clink when struck, and each has a different pitch, so that the ear of the clerk readily distill- guiehes them. Moreover, they are not so liable to be con- founded with the clinking of machinery or other sounds, and hence are peculiarly suitable for use in railway signal boxes. The London, Brighton, and South Coast, the Great Northern, and other railway companies have adopted them, and the instrument is now being tried on the Postal Tele- graph lines. The telephone has proved its value in the re- cent Egyptian campaign; but speech is so apt to be dis- turbed by induction and other influences, that for Army purposes the Morse sounder Is perhaps more reliable. In the Russian army, however, the telephone is employed as a sounder, the signals received on it being Morse signals, sent

, by an ordinary Morse key. This is the " telekal" of Colonel Jacobi, and consists of a battery, key, line, and telephone; each Morse signal causing a clicking sound in the diaphragm of the telephone. An improvement on this plan has recently been made by M. L. Wiessenbrach, and. adopted into the Belgian army. In this the battery and Morse key are dis- carded, and the signals made by striking the plate of the telephone, which is used as a transmitter as well as receiver. These telephones consist of a powerful horseshoe magnet with coils round its poles, and a large iron disc over them as in the Gower-Bell telephone. A jointed hammer lever is fixed on the diaphragm and on working it the hammer strikes the plate and induces a pulse of electricity in the coils at every blow by magneto-electric action. This pulse traverses the line and causes the telephone at the other end to click. Long signals or "dashes' are distinguished from short or "dot" signals by the time between the pulse gene- rated on depressing the hammer, and the reverse pulse due to the return of the hammer to its normal position. THE CAIISE OF SIMS-HEADACHE.—Dr. SAVage, of Jack- son, Tennessee (in The Medical and Surgical Reporter and Edinburgh Medical Revie,c), announces that he has dis- covered the real Cause of sick-headache to be hypermetro- pia and astigmatism, either alone or combined, and that its successful treatment censequently consists in the use of a properly, fitted glass. In support of his views, he gives a detailed account of four- cases occurring in the persons of his mother, his sister, his preceptor, and himself. His mother had long suffered from sick-headache; but, as she grew older, the attacks because less frequent, and, at the age of 58, she became entirely free from them. At the same time, she noticed that her vision for distant objects was failing. Dr. Savage examined her, and found that her once latent hypermetropia had been converted by loss of power in her ciliary muscle into a wholly manifest hyper- metropia. The question occurred to him, could not her far- sightedness have been the predisposing cause of her sick- headache, and would not the simple glasses he was then able to give her have transformed her years of suffering into years of ease? He was a sufferer himself. In the latter part of March of this year, premonitory symptoms of an attack of sick-headache appeared. Instead of taking his accustomed dose of chloride of sodium, he pat three or four drops of a one per cent. solution of atropia into his left eye, the headache being confined to that side. In half an hour, his ciliary muscle was at rest, he was free from pain, and I had no inclination to vomit, as on former occasions. The atropia had relieved the tension of. his ciliary muscle, put- ting it to rest, and thus relieving its pain; and, there being no farther cause for sympathy on the part of the head and stomach, the pain and nausea ceased. His vision was perfect before; now, however, hypermetropia and astig- matism existed in his eye; so that, to overcome the defect, he required a combination of a convex spherical lens of forty-two inches focal distance, and a convex cylindrical of sixty inches focal distance, with its axis set at an angle of 90 deg. He afterwards found the right eye also hyper- metropic and astigmatic, and gave it the proper correction. Since then, with one week's exception, he has done all his reading, ac., with the aid of the glasses. During the week he laid them aside, he had a severe attack of sick-headache, and does not, in consequence, intend to repeat his folly. In his sister's case, the doctor found one eye hypermetrople, the other hypermetrople and astigmatic. The proper glass for each eye was given her, and now her sick head-ache is a thing of the past. His preceptor he found hypermetropic ; and in his case, also, after the use of convex lenses, the sick . .

headache disappeared. The predisposition to sick•headache, In most persons, ceases between the ages of 50 and 60. Dr. Savage offers as an explanation of this, that, about this time, a latent hypermetropia is converted into a manifest hyper- metropia, the ciliary muscle that has had to work so hard during so many years being worn out, and ceasing its labonrs, and thus there is no further cause for sympathy on the part of the head and stomach. The periodicity of the attacks, he thinks, may be explained by the eye being able to bear for a time the excesiive work it is made to do, when at length its distress is made known by an explosive attack of sick-headache, the eye and head aching indescribably, and the stomach, through sympathy, so desperately nauseated as to unload itself of its contents. Even before the attack

comes on, the stomach performs its functions sluggishly, through sympathy for the overworked eye. The exciting cause for the sick headache, he is of opinion, is always to be found in the over-use of a hypermetropic or astigmatic eye. —British Medical Journal.,

Erskine observed, on coming into court one day, that Mr. Balfour, a brother barrister, had his ankle hound up with a silk handkerchief. " What's the matter, Balfour ?" he in- quired. The sufferer, whose mode of expressing himself was always very elaborate, replied—" I was taking a roman- tic ramble in my brother's grounds, when, coming to a gate, I had te climb over it, by which I came in contact with the first bar and graged the epidermis of my leg, which has caused a slight extravasation of blood." "You may thank your lucky stars," observed Erskine, "that your brother's gate was not so lofty as your style, or you must have broken your neck."

MARRIED OR Sniem—lt is hard to tell whether married people are happier than single ones or whether single ones are most blest. With the gout in his big toe, and no one to find fault with, bachelor is apt to envy Benedict; while, during the progress of a curtain lecture, Benedict depre- ciates the joys of wedded life. Single people have more peace and quietness, but now and then they bud themselves rather too severely let alone. Married people rejoice in the joys of companionship, but as there may be too mach of a good thing, they, perhaps, sometimes envy St. /Simon fitylites, who lived on the top of a pillar and "had his meals sent up to him" in a bahket. _ -

London, W.C., and reprinted by permission.] THE ELCHOS. What a graceful and dignified speech was that which Lord Elcho delivered in the British House of Commons on the Zulu War. The modern fashion is to scream at our enemies lie fish-fags, and blackguard them like coster- mongers. Poor Shere Ali was the object of our abuse so long as he lived; now it is Cetewayo's turn. We have it on the word of Lord Elcho that he is a gorilla; we have it also from Lord Elcho, on the eminent authority of a Ger- man newspaper, that he caught his brother alive and tor- tured him to death. True, that a better authority, Bishop Colenso, declares that there is no foundation for the story. No matter, Cetewayo is our enemy, and if the stories about • him are not true they ought to be. Impelled, I suppose by the 4' gorilla" speech, a correspon- dent asks me—Who is Lord Elcho, and how comes it that he represents a Scottish constituency ? He is the eldest son of the Earl of Wemyss and March, and has been for many years member for Haddingtonshire —formerly as a Liberal' and latterly as a Conservative; and he showed his apprecia: tiou of his constituents by flinging the contents of his cigar case among them on the hustings, when the seat was con- tested by that renowned Scottish farmer, the late Mr. Hope, of Fenton Barns. He sits for the county, not because the Haddingtonshire farmers are less Liberal that those of most other Scotch constituencies, but because his father owns 10,136 acres of land in that county. Besides these estates the Earl has 4,789 acres at Stanway, in Gloucestershire, obtained either by purchase er marriage. A century and a half ago Stanway was held by the Tracy family, who had a grant of the same at the dissolution of the monasteries. The Earl also has 3,010 acres in the neighbourhood of Elcho, Perth- shire, where the family once had a castle; 1,261 acres in, Berwick, and 1,504 in Midlothian-61,947 acres in all; with a gross rent-roll of £56,742. The Wemyss family claimed to be descended from that Macduff, Thane of Fife, who slew the murderer and usurper, Macbeth. It must be remembered, however, that it is only in tragedy that Macbeth was a murderer and usurper. Duncan was killed at Botitgowan, near Elgin, which, as Mr. Burton remarks, was near, if not actually within the terri- tory ruled by Macbeda ; Duncan being there with aggressive designs. How the Wernyse fatni,y tirst obtained lands in Fife I know not, but in the fourteenth century they had two additional grants from the King, and another in the six- teeth. Their connection with Fife appears now to be merely titular, as they have sloughed off the old skin; and while the name of Wemyss represents their ancient origin, those of Clurteris and Douglas indicate the manner in which they have acquired most of their present possessions. Until the reign of Charles I. they were commoners ; but that menarch ereate4 Vire *mad of the house Lord Elcho, and subaujuently Earl of Wemyss. These favours did not hin- der him from manifesting his Covenanting sympathies taring the Civil War, and his son, Lord Elcho' who married a daughter of Balfour of Burleigh, followed his: example, and was defeated at a battle in Perthshire by Montrose. By a subsequent marriage, this last had an only daughter, in whose favour a new patent of peerage was obtained. Her son, who was Lord High Admiral of Scotland, and a Com- missioner of' the Treaty of Union, married the daughter of the first Duke of Queensberry. It is through this alliance that the Wernyss family derive a very large portion of their property. The first Douglas, Duke of Queensberry, who died at the age of forty-eight, according to Burnet, who describes him as "very covetous," came into a much impaired fortune, but he greatly increased it. For a long time he was Lord High Treasurer of Scotland, and rendered himself odious by exacting ruinous fines from the Presbyterian gentry, who obeyed the law by going to church, but left their wives at home. He increased his fortune 80 much that he purchased for his second son who was created Earl of March, the lands and lordship of Neidpath, in Peebles, from the Hays, ances- tors of the Marquis of Tweeddale. It was not all of the Earl of March's lands that were obtained by purchase. The Duke of Queensberry in 1688 obtained a grant of the principal part of the revenue of the Cross Church, Peebles, consisting of sundry houses in the West Port, Edinburgh, of lands in the parish of Cramond, and 50 acres of rich glebe lauds—only four acres being left for the minister. This property he gave to the Earl of March. In 1707 there was an additional grant. "Among other favours," says the "Statistical Ac- count of Scotland," "he obtained the grant of Forton, and that donative had been deemed of so much value that it was named in the deed of entail of the March estates." The issue of the Earl of March subsequently succeeded to the Queensberry title and estates, but at the death of the fourth Duke without issue the Dukedom passed to the Duke of Buc- clench, the Marquisate to another kinsman, and the Earl- dom of March, with the estates held by the first Earl, to the seventh Earl of Wemyss. But in the meantime, the fourth Earl had contractei a _ _

splendid marriage with the daughter and heiress of Colonel Francis Charteris, of Amisfield, Haddingtonshire. Of this personage I have had some difficulty in gaining information, except that in his own day he is described as "notorious," and a "gambler," and that he was tried and condemned for a heinous crime, with difficulty obtaining a pardon. Look- ing over the works of Swift, edited by Sir Walter Scott, I came across the following remarkable epitaph, with the following foot-note by the editor:—"This epitaph on a man infamous for all manner of vices was written by Dr. Arbuthnot." It runs as follows:—" Here continueth to rot the body of Francis Chartres, who, with an inflexible con- stancy and inimitable uniformity of life, persisted, in spite of age and infirmities, in the practice of every human vice excepting prodigality and hypocrisy ; his insatiable a arice exempted him from the first, his matchless impudence from the second. Nor was he more singular in the undeviating suavity of his manners than successful in accumulating wealth; for, without trade or profession, without trust of public money, and without bribe-worthy service,he acquired —or, more properly, created—a ministerial estate. He was the only person of his time who could cheat .without the mask of honesty;' retain his primeval manners when possessed of £lO,OOO a year; and, having daily deserved the gibbet for what he did, was at last condemned for what he could not do. 0, indignant reader, think not his life useless to mankind! Providence connived at his execrable designs to give to after ages conspicuous proof and example of how small estimation is exorbitant wealth in the sight of God, by his bestowing it on the most unworthy of all mor- tals," I think that this will do as a companion picture to Lord Elcho's gorilla. If Dr. Arbuthnot had lived till now, he might have found another respect in which the life of Colonel Charteris was not useless to mankind, inasmuch as we owe it to his acquisition of property that Lord Elcho sits for Haddingtonshire. The ekeat son of the fourth Earl of •Wemysa was engaged in the Jacobite Rebellion of 1745, and was attaiuted in consequence. The father died in 1756, hut the son lived on an exile till 1787. At that time the Wemyss family had a narrow escape of being snuffed out, but as the next brother had not been implicated in the rebellion, he was mercifully allowed to succeed to the family title and estates. It only remains to be said that the Wemyss family, unlike most of the great Scotch houses, have never shown voracious tax-eating propensities. They have furnished at various times not a few gallant soldiers to the British Army and officers in the Navy. If they are too belligerent in their propensities, at any rate, unlike the Jingo mob who howl for war without the least intention of fighting themselves, the family of Wemyss are always ready to take a fair share of the risks. A younger brother of Lord Elcho was killed at Balaclava, and more recently his lordship's second and eldest surviving son died at sea of fever and dysentery, brought on by the hardships of the campaign in Ashantee. Charteris-Douglas-Wemyss; it seems a strange combination —the successful gambler, the oppressor of the Presbyterians, and the soldier of the Covenant. Were I a Scotchman' 1 should regard the worldly successes of the first and second as far less glorious than the defeat of the third.

HOUSEHOLD PETS. A KENNEL DlASY.—Every dog owner who goes in for breeding or exhibiting should keep a record of the pedigrees, progeny, and successes of his animals, as well as the ex- penses connected with the same, not only for his own satis- faction, bat for pecuniary purposes also. A dog with an undoubted pedigree will sell for a very great deal more than one without such a pedigree, however handsome the latter may be. In fact, as there is the belief that "blood will tell," a well-descended dog is indeed a valuable property. Of course, the owner of a single house dog need not trouble himself in this way, and if even he has a pedigree dog he can easily keep its record; but the owner of several dogs needs something more, and few have succeeded in devising a proper system for themselves. To meet this want a kennel diary has been framed at the Bazaar office, London, which provides just the thing needed. It contains an index diary, in which each dog's name is entered, with references to the other sections; an owner's diary, a breeder's diary, a diary of pups, a stud diary, an exhibition diary, a general diary, a pedigree diary, and pages on which receipts and expendi- ture can be entered, together with a general balance sheet at the end. It is very well arranged, and by a simple yet novel arrangement each section can easily be found, and will be a boon to many, bringing order where chaos has hereto- fore reigned. PLGRONs' FOOD.—rigeon keeper' ire very fond of using oily grains for their birds, under the impression that as these foods produce heat they must be good. But this Is a mistake, as the question of condition and habits of the birds must be taken into account. Foods such as hemp, rape, and ether heating seeds should only be given under very special cireumstances, and neer as a regular article of diet. Some, indeed, bays recourse to meat—a most objec- tionable food for pigeons. This is all wrong, as these sub- stances increase the animal heat of the pigeon and the lia- bility to disease. The thirst is increased also, and homers, especially in travelling, either stiffer through inability to find water for quenching it, or lose time in seeking for water and refreshing themselves ' • whilst aviary-confined birds get many diseases which the homer could throw off. The best grains during all seasons are beans, peas, tares, dart, with a very little of the small Indian corn during the winter. Always buy good sound food, which, in the case of beans, peas, and tares, should be a year old. Damaged grain is dear at a gift, and ought not to be used in any case, as it does a positive injury instead of any good. Pigeons are very fond of salt, and know no moderation in the use of it. It is a mistake to leave large lumps of salt about in the loft, for whilst a little is an aid to digestion, as well as a gratification, too much is disastrous, increases the animal heat, and produces emaciation. Matter containing limo is indispensable to the maintenance of health in pigeons, and for this shells of ordinary fowls eggs are about the best thing that can be giv,n, as they contain e trbsnate of lime, phosphate of lime, and animal gluten. RABBITS.—A HINT FOR THE SEASON.—Very often the wood of which hutches are made is nine, and by degrees gets into a shrunken condition. This leaves spaces between the various pieces of wood which let in the wind, make the inmates uncomfortable, and thus they get cold. Thus many rabbit owners, whose hutches are in the condition named above, on going to feed their pets some morning, find that they have closed eyes, with a thick white matter oozing out of them; or, perhaps, they will find them breathing heavily with short heavy gasps, and exhibiting similar symptoms to what we find in human beings attacked with certain kinds of fever. They will be crouching in one corner of the hutch, endeavouring as it were to get into as small a space as possible, and presenting altogether a most woe- begene appearance. As cold in human beings is the first step in almost all acute diseases, so it is with animals of every kind, rabbits being no exception to this law. If they are in an otherwise healthy condition, proper treatment will soon enable them to throw a cold off; but if there is any inherent taint or tendency, if improper feeding has upset the stomach and its functions, or vitiated the blood, then there is trouble in store. Of course, the first thing is to stop up all crevices, which can either be done with narrow strips of wood, or patty, both of which are equally effica- cious if well done, but if not, then there will be no repairing the damage. It will be better to remove the rabbits to a hutch indoors in a warm place, in order to fight back the cold, and treat by giving warm mashes in watch some homoa)pathic tincturet of aconite has been put, say three drops to a mash ; or give the mash and a copaiha capsule twice a day. Meanwhile the other hutch can be repaired, re-painted, and re •whitewashed, and got into a proper state for the reception of its inmates when they have completely recovered. It is stated that Mr. Sexton will move an address to the Crewn praying for the removal of Mr. Justice Lawson from the b•ncli. The contest for the representation of Ennis has resulted in the return of Mr. J. Kenny, Mr. Parnell's candidate, by 138 votes against 95 recorded for M. R. W. Carey Reeves. The house of Mr. Redmond Roach, J.P., at Maglass, Castle- island, was attacked on Wednesday night by a band of armed men, numbering about 40. They fired several shots and peremptorily demanded admittance. After taking two guns they decamped. While twe bailiffs were executing a decree about a loan near Youghal, en Tuesday, they were attacked and beaten. During the struggle the wife of the farmer against whom the decree was issned received a blow from some heavy instru- ment, and is reported seriously hurt. In the Chancery Division, on Monday, an injunction was granted by Mr. Justice Chitty in the case of "Guinness v. the Latd Corporation of Ireland," restraining the defendants from allotting any more A shares, and from applying any part of the proceeds of the B shares to pay the dividend on tke A shares. Tuaninus FIRE AT AN IRISH FARM: CATTLE, BURNED TO DEATIL—A most destructive fire took place on Saturday nigh', at the Castle Farm, Lisrnore, County Waterford. The premises are the most extensive on the Duke of Devonshire's Irish estates, and nearly the whole of the buildings were totally destroyed; also a large quantty of valuable machinery and farming implements. Between thirty and forty head of valuable cattle were burnt to death or suffocated. The judges of the Irish Court of Exchequer had on Thursday to give an opinion on the Arrears Act. The plaintiff, the executor of a deceased landlord, claimed that the defendant, a tenant, was not entitled to the bent of the Act in respect of certain arrears, this contention being based on a particular construction of the defining words "landlord for the time being." The Court was against the plaintiff, remarking that both the language and the policy of the Arrears Act were against the narrow construction sought to be given to the section in question. ATTEMPT TO ASSASSINATE JUSTICE LAWSON.—A daring attempt to assassinate Mr. Justice Lawson was made on Saturday, while walking in the streets of Dublin. The _ _ _

learned judge, who is always guarded by four attendants, was going through L,Anster-street, accompanied by his son, when a man named Patrick Delaney crossed deliberetelY over towards him, at the same time holdin his hand inside the breast of his Coat. He was at once seized by the guards, who were vigilant, and on being secured was found to be armed with a loa,led revolver of new make. The judge treated the matter coolly, and dined soon afterwards with the benchers of King's Inns, to whose hall he was proceed- ing at the time. Delaney was brought up in the Dublin Police Court, on Monday, charged with attempting to assas- sinate Mr. Justice Lawson. The only evidence taken was that of M'Donnell, who captured Delaney. He stated that in passing through Merrion-square Delaney nudged his arm and said, "It's all right." It was this action which aroused M•Donnell's suspicion, and when Delaney sharply bolted across the street in front of the judge, M'Donnell followed, and was just in time to save Mr. Justice Lawson's life. The expressiou, "It's all right," may be taken to imply that Delaney mistook M-Donnell for an accomplice, and the statement that at the time of the arrest two men hailed a tramway car and then disappeared will he regarded as corro- boratiye of this. It is very doubtful, however, whether the police will be able to trace these men. THE SELECT COMMITTEE ON MR. GRAY'S IMPRISONMENT. —The Select Committee upon the question of privilege connected with the imprisonment of Mr. Gray, M.P., laid their report upon the table of the House of Commons on Tuesday evening. The report is identical with that adopted in the Whalley case, and has been drawn up by the Attor- ley-General, the chairman. It narrates briefly the facts of the present case, states that Mr. Gray was allowed to make a statement before the committee, which was, however, mostly irrelevant to the point at issue ; that Mr. Justice Lawson acted within his powers in ordering Mr. Gray's im- prisonment; that the judge had further acted properly in reporting the matter to the House of Commons; and that, finally, in the opinion of the committee, there was no oeca- sion for the House to take further notice of the matter. Mr. Dillwyn, who dissents from the conclusions arrived at, has prepared a separate draft report, maintaining that Mr. Gray Was not guilty of contempt of court; that Parliament has never abandoned its right to inquire into such charge; and that the learned judge had no right, under all the circum- stances, to commit a member to prison. Besides exonerating Mr. Gray, Mr. Dillwyn recommends that the whole subject of the state of the law respecting punishments for contempt of court should be inquired into. Mr. Sexton also sub- mitted a separate draft report representing the views of the minority, expressing a more decisive condemnation of the conduct of Mr. Justice Lawson, and recommending that the power of the judges to punish for contempt should he de- fined by the statute. Mr. Parnell and Mr. Healy were ab- sent from Tuesday's committee meeting.

AG AND TEE CORN TRADE The Mark Lail says :—" The weather during the past week has varied greatly in different localities. In the south-east it has been fine, bright, cold, and seasonable since Tuesday, whereas in the west midland counties, and especially in the north, there have been violent storms of hail, snow, and rair, accom- panied by destructive lightning and followed by disastrous floods. Under these circumstances, progress with wheat sowing has been small at best, and on a very restricted local area. The bulk of grain has come to band damp, and has been neglected by millers. The trade throughout the week has been very quiet, and prices have not shown any advance on Monday's currencies, which were barely those of the previous week. Country flour is coming forward freely, and values remain at Monday's rates. Fine English and Scotch barleys have been against buyers, and the same may be said ef heavy oats. Beans and peas remain firm. There was a better demand for foreign wheat off stands in London on Friday, but prices could not be raised above Monday's quota- tions. Supply on the spot has been moderate, and that off the coast very meagre. In Liverpool, on Friday, red winter wheat commanded an advance of Id to 2,1 par centai."

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

At a meeting of representative miners, held at Wolver- hampton on Tuesday, it was resolved to take steps to obtain an advance of 5 per cent, on the present state of wages paid in South Staffordshire and East Worcestershire, and also to terminate the present agreement in the Cannock Chase district.

It is announced that the Clyde shipjoiners' strike has now kerminated, after lasting twelve weeks. It has cost about .£lOO,OOO. Three-fourths of this sum represents penalties incurred by employers for delay in contracts. The other four that represents loss of wages by maintenance of the men on strike. Many men who have resumed work were work- ing overtime all Monday night, so great is the demand upon their service'.

Buts or SALE AND FAILURES—III the week ending Nov- ember 11th, 1882, there were 193 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 813 over those of the correspond- ing period last year; and the failures numbered 207, a decrease of 28. The totals for portion of year to November 11th, 1882, are bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 39,997, a;decrease of 3,810; the failures gazetted number 9,202, a decrease of 811.—Stubbs' Mercantile Gazette. THEI LANCASIIIRIZ COAL TRADE.—A falling off in the demand, which was anticipated after the large buying prior to the recent advance in prices, is to some extent being realised. . In the Manchester district prices are firm at the advanced lists which came into force at the commencement 'of the month, and the leading colliery Arms in other die- ' tricts are also still holding to their prices. For steam and I forge coals there is'a moderately good demand. Engine classes of fuel, although fairly plentiful, move off 'tolerably r well, and sellers are not disposed to contract sforward for slack at present rates. At the pit-mouth .prices average about as under :—Best coal, 105 6d to lie; seconds, 8s to 9s; and common round coal, 63 6.1 to 7s 61 per ton, accord- ing to quality. Burgy about ss, and good ordinary slack 3s to 4s, with best sorts fetching in some cases 4s 3d to 4s ed per ton. Shipping is quiet, and good steam coal delivered either at Garston docks or on the high level, Liverpooi, does not realise more than an average price of 8s 151 per ton. Tars LANCASIIIRB IRON TRADE.—The iron market of the district continues very quiet, and buyers seem to be confi- dent that prices will have to give way. Makers, however, although they are rather easier to deal with, are not disposed to make any material concession to secure orders, and where there is underselling it is chiefly confined to holders of second-band iron. There was a good attendance on 'Change oa Tuesday, but the inquiry was very limited, and the actual business transacted small. Lancashire makers of pig iron who are well sold are firm at 48s to 50e, less 2.4 for forge and foundry, delivered equal to Manchester, and district brands remain at an average of 49s ed for Lincolnshire and 51s for Derbyshire, less 4, but sales are limited to a few occasional orders for small quantities. Finished iron makers have as a rule still plenty of work in hand, and do not press sales. There is, however, less buoyancy in the market, and both for home requirements and shipment tbe demand at present is only dull. For bar iron delivered into the Manchester distt iet NlAkers' prices remain on the basis of £6 10a to Sd 15s per ton.

div.head: MkAMTPtASNA MURDERS,
div.p: THE MkAMTPtASNA MURDERS,

Iu Dublin, on Monday morning, Mr. Justice Barry com- menced the trials of the men charged with being participa- tors in the massacre of a family named Joyce at Maamtrasna, in county Galway, in August last. At the outset, counsel for the defence sought to obtain still another postponement, but the judge decided that the case must proceed. It was arranged that the accused men should be tried separately, and the first of the prisoners arraigned was Patrick Joyce, of Shanballycahill, a young man. The Attorney-General, having stated the principal facts in the crime, said that one of the persons who had been committed for trial—Anthony Philbin—had volunteered a statement, and his name had been struck out of the indictment. The trial was then pro- ceeded with. Evidence was first given of the discovery of the murders, and a more horrible story was probably never told in a court of justice. Then the prosecution called an elderly man named Anthony Joyce, who deposed to having, in company with twp relatives, fellovred a party of ten men, amongst them the prisoner, to the house where the tragedy was enacted. Some of the ten went in and some stayed out- side, and the witness and his relatives lay in concealment and heard the cries of the victims.

The trial was resumed on Tuesday, when two "ap- provers," who were amongst those arrested by the police for complicity in the crime, gave evidence. Anthony Philbin was the first of the two, and he deposed to accompanyins, the murderous gang as far as the house at Maamtrasna, and to the prisoner at the bar being one of the men who broke in the door and entered the place. The witness said he heard screams and the firing of a shot, and he got frightened and went away. He was severely cross-examined by the coun- sel for the defence, and in explanation of his haying accom- panied the party to the house he said his brother-in-law, who was the first of the number he met• that night, merely told him that he wanted to see "the boys," and he (Phil- bin) "had no idea that he was going to see murder." The second 4. approver" was Thomas Casey, Philhin's brother-in- law, whose evidence brought into the affair two additional men named Kelly and Neill. Casey said he had not seen the former since the night of the tragedy, that he saw him for the first time last summer, that he had not seen Neill since the murders, that this man was a " pedlar," and that about a year previously he gave witness a revolver "to keep for him." This witnessl like Philbin, said that he himself slid not enter the house, and that he ran away when he had heard one shot fired. The prisoner at the bar, he asserted, was one of those who entered the place. In cross-examina- tion Casey, replying to a question whether he had given this information to save his life, said he had. Asked if he knew when on the way to Maamtrasna that there would be a murder, he replied that he knew "something was to be up," for Neill told him so. The police officer who arrested the prisoner at the bar three days after the murders, said the prisoner asked him *whether Philbin bad been arrested. An analyst who had examined a pair of trousers found in the house of the prisoner at the bar, said they had evict, ntly been recently washed. They still, however, bore blood stains, but he conld not tell whether the stains were of human blood. A piteous incident in Tuesday's pro- ceedings was the production of the sole survivor of the massacre, a little fellow nine years old, who himself was cruelly assaulted, and still carries marks of his wounds. The child was questioned by te counsel for the prosecu- tion to test his sense of responsibility. He had never been at school or chapel, had not learned his catechism, and did not say his prayers, but he " knew what it was to tell a lie." To the question "did he know where he would go to if he told a lie," the boy answered "No," and the Attorney- General felt compelled to abandon the examination of what must have proved a most important witness. The case for the Crown now closed, and counsel for the defence addressed the jury.

At the opening of the Court on Wednesday morning, Mr. Justice Barry commenced his charge to the jury. The learned Judge truly remarked that the enormity of the crime under investigation was such as to have startled the civilised world. He gave full weight to the argument of the counsel of the prisoner at the bar that no motive had been shown, but pointed out that the crime was so terrible that it would be difficult to suggest a motive for it. When one spoke of motive in a case like this one bacame lost in mystery and uncertainty. The jury were only five or six minutes in coming to a verdict. That verdict was what everybody was prepared for—" guilty." In sentencing the prisoner to be hanged within Galway Gaol on the 15th December the Judge told him that he had no mercy to ex- pect at the bands of man. During the closing scene of the trial his Lordship was deeply moved, but the convict betrayed no emotion whatever.

The Attorney-General entered a nolle proseyui to the in- dictments against the two "approvers," Anthony Philbin and Thomas Casey. Patrick Casey, the reputed leader of the gang of assassins, was then arraigned.

The trial of Casey was resumed in Dublin, on Thursday morning. Thomas Casey, one .of the two " approvers " who accompanied the party Jo Maamtrasna, said that the day before the murders the prisoner at the bar told him that on the following night he must go in a direction indicated, and bring Philbin with him, and by this order witness understood that he was to go as far as Michael Casey's house. At a fair previous to this the prisoner told him that something would have. to be done to John Joyce. The pri- soner was one of five men whom he saw go close to the door of the house, but he could not say who went in. The witness described the manner in which Kelly and Nee (two men not in custody) joined the party on the way to the scene of the outrage, and said he knew they were the authors of it—" the way Nee was talking." Kelly was a stranger in the district. Nee was a pedlar. He would not hays known what Kelly was only for Nee. It was Nee that directed witness and was telling witness about it. A question as to Nee's comm unication to the witness was objected to by the the prisoner's counsel, and the question was not pressed. The case for the prosecution was closed, and the defence, an alibi, gone into ; and the court adjourned.

div.head: MRS. E. PARKER ON TEMPERANCE.
div.p: MRS. E. PARKER ON TEMPERANCE.

The autumnal anrual conference of the British Womea's Temperance Association has been held at Bolton, under the presidency of the founder of the Association, Mrs. E. Parker, of renketl, who spoke as follows :—Beloved sisters and co- workers, it is with no common feelings of joy that I greet you to-day in my own native town, hallowed by so many precious memories of ray childhood. When I think of the day, four years ago, when in the Boardroom (kindly lent by the British Temperance League), the seed sown in weak- ness has been raised in power, and now, chiefly through the zeal of the women there, thirty-three branches proclaim eur dear old Lancashire a banner country for temperance, and Bolton is its chief town. (Applause.) May this autumnal meeting be a very pentecost of power from on high, and may every delegate feel that henceforth she is prepared to be whole-hearted in this blessed temperance work for our native land. Let protection for our homes be the watch- word all along the line. It is high time that the question is it right, should take the place of is it expedient, or is it politic, when the mists of earth shall fade away from our vision, and the great Recorder shall testify of the deeds done in the body. Oh, may it be said of each cf us, "She hath done what she could."

On the ladder of God which upward leads, The steps of progress are human needs. And surely the greatest need of society to-day is its purifica- tion from strong drink, with all its attendant evils It is for this that we must work, and I trust that from this conference may go forth a power that shall be felt to the ends of the earth. Let our children grow np in homes purified from the drink, and let us bring our influence to bear on Sunday school committees, that sound temperance teaching may second our efforts. It is not enough that we send out our lifeboats to save the wrecked ones, we must plant beacon lights on the rocks, so that the untrained mariners on life's treacherous sea may be warned to avoid them. An added power has been given to women householders—for which we tsbould reverently thank heaven, and pray that we may use it wisely and vell. I mean the municipal and school board franchise. The ballot is A weapon that is firmer set, And better than the bayonet, • A weapon that comes down as still As snowflakes fall upon the sod, And executes our freedom will As lightning does the will of God. Let us shrink from no duty, public or private, where God shall lead the way. The time is short, eternity is at hand, Let us work in faith. There is such a thing as resting in labour, going from strength leaning upon God. And now, my sisters, a gate is opened to us that shall be shut no more, it is to bless humanity. Let us arise and bless the nations— Work on, work on, nor doubt, nor fear, From age to age this truth shall cheer; Whate'er may die and be forgot, Work done for God it dieth not. (Loud applause.)

Tiuz SURRENDER or ARABI PACRA.—Further gnestions Were put regarding the surreud.r of Arabi and the prepara- tions for his trial. Sir C. Diu ma stateu in reply that the IlnlY variations from the procedure usual in such cases according to Egyptian practice were in favour of the atensed, allowing him counsel and a public trial. The under- Standing was that Arabi would be tried under the Egyptian Military code as varied by the conditions agreed upon by Counsel ....The PRIME MINISTER stated he was net prepared while judicial proceedings were pending in Egypt to name a dais '7 for the discussion of the motion of which Mr. Bourke 'tad given notice as to the surrender of Arabi, but if there Was any disposition to ask the House to pass a vote of ,eensure on the general conduct of affairs in gYpt, he should be prepared to give an early day for its Wecussion. Mr. Gladstone subsequently stated that he '-trtained no doubt that limb' Paella would not be put to
elite'
death without the assent of Her Majesty's Government.

_ Mr. BRADLAUGH.—The SrEexnu read a letter from Mr. Btadlaugh, in which the hon. member claimed to be heard at the bar in order that he may state the grounds of law on Which he claims to be entitled to take his seat in the House. LABOUCHERE gave notice that he should on the first occasion he could do so consistently with the rules of the liouse, move that Mr. liradlaugh be heard at the bar. • STANDING COMMITTEES —The PRIME MINISTRR informed S. Northcote that the resolution respecting Standing winmittees was of an experimental character, and as the Session was now so far advanced it would be proposed to give them effect from the opening of the next session. PROCEDURE RULES. Mr. Gr.snsTorrit proposed his 1 second procedure rule, Providing "That no motion for the adjournment of the House shall be made before the orders Of the day or notices of motions have been entered upon, except by leave of the House, the granting of such leave, if disputed, being determined upon question put forthwith ; but .1k 0 division shall be taken thereupon unless demanded by 4(:)rrY members rising in their places, nor until after the cluestions on the paper have been disposed of." Five imprac- ticable amendments were moved in rapid succession, and either negatived or withdrawn.—Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL then moved a sixth, and in the course of his speech most Scandalously insulted the Government on the subject of the • ‘`Kilmainham Treaty."—Mr. GrLADSTONE then followed arid a very painful scene occurred, the right hon. gentleman Passionately peotfsting against the existence of any such treaty amid the jeers and taunts of the Tory party.—Ulti- raately the House accepted a portion of Lord Randolph's Proposal.

div.head: ROUSE OF COMMONS.-TIISDAY.
div.p: ROUSE OF COMMONS.-TIISDAY.

OUR RELATIONS IN EGYPT.—The PRIME MINISTER stated • that the Government thought the time had come when they tight state briefly their Egyptian arrangements. Since the • occupation of Cairo on the 14th of September the Govern- ' tient had been occupied in bringing away the troops, with the exception of such force as appeared to be necessary, tinder the existing circumstances to remain there for a cer- tain time. The maximum of 33,000 men had been reduced to 12,000. The Government would now propose a Conven- tion with Egypt, which would have reference to the tem- ,' Perary arrangements for the maintenance of order and SOCUlity in the county. No claim had been made for the %EPenses of our military expedition but now the question Would have to he considered between the Egyptian Ciovernment and the British Government of how the peace and security of the country were to he claintained, and it would form the subject of the Proposed Convention, which he had no doubt the Govern- tent would be able to proceed with in the course of a few • Weeks, and before Parliament met in the ensuing session t.they should be able to insert in the estimates whatever par- ' ,utoulars it might be proper to give to Parliament to enable It to express its judgment on the arrangement that might be Inade.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE complained that information was ?Ping withheld, and he asked for fuller information as to `no purposes for which additional expenditure beyond the 'Cote in August was now going on. He thought great mis- fOttune would result from the reticence shown by the Govern- Zlect, and he recorded a protest against their silence on the hject.—Later in the evening Captain AYLMER desired to ipnow if any convention or, agreement had been made between England and Egypt. Mr. GLADSTONE replied ' that none whatever existed. As to the cost of the Indian contingent, the estimate made in the summer would have to be reconsidered, but he hoped before the prorogation to take a statement on the subject. A Convention would be Pro Posed, and it would be presented to Parliament when it Ites completed. The Convention would be confined to the ..l'ailitary occupation, and would not refer to any other ,reatters.—Mr. SALT expressed An opinion that any expend'- tire beyond the £2,300,000 voted was contrary to the provi- Pions of the Appropriation Act, and as he thought it of teroPortance that a more definite statement as to the expendi- Lure should be made, he gave notice that he should refer to the subject again on Monday. ,TRE PROCEDURE RULES—The debate on the second F,ocedure rule was then resumed.—Lord R. CHURCHILL toyed an amendment providing that the rule should not ItPlaly when any member by leave of the House had made a etatement other than in answer to a question.—Mr. GLAD- TONE opposed and Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE warmly sup- , Ported the proposition. UltimateVe the amendment was re- Jetted by 123 to 85.—Mr. FOWLER next moved his im- portant amendment, the principle of which was accepted by the Government. The Ministerial rule, as amended by the Pertial adoption of Lord Randolph Churchill's amendment - tit Monday night, stood as follows :—"That no motion for tht adjournment of the House shall be made until all `Le questions on the notice-paper have been disposed of, :rd no such motion shall be made before the orders of the itaY or notices of motions have been entered upon [except by ielve of the House; the granting of such leave, if disputed, ,1449 determined upon question put fo,thwith ; but no division I ",11 be taken thereupon] unless demanded by forty ! 4gernbers rising in their places, nor until after the I,ilreations on the notice-paper have been disposed of."— FOWLER now proposed to leave out the words printed in thus enabling a certain number of members not eetuelrely to challenge a division as to whether a motion for 'Clournmeut should be put, but absolutely to authorise the naging forward of such a motion.—Mr. Greansrorex, who Vinted out that the Government were merely doing for the ;ruse what the House had failed to do for itself, said be .:Leerfully accepted this principle, tholgh with con- , ;derable misgivings. He suggested forty as the number ,110 Should have tho power of determining that the c'tion should made, but proposed as a necessary restric- „,°ll that "it should be binding upon the person who might the adjournment to declare that he did so for the pur- -28 of discussing a defluite urgent public matter."
