FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE. THE CONDITION OF EGYPT. Monday was the Mussulman New Year's Day, and, in accordance with usual custom, the Khedive held a grand reception. In addition to the patriarchs and officials, His Highness received Lord Dufferin and Sir A. Alison. It is now stated that all the European powers except France have agreed to a purely English Control in Egypt. Germany and Italy, it is said, stipulated for a European sur- veillance, and Russia tacitly consented upon discovering that an anti-English coalition with France could not be brought about. That the English Government were sure of their position before going the length of advising the Khedive to pronounce the demise of the Control is regarded every- where as certain, and France has no course but to acquiesce in what has already become an accomplished fact. In a letter addressed to a London contemporary, Arabi Pasha declares that the Egyptian revolt was made in accord- anCe with the laws of God and man, and in accordance with a solemn decree of the Council under the presidency of the Khedive and Dervish Pasha, the envoy of the Sultan. He adds that the whole Egyptian nation was unanimous an to the necessity of suspending Tewfik Pasha for having transgressed the highest and diviae law. An English gentleman who has just returned from Zagazig learned there that 150 persons charged with political offences are now confined in the prison of that town. These are most cruelly treated, and many have been severely flogged. The two Notables who applied to Mr. Broadlev to defend them were chained together and con- fined in a dark cell. There is every reason to believe that both men are the victims of a private grudge on the part of the Governor, who, some years ago, had an important law- suit against them, but was defeated, and was, in consequence of the affair, turned out of office.

Baker Pasha's scheme for the reorganisation of the Egyptian army has so far progressed that a thousand men have already been equipped and despatched for the Soudan. Much greater progress would have been made were it not for the delay on the part of the British Government in ex- pressing their definite views en the subject. The army, as reconstructed by Baker Pasha, will be a purely Egyptian force, with the exception of a certain number of English officers and a small corps of Albanian riflemen. We learn from Cairo that Mr. Broadley has written to Sir Charles Wilson complaining of the treatment experienced by Emin Bey-el-Shemsy at Zagazig. It is stated that the prisoner, who was a large cotton grower at Zagazig, is em- ployed in watering the streets there. He and some other prisoners have given retainers to Mr. Broadley and Mr. Napier. According to a telegram from Constantinople which ap- pears in the Vienna papers, the Sultan has addressed a com- munication to the Khedive, in Welch he enters into explana- tions respecting those papers found in Arabi's possession, which were said to be of a nature :gravely compromising his Majesty. • Referring to the trial of Arabi and his associates, the Cairo correspondent of the Times says that difficulties have arisen between the Commission for Preliminary Inquiry and the prisoners' counsel. The former desire to limit the period allowed for the cross-examination of the witnesses already examined, and for the prcduction of fresh evidence for the defence, to 30 days. They also require the surrender of all papers tendered in evidence before the court-martial begins. The counsel for the defence maintain that, as no time was fixed by the original agreement, none can be im- posed upon them now. A shocking occurrence took place at Alexandria the other night. A Russian subject was found murdered in a street near the Arsenal, and it is believed that the culprit is a native watchman who was on duty at the time. The man was arrested, and in his possession was found a heavy bludgeon, covered with blood. The affair has caused a great sensation. The police report that the death was caused by the deceased falling from the roof of a house. . .

The Daily -Netc;:s Constantinople correspondent says the Porte is still of opinion that it is expedient to send a Turkish Commissioner to Egypt. Lord Granville has replied that he sees no practical advantage to be gained by each a step, but, on the contrary, many disadvantages. It is rumoured, the correspondent adds, that another Power may support the suggestion of the Porte. Latest accounts from Egypt states that Lord Dufferin confers daily with important Egyptian officials with regard to the state of the country. It is considered probable that the " capitulations " with Earopeati Powers, which prac- tically remove the subjects from the control of native courts, will be swept away like the Dual Control. Unquestionably, says a correspondent of a London contemporary, the capitu- lations have worked ill. "They have been the means of Egypt being flooded with the sweepings of Southern Europe." The deficit in the revenue of the current financial year is estimated at about £120,000, as against the expected surplus of £282,000. There is a rumour that England is in negotiation with the house of Rothschild for the purchase of the Domain estates from the Egyptian Government. Some attention is again being given to the proceedings against Arabi in consequence of the statements which have been made in self-defence by Snleiman Daoud, one of the refugees who were arrested in Crete. This man admits that he gave the order to set fire to Alexandria, but alleges that he received peremptory orders to do so from Arabi. He also alleges that the Dictator ordered him to murder the Khedive at Ramleh, but that Sultan Pasha persuaded him to disobey the order. With regard to these men, accuser and accused, the Times correspondent says that both Lave "a wide reputa- tion as liars." The health of the army of occupation is again said to be very unsatisfactory.

It is officially announced that General Count Menabrea has been appointed Italian Ambassador to the French Re- public. Attempts are being made to resume the intimate relations between the Germun Empire and the Porte which, existing until recently, were supposed to have been broken off. . .

Albert Bierstadt's home, Mallaston, at Irvington on the Hudson River, above New York, with several valuable paintings and art treasures, was burnt on Friday. The loss amounts to 150,000 dollars. The houge was un- occupied. A passenger train has gone over a trestle bridge, near Bradford, in the Pennsylvania oil region, with disastrous results. The cars fell a distance of twenty feet. The en- gineer, stoker, and several passengers lost their lives, and many who were not killed outright received serious in- juries. There are reports in Paris that the Finance Minister has discovered that his secretaries have been mistaken in their reckonings, and that the treasury has only about Sixty million francs to the good instead of one hundred and fifty-nine million francs as was promised. The difficulty is to be met by M. Tirarcl reducing his demand for public works inaugurated by the De Freycinet Cabinet. THE CUBAN REFUGEES. - It is said to be believed in Madrid that the British Government, when it learns the result of the inquiry at Gibraltar, will desist from making any official communication to the Spanish Government on the subject of the Cuban refugees. Spain, it is added, considers herself fully justified in not giving them up. The Daily News correspondent fears that if it can be proved that the capture took place on Spanish territory the British appeal to Spain has not the slightest chance of a favourable hearing. GREAT ROBBERY IN PARIS.—A Paris correspondent writes that a sum of money, amounting to nearly 70,000 f., was last week abstracted from a safe in the office of Mr. Geo. Waters, agent to the London, Chatham, and Dover Railway and several steamship companies. The office door had been entered by a false key, but the safe had been broken open. The matter was promptly put into the hands of M. Taylor, Commissary of Police for the Chaussee dAntin quarter, but so far nothing seems to have transpired to throw any light on the affair.

OPENING OF zirn PRUSSIAN DIET.—On Tuesday the new Prassian Diet was opened by the Emperor William in per- son. In the Speech from the Throne his Majesty announced that a Bill authorising a loan would be presented with the estimates. Reduction oft taxation in favour of the poorer classes were also announced. Measures for establishing further railway communication and for constructing a canal connecting the great streams in the west would be submitted to Parliament. The resumption of diplomatic intercourse with the Roman Curia had assisted in strengthening the friendly relations of the Emperor with the Supreme Head of the Catholic Church. In conclusion, the Speech said that the relations of Germany with all foreign Governments justi- fied the conviction that the benefits of peace were assured. ANOTHER DUEL IN PRANCE.—Not much discernment was necessary to predict that if the French continued to indulge their passion for duelling unpleasant results must follow at some time or other. It seems that a pair of duellists, whom we are only allowed to know as M. T. and Count T. fought with revolvers, near Paris, on Sunday morning. The Count, who is a Russian, had maligned a lady. The com- batants appear to have fired at a distanct of twenty paces. The Count was shot in the shoulder at the first fire, and the second ball struck him on the forehead, but his skull was so solidly constructed—a characteristic of duellists—as to turn the ball, and there being a staff of surgeons at hand, he may be expected to live. When last heard of he was enveloped in surgical bandages, and making his way to the likissian frontier. A Nirir YORK MERCHANT'S FORTUNE.—It will be re- membered that some time ago Mr. Andrew Thomson Stuart, the celebrated New York warehouseman, died and left be- hind him a fortune equal to about $85,000,000. The de- ceased died intestate, but by the law of the United States one-third of this colossal amount went to his wife, .yho before he married her was a checker in the lace department of his extensive buliness. For some time there was a diffi- culty in finding out who were entitled to the other two- thirds of Mr. Stuart's fortune, but the heirs, it is said, have at last been discovered. Mr. Stuart was a Scotchinan, and relatives of his, it appears, reside near Lockerbie in Dum- frieshire. There is also a relative resident in America, and altogether there will be seventeen participants in Mr. Stuart's fortune beside the widow, who will have the plea- sure of dividing amongst them the nice little sum of be- tween £12,000,000 and £13,000,000 sterling. ATTEM7rnto THE SULTAN'S LIFE.—The Tayblatt of Vienna has received the following intelligence from Con- stantinople :—" On Friday, Nov. 3, the Sultan was about to leave the palace to pay his weekly visit to the Mosque. Fol- lowed by his militNry suite, he had left the inner apartments of the Yildiz Kiosk, and was passing through the smoking - room, with the ruby-coloured glass cupola, when one of the Halberdier Guards on duty at the outer door made a rush towards him. Aide-de-camp Major Seizo,t Bey seized the man by the arm, and handed him over to the custody of the soldiers. His name is Muzri Hafuss, and he is an Arab by birth. He denied having intended to take the Sultan's life, and says he was only a little awkward in presenting arms. It was discovered, however, that he had previously adjusted

the steel point on his halberd, which is usual only for out- door duty. The point is hidden by a tuft of peacecks' feathers, and thus escaped notice. He had also made several suspicious remarks to his comrades in the guard-room, and given one of them a black amber cigar holder, saying he would nt,t require it any longer. The whole affair has been kept as secret as possible. The Chief Eunuch and Ferik Vitalis Pasha has been entrusted with the preliminary investigation." A DUEL WITH HORSEWHIPS.—A duel, not unjustly des- cribed as" bloody, cruel, and novel," has just been fought in Guilford, in North Carolina, between Mr. Johnston and Mr. Saks Williams. Both wooed the same nymph, and jealousy found utterance in harsh words. A duel was arranged; the weapons, as in a caricature by Mr. Caldecott, were to be horsewhips. Churls fought with clubs in the Middle Ages, less undignified instruments. The men were put at three feet from each other, each behind a crease. They fought in a hard and level spot on a field, and they fought in their, ,shirts. The seconds tried to patch up a peace in vain. The question was put, "Gentlemen, are you ready ?" then "strike " Itas called, and Johnston and Williams, like knights in Mallory, "so lashed at each other that it was marvel.". First blood was soon drawn, but neither flinched, and when the right band was weary, they flogged each other with the left. Since King Padella and King Valoros3 piously chastised each other in a humble but resolute spirit, there never has been such a horsewhipping. Time was called after a half-hour rally, but fightieg went on, with intervals for rest and refreshment, during three hours. The seconds then decreed that honour was satisfied, and if honour can be satisfied by the reception of a good flogging, both men had every reason to be contented. "Both men are suffering terribly," but we do not hear what the lady for whom they fought thinks of her lovers. "He'. more like a friend than a husband," said a poor woman whose lord never beat her.

k. " MISCELLANEOUS. The statue of Lord Beaconsfield is undergoing the process of moulding, gind it will be ready for casting at Christmas. It has been decided that the ceremony of unveiling shall not take place till Parliament meets next year. The Colston banquets were held at Bristol on Monday. The principal speaker at the Liberal gathering was Mr. Campbell-Bannerman. Among the guests at the Con- servative banquet were Sir M. Hicks-Beach, Sir Hardinge .Giffard, and Mr. Raikes. '1 here was a keen competition on Saturday at the sale of the famous Sunderland Library for a copy of Petrarch's " Triumphi," which was printed in 1488, and contains two sets of valuable engravings. It was secured by Mr. Quaritch for the large sum of £1,950. At Warwick Assizes, on Wednesday, Albert Woolf (18), fitter, was sentenced to 21 months' imprisonment with hard labour for stabbing his sweetheart at Birmingham. It was alleged that the prosecutrix jilted the prisoner, who conse- quently stabbed her dangerously. TEN SEAMEN DROWNED.—On Tuesday night the German barque Wedan, of Aspenrade, from Hamburg, bound to Shanghai, with general cargo, went to pieces on the Gun- fleet Sands. The mizenmast was seen to fall, and ten of the crew were carried overt:lsm' d with it and drowned.

Cn Monday night in the House of Commons a new writ was issued for the election of a member for Salisbury in the room of Mr. W. H. Grenfell, who has accepted the office of one of the Grooms-in-Waiting to Her Majesty. Mr. Gren- fell offers himself for re-election, and will be epposed by Mr. Coleridge Kennard, a Conservative. _ _

TRH -ST. LUKE'S MYSTERY: STATEMENT BY MRS. STRANGER.—Mrs. Stranger, wife of the missing baker of St. Luke's, has made a statement, in which she says she cannot believe her husband has been murdered. He was, she says, a very violent and passionate man, and he had for a long time said he would leave her and go away for ever without leaving her a penny. She was a long time before she came to conclude that her husband had left her for good, and she is anxious that his whereabouts should be traced and the mystery cleared up.

Two HIINDRED COLLIERS IMPRISONED IN A PIT.—A serious accident occurred at East Holywell Colliery, near Backworth, Northumberland, on Saturday. While coals were being drawn, the cages got out of the slides, and corn- ing in collission a complete block ensued. Two hundred men and boys were imprisoned in the pit. It was contrived to send them food, and on Sunday afternoon, the cages be- ing put right, they were released, the boys after thirty hours and the men after twenty-seven hours' imprisonment. A DUST CONTRACTOR'S BENEFACTION.—A petition in the matter of Dodd's Trusts' came before Mr. Justice Chitty, on Saturday. The testator Dodd was an extensive dust contractor in London, and died worth a very large sum of money, and among the numerous bequests made by his will was the sum of £5,000 to a French foundling orphan house in Paris. There being more than on. of this description of refuge in Paris, an ambiguity as to the object of the testator's bounty was suggested, and the peti- tion was presented for the decision of the :court on the point. Mr. Justice Chitty directed an inquiry.

EXECUTION OF THE BODMIN MURDERER.— William Meager Bartlett, mine manager at Lanlivery, was executed at Bodmin, on Monday morning, for the murder of his ille- gitimate child. The morning was intensely cold. The re- presentatives of the Press, with about a dozen others and a few policemen, were the only persons outside the prison when at one minute after eight the hoisting of the black flag announced that the sentence had been carried out. The condemned man had confessed his crime, and bad acknowledged the justice of his sentence. A POLITICAL ANECDOTE. The following anecdote, which is circulating in Paris among the members of the diplomatic world, and which one of them affirms he has had from a perfectly trustworthy source, throws a decisive light on the Porte's intention of sending a commission to Egypt te act alongside Lord Duffed°. Musurus Pasha, a few days ago, called on Lord Granville to announce to him that the Porte proposed to send this commission' evidently witk a view to sounding the intentions of the British Cabinet on the subject. "1 thank you very mach for your communi- cation," Lord Granville courteously replied, "but if the Porte really did send such a commission to Egypt it would be boycotted."

SHOCKING DISCOVERY IN SALFORD. A shocking dis- covery was made on Monday morning in Salford. A carter, employed by Messrs. Robert Neill and Sons, contractors,was passing under No. 1 railway arch, Greengate, shortly before twelve o'clock, when he observed something lying on the roadway. On examination it was found to be the dead body of a man. The body was doubled up with the head bent under the breast, and the flesh of the face, neck, and hands had evidently been eaten away by rats. The deceased's neck appeared to have been broken as by a fall. The remains were removed to the mortuary in Silk-street. In the pockets were found 9s. 7d., three Roman Catholic medals, and other articles. The body has been identified as that of a person named Kinsella, an assistant to a cattle dealer from Dublin. IMPROVEMENTS IN Boua-sTREarr. Messrs. Kirkland, whose names have become familiar to Liverpool residents, have recently opened a splendidly-appointed grillroom in connection with their establishment in Bold-street, for the accommodation of ladies and gentlemen whose business takes them to the fashionable locality in the course of the day. The dining and luncheon room, separated from the shop by a handsome stained-glass screen, is commodious and comfortable, and in upstairs parts of the premises have been fitted up smoking and dining rooms for gentle- men, lavatories Jac. The milk-brown bread manufactured by Messrs. Kirkland has met with the greatest success,and the addition of their Vienna bakery in Hardman-street has given still greater eclat to the daily and varied products of this enterprising firm. THE PRESTON ELECTION.—Two Conservative candidates are now wooing the electors of Preston, the Guild Hall Club, after many rebuffs having secured a candidate in the person of Mr. R. W. Hai-ary, who has previously had Par- liamentary experience as member for North Staffordshire. Mr. Tomlinson, the workingmen's Conservative candidate, continues to press his clkirns upon the constituency, and is determined to proceed to the poll. Mr. Hanbury on Satur- day published his address, and in the evening addressed a I meeting in terms which suggests that he means to carry the election by being more truculent than his opponent in his attacks upon Mr. Gladstone and his Government. The fact that two Conservatives are in the field is encouraging the ' Liberal party to make an attempt to secure the seat, and Mr. S. B. Galion is mentioned as a probable candidate. SIR GARNET WOLSELEY AND HIS SLANDERERS.—Sh Garnet Wolseley has given the reply which every one ex- pected to the slanders of a portion of the Irish press. Mr. M'Coan, M.P., who felt it his duty to inform Sir Garnet of the libels that were being published, has received a letter in which the General says that " any duty,in connection with a civil war in Ireland would be of all others most repugnant to his feelings." He adds the expression of a fervent desire 'to see Ireland loyai, peaceful, and prosperous." Unfor- tunately, there are too many Irishmen whose trade it is to make Ireland disloyal and disturbed, and who will continua to do their worst, by the malignant distortion of everything that is said or intended in England with regard ta their country, to delay the happy period which Sir Garnet Wolseley anticipates. The Freeman apologises for the proved untrustworthiness of its special " knowledge," and expresses its regret for having been the medium of circulating the statements. THE CLOSURE RESOLUTION.—The Closure resolution takes effect at once so far as this session is concerned, but the question of constituting it a standing order remains to be considered. The exact text of the new rule, as sanctioned bg the House on Friday night, is as follows :—" That when it shall appear to Mr. Speaker, or the Chairman of Ways and Meaas in a committee of the whole House, during any debate, that the subject has been adequately discussed, and that it is tho evident sense of the House, or of the com- mittee, that the question be now put, he may so inform the House or the committee; and if a motion be made 'That the question be now put,' Mr. Speaker, or the Chairman, shall forthwith put such question; and if the same be decided in the affirmative, the question under discussion shall be put forthwith, provided that the question, that the question be now put,' shall not be decided in the affirmative, if a division be taken, unless it shall appear to have been supported by more than 200 members, or rimless it shall appear to have been opposed by less than 40 members and supported by more than 100 members. A LANCASHIRE CLERGYMAN'S MATRIMONIAL SUIT.—The case of Cator v. Cator came before Sir J. Hannen on Saturday. It was a petition presented by the wife for judicial separation from her husband, the Rev. Joseph Samuel (otherwise Cator), of St. Luke's Church, Chorlton- on-Medlock, on the ground of cruelty. Mr. Pritchard ap- peared for the petitioner. The respondent was not repre- sented by counsel.—The learned counsel said the petition was originally for dissolution of marriage on the ground of cruelty and ;clultery,:but as there was some difficulty, and there was a family of nine children living, it had been deter mined to ask the court for a decree of judicial separation. The respondent's real name was Samuel, but after their marriage he assumed the name ef Cator.—Mrs. Martha Ann Cator, said she was married to the respondent on the 20th of June, 1862 —Sir J. Hannen :What was the respondent? He is described in the certificate as a stationer. Witness: Yes, my lord, so he was at the time of the marriage, but he is now a clergyman in the Church of England.—The evidence was then proceeded with. The respondent got into difficulty, and he then introduced a lady into the house as a lodger, whose money, he said, would be of great assistance to them. Witness objected to the arrangement, and then quarrels arose between them. She insisted on the lady leaving the house ; he as strongly determined such should not be the case, and he became very violent. The respondent appeared to be enamoured of that lady. The quarrelling went on, and the lady eventually left, and on one occasion he (respondent) was writing a letter to the lady when she (petitioner) interfered and remonstrated with him on his improper conduct. After that quarrels continued, and the respondent told her she could get a divorce, as he had committed adultery many times. She said something about judicial separation, lhut the respondent said he would have nothing but a dissolution of the marriage. On another occasion he came into the kitchen And told her it was necessary she should plead cruelty as well as adultery in order to obtain a decree for divorce, and thereupon knocked her down as she was ironing. He then said, "Now you can .get a divorce, and if you are quiet you cm keep it out of the papers. Nobody will be any the wiser, and I shall think you a sensible woman." She left the rectory the next day. Lena " Cator, daughter of the petitioner, gave evidence to corroborate her mother's evidence as to the acts of cruelty committed by her father. She bad seen him strike her and otherwise ill-use her.— His Lordship made a decree for judicial separation, with costs.

I Her Majesty has fixed the 2nd December for the opening of the new Law Courts. Hugh Grant, the man under sentence of death in Carlisle Gaol for the murder of his infant daughter at Workington, has been respited during her Majesty's pleasure. Sir Stafford Northcote has been recommended by Sir W. Jenner to go abroad as soon as his Parliamentary duties allow.

Lord Fitzgerald, the newly-appointed Lord of Appeal, took his seat for the first time on Tuesdoy at the Judicial Com- mittee of the Privy Council. - Professor James Stuart has consented to contest Cam- bridge University in the Liberal interest, so that Mr. Raikes will have to fight for the seat.

At the International Food Exhibition just held at Knightsbridge, London, a gold medal was awarded to the Montserrat lime fruit juice sauce. Only four gold medals in all were awarded at this exhibition. An attempt to upset a taain is reported to have been made on Sunday, by two boys, on the 135,idport line of the Great Western Railway, by placing, .a large pieoe of iron en the metals. A ganger discovered the obstruction in time to avert a catastrophe. • In reply to a representation from the Inverness authori- ties, the Government have declined to send a military or naval force to the Island of Skye to protect the officers who are attempting to serve writs on the tenantry. It has con- sequently been decided to augment the police force for the purpose.

• The contract for the completion of the Forth bridge has been settled, the successful firms being those of Sir Thos. Selby Lancree, Bart., C.E., London, and Messrs. William Arrol and Co., Dalmarnock ironworks, Glasgow, who under- take the gigantic work jointly. The amount of the contract £1,600,000. A shocking discovery was made late on Monday night at the Stratford Collieries, near Barnsley. Two men, named Joseph Hudson, 54, and Henry lolling, 51, both of Dod- worth, were almost buried alive by a fall of stone. The deceased ought to have left work at two o'clock, but being missed'search was made. Both were found alive, but died in a few minutes.

A MUNIFICENT GIFT.-At a meeting of the Court of Governors of the Stratford-on-Avon Infirmary, on Tuesday, Dr. Kingsley stated that be was now in a posiion totell them that the persons who bad placed the sum of £6,000 in his hand for the erection of a new institution were Mr. and Miss Gibbins, of Eatington—the same donors who two or three years ago presented £4,000 to the Stratford Nursing Home. An eligible site has been secured, and building operations will be commenced forthwith.

ST. Joares, MILES PLATTING.-Sir Percival Heywood, patron of the benefice of St. John's, Miles Platting, has in- formed the Bishop of Manchester that he has nominated the Rev. Harry Cowgill, the former curate of the church, to the rectory. Mr. Cowgill has been at St. John's for five or six years. He was in thorough sympathy with the late rector during whose imprisonment he had charge of the church' It is anticipated that Ir. Cowgill, if he is instituted, will continue the ritual and observances adopted by the late rector.

Two sisters, named Cooper, in 1879, entrusted a firm of solicitors with the sum of £2,700 for investment. In 1881, when the firm suspended payment, it was found that the money had not been invested, but had been applied by Mr. Turner, one of the partners, to his own purposes. The Misses Cooper, on Saturday, sued the other partner, Mr. Pritchard, for the amount. Mr. Baron Pollock said he had no doubt this was a partnership transaction, and, notwith- standing the bankruptcy, Mr. Pritchard was liable for acts of his partner, even though they were dishonest. Judgment was therefore given for the plaintiffs, with interest. THE POET LAUREATE'S NEW DRAmA : REMARKABLE SCENE IN THE THEATRE.—During the performance of the Poet Laureat.i's play, "The Promise of May," at the Globe Theatre, London, on Tuesday night, the Marquis of Queens- berry rose in the stalls and protested against the exposi- tion of the principles of freethought given by one of the oharacters. The act was allowed to proceed to its close, but immediately after the fall of the curtain the Marquis again rose, apparently under the influence of considerable excite- ment, announced himself as a free thinker, and accused Mr. Tennyson of presenting a travesty of free thinking senti- ments. There was much confusion, and ultimately it was found necessary to urge the Marquis to leave the house.

THE NITIJNAL UNION Or CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIL- TIONS.—The annual conference of the National Union of Conservative Constitutional Associations was held in Bristol, on Tuesday, when there was a numerous at!en- dance of delegates from all parts of the kingdom. Earl Percy presided. The report congratulated the members on the work done during the past year-200 new associations having been opened in different parts of the kingdom. The President, in moving the adoption of the report, said thaL, although the organisation was becoming more perfect, they must not solely depend upon organisation, but should endeavour to educate the public mind to true political prin- ciples. The Duke of Beaufort was elected president for the coming year. _

THE CLLYCROSS COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—R is now known that thirty-three widows and about one hundred children have been left destitute by the Claycross Colliery disaster. Towards their maintenance the Claycross Com- pany have headed a subscription list with 500. Mr. Jack- son, one of the proprietors, went down, on Monday, with the manager, and made a thorough examination of that part of the mine where the greatest force of the explosion was felt. The engines were subsequently examined, with the result that it is anticipated the pit will be speedily again in working condition. The Government inspection of the mine took ploce on Tuesday. The Government inspector, Mr. A. H. Stoke, accompanied by several managers of ad- jacent collieries, spent about five hours in the mine. THE GREAT ROBBERY OF BONDS—The Russian ox-officer Novitzky, who is alleged to have assaulted and robbed an (Mem magistrate in London in August last of over £15,000 worth of bonds, and who has been arrested in Hamburg, will be brought to England under an extradition warrant by Detective-Inspector Moser, of Scotland-yard, who had traced him from London through nearly all the countries and cities of the continent. Inspector Moser found that some of the bwids had been cashed or placed in the hands of backers at Dresden, Prague, Vienna Buda-Pesth, Bucharest, and other places. At Hamburg, however, Novitzky's movements ex- cited suspicion, and the police, who apprehended him, telegraphed for Inspector Moser, who at once identified him from a photograph. The whole of the valuables stolen have been recovered, and it is therefore evident that Novitzky possessed considerable funds of his own, out of which he defrayed the necessarilly large expenses connected with his flight. It has been ascertained that Novitzky was formerly an officer Is the Russian army, and fought bravely at the battle of Inkerman. M. Savitch, who has remained in Eng- land since the robbery, will prosecute Novitzky when brought up at Bow-street. Tit a SCHOOL BOARD CONTEST IN MANCIIESTER.—The result of the School Board elections for Manchester was declared on Monday evening. There were IS candidates for 15 seats—namely, seven Churchmen, six unsectarian, three Roman Catholics, one Independent, and one Land League nominee. The process of counting began at nine o'clock a.m. on Monday, at the Town Hall, and was conducted under the persenal supervision of the Mayor, with a staff of 75 clerks. The result was declared s'iortly after eight o'clock on Monday night, six of the Church candidates, the six unsectarian candidates, and the three Roman Catholics being elected. A re-count was demanded on behalf of the seventh Church candidate, who was only a little over 200 votes below the unsectarian candidate next above him. Mr. Kenny, the Land League candidate for Ennis, was one of the dere ited candidates. The total number of votes recorded was 27,860. THE LIBERAL DEFECTION ON THE CLOTURE.—The fol- lowing analysis of the lists on the three vital divisions on the first rule will be found useful. It supplies the best pos- sible illustration of the numerical insignificance of the Liberals who oppose the cloture. All the other English and Scotch Liberals who do not appear in the list have either voted or paired in favour of the cloture, or have been un- unavoidably absent : AMENDMENTS MARRIOTT. GIBSON. W. Absent For Against Fitzwilliam, Hon. W. ...... Against For Absent Fitzwilliarn, Hon. H Against For Absent Fort, Mr. Against For Against Grey, Mr. Albert Against For Against Jenkins, Mr. D Against For Against Lubbock, Sir John Against For Absent Mar lett. Mt Far For For Nicholson, Mr. W Against For Against Rylands, Mr. P. Against Absent Paired agst Stafford, Marquis of Absent For Against Taylor, Mr. P. A. Absent Absent Against Torrens, Mr. W. M4O Absent Absent Absent Walter, Mr. John For For Absent Watkin, Sir E. Considerable doubt exists as to whether Sir Edward Watkin I ought still to be classed among Liberals. Rumour flays I that he is no longer included among the Ministerialists by the whips.—Pall Mall Gazette. POOR Lam AMENDMENT.—On Tuesday afternoon a depu- tation of nearly 50 members or clerks of boards of guar- dians in Lancashire and Cheshire had an interview with Mr. Dodson, President of the Local Government Board, to urge certain amendments in the Poor Law, especially so as to secure uniformity of assessment and the triennial election of guardians. Mr. W. Agnew, M.P., introduced the depu- tation, and it was accompanied by Mr. Leake, M.P., and Mr. Summers, M.P. Mr. Dodson. in reply, said that within the last 15 years seven or eight Valuation Bills had been intro- duced into !Parliament, and he was bound to say that the experience of the Ministers who introduced them had not been encouraging, but ,he supposed that there was now a more generel approximation to a concensus as to what should be done, and therefore when Parliament was once more able to devote time to this subject, as he hoped it ere long might be able to do, there might be a chance of arriving at a satisfactory conclusion on the subject. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the other subject, a Committee of the House of Commons reported some years ago in favour of the triennial election of Guardians, but without making any recommendation as to one-third of each board retiring annually by rotation. The subject would require to be very carefully considered, and upon which the authori- ties would have to learn the opinions not only of the guar- dians themselves, but also of the ratepayers. In conclusion Mr. Dodson referren to the desirableness of also considering whether some change should not be made in the mode of electing guardians, especially so far as the present system of votine• papers is concerned. After thanking the right hon. gentleman for receiving them the deputation retired.

The Birmingham School Board election resulted in the re.urn of nine Liberals, one Independent Liberal, one Roman Catholic, and four Churchmen, being a loss of one seat to the latter. It was resolved on Thursday, at a meeting held at Lord Salisbury's house to raise X.,50,000, in order to purchase the library of the late Dr. Linsey, and preserve it as a memo- rial of that distinguished and ecclesiastic thinker. The proposal to confer the freed3m of the city of Edin- burgh on Lord Salisbury when he visits that city next week has not been abandoned. It will take' it is expected, a definite shape in the course of the next three flays, as the usual meeting of the Town Council takes place next Tuesday. At Portadown, on Wednesday night, a man living apart from his wife, entered her place of residence, and found her in th.e bedroom with a man. The outraged husband then attacked the man with a pair of tongs, and injured him so severely that his life is despaired .of. The husband was arrested.

On Thursday morning, while five pilots belonging to Bamtisland were attempting to reach a steamer in distress in the Firth of Forth, the boat swamped, owing to ths temptestuous state of the Firth, and the five men were drowned. Four of the men were married, and leave families. The boat has been found, but the bodies have not been recovered.

Wavertree, one of the suburbs of Liverpool, was in a state of great excitement on Thursday morning, owing to the occurrence of a fatal fire. At an early hour, the family of Mrs. Yanher vi ere aroused by a smell of fire, and dis- covered the house in flames. All inmates escaped but the servant girl, Mary Ann Dogherty, ap,A 10, returned for sonic purpose, and being overcome by the smoke was burnt to death. Her return was unknown to those about. The house was utterly destroyed. _ _

The Rev. Dr. -Culross,-of Adelaide Place Church, Glas- gow, the largest Baptist congregation in Scotland, has inti- mated his declinatura of the invitation to become principal of Bristol College, in succession to the Rev. Dr. Gotch. A few days ago Dr. Culross also declined the appointment of permanent tutor to the Baptist Union of Scotland. At the Sheffield Town Hall, on Thursday, William Doma- kin, foreman fireman at the Nunnery Colliery, was fined .E 2 and costs for a very gross breach of the Mines Regulation Act. He was found drunk in the pit, and owing to his in- ability to attend to the fires the ventilating fan only made thirty instead of sixty-four revolutions per minute, and the lives of a large number of men were endangered. At the Liverpool Assizes. on Wednesday, Mary Forbes was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude for setting fire to her husband's house at Great Crosby, with the intent to defraud an insurance company, the furniture being in- sured for £l,OOO. At the conclusion of the trial of Mrs. Forbes, her husband was arrested as he was leaving the court on the charge of being implicated in the arson. On Thursday morning, about half-past eleven o'clock, the Queen, who was accompanied by the Princess Beatrice and the Duke and Duchess of Connaught, drove, attended by the :mite, from the Castle, to the Spital Barracks, Windsor, and inspected the squadron of the 2nd Life Guards, which has just returned from Egypt. The Royal party returned, after the visit, to the Palace. DARING CATTLE ROBBERY. On Wednesday, a young man named Clement Leith was committed for trial at Wed- nosbury for stealing two valuable cows from a field. In consequence of his keeping bad company, and in order to obtain £4O, he went into a field belonging to a butcher, took two cows, and afterwards sold them for £34. The robbery was not detected until after the cows were slaughtered..

On Thursday morning Jane Chambers, aged 15, died at the Leicester Infirmary from injuries sustained at a level crossing on the Midland Riilwav at Colville. Deceased was going home from work, and was standing on one line while a train passed over the other, when she was knocked down by a goods train. One limb was torn from the body, and the other smashed, and a wheel also passed over her body. Thomas Hollingworth, draper, was charged at Oldham on Thursday, with employing five girts as dressmakers is con- travention of the Workshops Act. Factory-Inspector Hoare found the girls employed at a quarter to ten on Saturday night. The defence was that a number of mourning orders came in which had to be executed early. The defendant was fined 50s and costs.

Before the Bolton magistrates, on Thureday morning, the proprietors of the Persian Mill, recently destroyed by fire, were summoned for £5, the amount of the poor rate which was paid in May to cover the year. The mill was burnt down in August, and the proprietors claimed a reduction. An order was made for payment, the Bench remarking that it was a hardship, but lot injustice. Messrs Bayley were granted a case for a superior court. At Oldham, on Thursday, John Farrow, secretary of the Oldham Grounds Company, was charged with selling in- toxicating drink without a license. The officers of the Inland Revenue went on the 16th September to the grounds on the occasion of a great wrestling match, and drink was supplied to people who entered. Complaints had been received from publicans, because of the drinking at the grounds militating against their business.. A fine of £35 and costs was inflicted. A STIIDINTS' RIOT AT ABERDEEN.-Dr. Alexander Bain, Lord Rector of Aberdeen University, delivered his address to the students on Wednesday. Great confusion ensued when the Lord Rector appeared, and he spoke for a con- siderable time to the reporters. Furniture was broken and peas and crackers thrown about. Eventually the Lord Rector retired, after handing his address to the reporters. The scene afterwards became indescribable. Much damage was done and several persons were slightly injured. On Wednesday night, at the annual dinner of the Burnley and District Licensed Victuallers' Association. Councillor Bickerstaffe. of Blackpool, the chairman, said he could not usderstand the bishops and clergy mixing with Dissenting ministers on teetotal platforms when they had so much at stake in the shape of vested interests, villifying the character of their best friends. At some future time, when disestab- lishment came to the front, they might be glad of the assistance of those whom they were now trying to alienate. At half-past five on Thursday morning a shocking acci- dent occurred at the Carlton Main Colliery, owing to over- winding the machinery, ten men and boys being thrown out of the descending cage into the.pit bottom. They were all seriously injured, and narrowly escaped with their lives. Joseph Poppleton Roystone had both legs fractured, and two men named Latham and Tomlin had each a leg broken. The accident was causect by the engineman losing control of the machinery. The patent safety winding links saved the men from being smashed to pieces. A wedding was celebrated at Ipswich, on Wednesday, the bride being Miss Mary Charters, only daughter of Mr. G. Charters, of Stoke Park, Ipswich, and the bridegroom, Count Carl Esterhazy, of Presburg, Hungary. In the summer of this year, Mr. and Mrs. Charters, with their daughter, were cruising on the river Nile, when their boat was upset. Count Esterhazy was passing in kis yacht, and gallantly rescued the party. The acquaintance formed under these circumstances quickly ripened into a closer intimacy, and in the presence of a crowded congregation the nuptials of the young lady and her deliverer were celebratel on Wednesday. Count Esterhazy, who was dressed in the Hungarian Court costume, was accompanied by ount Csaky, similarly attired, and Captain Sebastiani, wearing the Uhlan uniform. Lord and Lady Gwdyr, Lady Broke Middleton, and Sir William and Lady MlCormac were amongst the wedding party. THB PALMER EXPEDITION. - The Admiralty have received further information from Suez, through Captain Stephens° n, of the Carysfort, as to the Palmer expedition. The officer in question, whose communication is dated Satur- day, states that Mattar Soffieh declares that he buried the money after Professor Palmer's party was attacked in Wady Sudr ; and on Thursday last Warren and party left Suez with Matter Soffieh to recover it. News were received from the party on Saturday morning stating that they had re- covered Professor Palmer's despatch box, containing private letters, £165 in cash, and £45 in notes, and a black bag, open, containing £l,OOO in gold. The bag had a label attached bearing the name " Euryalus." Matter Soffieh denies all knowledge of the remainder of the money. It seems that there were no notes or writing of any decription to show what took place after the party left Moses' Well. The search party was expected back to Suez on Sunday.

A GIPSY ^CHiRGBD WITH MURDERING HIS FATEDiII. At the Hampshire Assizes, on Tuesday, William James, a gipsy, aged 26, was tried for the murder of his father on the 30th August last. The chief witnesses against the prisoner were his mother, two brothers, and two sisters. The family had heen harvesting in the neighbourhood ef Petersfield, living in vans, and the prisoner had created some ill-feeling by his relations with a woman. On the I..st day of the harvest they were all at a public-house in Peterstield, and the prisoner challenged his brother-in-law to fight. Later in the night he struck his mother, and offered to fight any man of the tribe. There were one or two fights among the women, and ultimately the prisoner's father was found lying on his back in the road some distance from his van. The prisoner was heard to strike somebody, and to say that if he did not get up he would kill him. The deceased was re- moved to the Workhouse, where it was found that he had six ribs broken ; his head was sevsrely hurt, and he had suffered other injuries, it was believed, from prisoner having jumped upon him. He died four days afterwards.—The prisoner was found guilty of manslaughter, and sentenced to 20 years' penal servitude. TEE NATIONAL LIBERAL CLUB.—A thoroughly-represen- tative assembly of Liberals toot at Westminster Palace Hotel, on Thursday, to establish a National Liberal Club, and the meeting was crowned with complete success. Lord Northbrobk, who presided, explained that the object was to establish a club which would be a London centre for Liberals, and would be within the means of persons who are not wealthy. The Marquis of Hartington also dwelt upon this important point, remarking that the majority of the Liberals are to be found in the industrial classes, and it was therefore necessary to provide a centre at which Liberals from the country could meet in London. Lord Derby pro- posed the first list of members of the committee of the club, and in doing so slid the Liberals had ability in abundance for administrative and debating pur- poses, both in Parliament and out of it. They had plenty of reforming energy, but all their requirements and all their dangers lay in one direction—their want was a com- plete and cordial organisation. Their danger Was that of division and separation. This observation did not apply to their present condition, for their never was a time when the Liberal party was more united, but he referred to the past and what might oocur in the future. It is to sweep aivaY this danger that the National Liberal Club is being formed, and it only needs loyal support to ensure success. Sir W. Harcourt, Sir Henry James, Mr. W. H. Gladstone, and others also spoke, and the formation of the club, with Mr. Gladstone as its first president, was decided upon. The clut cannot fail to be highly appreciated by country Liberals, especially if the head of the party take a personal interest in promoting its success.

div.head: MAN STABBED IN THE STREET AT WIDNES.
div.p: A MAN STABBED IN THE STREET AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jour., a man named John Riley, was brought up in custody, charged with wounding Wm. Ratcliffe, a labourer, of 7, Alforde-street, Widnes, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm. From the evidence of the prosecutor it ap- peared that on Saturday evening he attended a dancing class at the Mersey Hotel, where he met the prisoner, whom he bad known for about two years. He. did not speak to the prisoner, nor did the latter address him. About ten o'clock the prosecutor, accompanied by Jun. Pickering, Thomas Davies, and several other young men, left the hotel and they proceeded along Waterloo-road. When they reached the end of Pitt-street, the prisoner, who was walking by the side of a young woman named Annie McLoughton, passed them. No words were exchanged. When the prisoner had got about 40 yards ahead he stopped. The young woman went on. Soon the prosecutor and his companions overtook the prisoner, who seized the former by the left arm, making use of a foul expression as he did so. Prosecutor replied to him, when the prisoner gave the former a sharp blow on the left breast, but whether with his open hand, or with his fist, the prosecutor was unable to say. Without in any way retaliating, Ratcliffe walked on. He did not know -what became of the prisoner. At that time the prosecutor was not aware that he was injured, but after a short time he felt blood running from his chest, and went to the window of a shop in the vicinity and opened his waistcoat. He saw that his shirt was dyed with blood. He staggered in his walk, and began to feel very ill and faint. He at once went to the surgery of Dr. O'Keeffe, who dresed his wound. An examination of his clothing showed that hie coat, waistcoat, shirt, and singlet were cut through to the left breast. He was still suffering from the effects of the wound, and was not able to go to his work.—ln cross-examination by Inspector Barnett, the prosecutor said he had never had any quarrel with Riley in his life; nor did he give him any provocation on the might in question.—The prisoner; Did you see me with a knife or anything P—Prosecutor : No.—The prisoner: Be- cause I had no knife to stab you with.—John Pickering, labourer, 13, Kent-street, Widnes, and Thomas Davies, joiner, living in Princess-street, gave evidence corroborative of this statement—Dr. O'Keeffe said the prosecutor went to his surgery about tea minutes to eleven on Saturday night. Prosecutor told him he was wounded in his left breast, and asked him to dress the wound. He examined him and found a small punctured wound under the nipple of the left breast, just over the heart. The wound merely penetrated the skin; if it had been deep it would have killed the man instantly. He dressed the wound, and then examined the clothing. He found a cut on the coat, waist- coat, shirt, and singlet corresponding with the position of the wound on the breast. The cut was like one made by a knife or scissors, as the wound was a clean one and not ragged.—The Clerk: Then you say that the man was stabbed by some sharp instrument ?—Dr. O'Keeffe: Yes. Ratcliffe seemed nervous when be went to the surgery. He appeared to be suffering from the shock. He had not recovered from the shock, and would not be able to follow his employment for several days.—P.C. Brydges deposed to apprehending the prisoner at his lodgings in Charlotte- street, Widnes. He first saw the prisoner in the street, but when the latter saw the officer he tried to escape. When arrested the prisoner resisted violently, but with assistance be was conveyed to the Police Station. In answer to the charge, the prisoner said "I did nothing to Wm. Ratcliffe, or anybody else, in Waterloo-road."—lnspector Barnett said in his opinion the case was one of premeditation, and he asked for the prisoner to be committed for trial.—The prisoner was then cautioned in the usual way, and he said "lam not guilty of stabbing."—He was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday. The Rev. Canon Barclay (chairman) presided, and there were also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood; Messrs. Mclntyre, Wm. Handley, E. A. Wallington, T. Norman, Knowles, Highfield, Ashton, Stokes, Andrews, Darbyshire, C. Rigby, W. Whittaker, G. S. Hazlehurst, and Henry Linaker (clerk).

div.head: AUDITOR IN QUEST OF A ROOM.
div.p: THE AUDITOR IN QUEST OF A ROOM.

The House Committee recommended that the application of the district auditor for the use of the Board-room, in which to hold his audit, be granted provided his audit did not interfere with the sittings of the Board.—Mr. C. RIGBY said he understood that the consideration of the matter was adjourned until that day in order that the Clerk might state his opinion whether the Guardians were compelled to find the auditor a room.—The CLERK : You are not bound to find him a room.—Mr. RIGBY : Then I should let him find his own. (Laughter.)—The CHAIRMAN: That is what he is trying to do.—Mr. W. HANDLEY observed that the Work- house was in the centre of the Union, although not perhaps so convenient a place as Frodsham. He thought the Guardians ought no longer to presume on Mr. Linalter's kindness in the matter. Mc. Linaker had accommodated the auditor at his office with serious inconvenience to himself.—The CHAIRMAN : Why could not the auditor engage the Public Hall at Frodsham ?—Mr. ASHTON sug- gested that there were several public-houses in the place.— The CLERK said the auditor refused to hold the audit in a public-house. He agreed with that refusal; a public-house was not the proper place.—Mr. RIGBY was of the same opinion.—The CLERK pointed out that it would be incon- venient far the officers if the audit was held at the Work- house.—Mr. NORMAN remarked that he understood the audit 'occupied several days, and he pointed out the incon- venience which would attend the andit were it held in the Board-room.—The CLERK: If you refuse to allow him the room he must fisd another place. Before the' audit wAs held at any office, the Board had always paid for a room. It was held at Frodsham Town Hall once or twice.—Mr. ASHTON : But you say we are not bound to pay for a room. —The CLERK: I don't think we are ; we have always done so.—Mr. NORMAN suggested that a letter should be forwarded to the auditor, stating that it was the general opinion of the Board that Frodsham was the most central and convenient place ; but that if ha could not engage a room there, the Guardians would allow hint to use the Board-room if his audit did not interfere with the Guar- dians' meetings.—Mr. ASHTON remarked that if the auditor used the Board-room there would be several small expenses incurred including the consumption of fuel, and if they were to study economy as they had done in the past they ought to refuse to allow the auditor the use of the room without remuneration. He would not move a resolution, but gave this Elsa, suggestion.—The CLERK: lam sorry you have not found that out during the years I have been providing coal and gas.—lt was ultimately decided to grant the auditor's request providing his audit did not clash with the meetings of the Board, informing him that the Board would suggest that Frodsham was the more convenient place for all the Guardians.

div.head: IMPROVEMENTS.
div.p: IMPROVEMENTS.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board, stating that an order bad been issued directing the Guardians to cause an engine and boiler house and new entrance gates to be erected at the Workhouse, at a cost not exceeding £216. Toe order also authorised the Guardians to expend the additional sum of £394 in making alterations and addi- tions at the Infirmary at the Workhouse, and to borrow the sums mentioned. APPOINTMENT OF A NURSE. The CLERK stated that the committee appointed to con- sider the applications for the position of nurse at the house met on the 10th November, and resolved that the applicants Mrs. Janet Ball and Catherine Parry be selected to attend the next meeting of the Board. A number of testimonials were now read, and the applicants were called into.the room and examined. Afterwards Mr. NORMiN moved, and Mr. HAZLEHURST seconded, a motion that Mrs. Parry be appointed.—Mr. Asirrow moved an amendment that Mrs. Ball be appointed.—Rev. J. LOCKWOOD seconded.—Eleven Guardians voted for the amendment and four for the original motion.—Mrs. Ball was declared elected, and she was called into the room and informed of the fact by the Chairman.

div.head: sreTn OF THE HOUSE.
div.p: sreTn OF THE HOUSE.

The Master's report showed that there were 200 inmates in the house, compared with 197 in the correspondirg week of last year. Thirteen vagrants had been relieved during the week, and the sum of £64 5s had been expended in out- door relief, being an increase on £1 10a 101 on the previous year. There were 33 boys and 32 girls in attendance at school, and 12 boys and 13 girls receiving industrial training.

div.head: DREADFUL WOUNDING CASE.
div.p: DREADFUL WOUNDING CASE.

A WOMAN'S LIP BIF FEN OFF AT RUNCORN. On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell and Captain Hazlehurst,James Robinson was brought up in custody charged with having, on the Ilth inst. unlawfully and malicious:y wounded his wife, Mary Robinson.—Mary Robinson said she was the wife of the pri- soner, and lived at the Cemetery Fields. She had been twice previously married, and had had children by each of her other husbands. These children now lived with her. On Saturday night, about ten o'clock, she was at home with her husband. About half-past ten one of her sons entered 1 the house, accompanied by two young women—"one that Ihe followed," and her companion. The prisoner charged the son with going with the Salvation Army. The latter denied that he had. Prisoner said he did not like the son going there. The son retorted that if he did not like it, he would pack his things up and go away. Witness said he should not go away. Blows were now exchanged between the son and the prisoner, and witness, as she had often done before, went between them. The husband and wife struck each other many times. While they were struggling to- gether the witness slipped to the ground, her head coming in contact with the end of the sofa. She was rendered un- conscious. When sbe regained her senses she was in the yard, and she discovered that her bottom lip was injured and was bleeding profusely. .bhe went to Dr. Bagnall's surgery, where her injuries were attended to. Her lip was not cut when she fell against the sofa.—ln cross-examina- tion by the prisoner, witnese admitted that she struck him a blow between the eyes after be had removed an organette which his son wished to play.—James Shaw said he was the son of the last witness. and lived with her. When he went home on Saturday night some words passed between him and the prisoner, and from words they got to blows. His mother tried to separate them. He saw her fall, but could , not say whether she came in contact with the sofa or not. I The prisoner had hold of his mother by the neck when she I fell. His mother was screaming, and he told the prisorer 'o release her. He did so, and left the house. Witness had previously seen the prisoner with his face clol.e to his mother's, and the latter screamed loudly. After the priso- ner had left the house he discovered that part of his mother's lip had gone. The prisoner in a short time entered the house, and witness said, 'You have bit her lip off." The prisoner replied, "No, I havn't," when witness said, "It's no one else." Ten minutes afterwards witness found the lip on the floor, and placed it on the chimney piece. He did not see it again. The piece was about quarter of an ir ch deep.—Martha Hannah Wilthenshaw, daughter to the first witness, said she saw her mother fall, and also her step- father with his head against hem When in that position her mother screamed. She afterwards 131 VI her stepfather wash his face in the scullery.—Dr. Bagnall deposed that shoat half-past eleven on Saturday night the prosecutrix went to his surgery. He found that the greater part of her lower lip was missing. The piece was taken out in a semi- circular form. He had never seen such a wound, and asked her how it had been done. It was such a wound as could be caused by a bite, or being cut off; it could not have been caused by a fall or a blow. The prosecutrix could not have bitten it off, because she had no teeth in front. P.C. Kelly stated that be apprehended the prisoner on Sunday morning at half-past twelve, at the Rancoru Soap and Alkali Com- pany's works. He had searched for the lip, but could not Ind it. Prisoner was cautioned in the usual way, and asked if he bad anything to say. He said he denied biting his wife's lip off. When his stepson went home on Saturday night he insisted upon playing an organette. Prisoner removed the instrument from one table to another, and whilst he was doing so the son struck him in the mouth. . When he had placed it on the table he turned round to face his stepson, when the mother struck him between the eyes with her fist. Then there were "five all at once pummel- ling into him," and when he got at liberty he went from the house. An older son than the one who had given evidence followed him and struck him three or four times. Then be returned to the house and sent his (the prisoner's) coat and hat into the yard, and told him to go, adding that that was about all be brought with him. The prisoner was committed to take his trial at next Knutsferd eessions.—The prosecu- trix: Will you allow bail for him ?—The Bench admitted prisoner to bail, himself in £4O and two sureties of £25 I each. _..._

The " friendly " actioq commenced by Mr. Jos. Gurney, of Northampton, against Mr. Bradlaugb, by which he nominally sought to recover the £5OO penalty prescribed by Act of Parliameßt from Mr. Bradlaugh for having sat and voted during a debate in Parliament without subscribing the oath, has been mentioned before Mr. Justice Mathew, in London. It was admitted to be a friendly suit instituted by Mr. Bradlangh's earnest supporters' who were anxious to have the question of his rights tested by the Courts. After some discussion, Mr. Justice Mathew said hq must decline to hear the case, as it was a collusive action and Mr. Brad. laugh was both plaintiff and defendant. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 18, 1882.(
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 18, 1882.(

particulars necessary to be considered in connection with the temporary.arrangements for the maintenance of order and security in the country. Naturally, the most important element in such a Convention will be the charge for the iz,ooo men, but that is just the point on which we are not favoured with information, for the very sufficient reason that the Convention has not been drafted. With many it may be doubtful whether Egypt should be called tipon to pay any portion of our expedition to Egypt; for ourselves we think she should be liberally dealt with in this respect, and that no charge whatever should be made upon her for our military operations. But with respect to our armed occupation of the country—which is only undertaken because Egypt is not, and will not be in a position to defend herself against internicene discord until her army has been, thoroughly reorganised—the case is very different, and her finances, we are disposed to think, may be farly, called upon to bear a fair share of the cost. The House of Commons, it has been often said, is the slave of pre- cedent, and happily a precedent for the course now about to be followed is to be found in the limited occupation of France after the battle of Waterloo. France at that time was invaded for the purpose of putting down a rebellious Power which had obtained sway in the country; just as the invasion of Egypt had its origin in a desire to deliver the country frcm the oppressive yoke of Arabi and his dis- loyal -army. The only difference, if difference it may be called, in the two cases is that Egypt was invaded by one Power only; while the invasion of France was undertaken by allied Powers. The principle, however, go- verning both the traneactions is the same, and France recouped England for her military occupation in the same way that Egypt will have to reimburse the invading Power for her services now. To us it is some satisfaction to know that the Convention is to be made with the Egyptian Government and not with the SULTAN, and we recognise in this a desire on the part ofl England to control rather than to augment the power which Turkey has hitherto been able to exercise in Egyptian affairs. During the negotiations which preceded the war, and whilst the military operations were in actual progress, the SULTAN was frequently found coquetting with the rebels. It will scarcely be disputed that the mission of- DERVISCH Pacha was a blind, and it is equally certain that ARABI Pacha would not have offered the resistance he did had he not ex- pected the active assistance of the Turkish army. Every step, therefore, taken in the direction of limiting the SULTAN'S sovereignty over Egypt will be heartily welcomed. "Egypt for the Egyptians" should be our watchword, and anything short of this will but inadequately recompense us for the trouble, expense, and bloodshed of the recent cam- paign; and? at t 4 same time, anything short of complete self-government for the Egyptian people must inevitably result in future trouble, We have every sympathy with Sir S. NORTHCOTE'S observation that the House is entitled to early and full in- formation—as to the employment of the forces of the Crown and the mode by which the expenses are to be met, and we feel sure that the Government are anxious to give as much information as they “m- -veniently can; but then, as Sir STAFFORD knows, the exigencies of the public service must be consulted, and it is only a sense of public duty that prevents the Govern- ment from disclosing all their intentions. At a time when diplomatic negotiations are going on it is extremely inconvenient; as we all know, to allow a word to slip, and- it would not be wise for the Government to state what its intentions are to-day when to- morrow the force of circumstances may com- pel them to modify their views. Above all it is very undesirable that finance should be dealt with in anything but a final and com- prehensive fashion ; and we are convinced it is only because this cannot now be done that the Government declines to enter into the financial details which Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE invites them to do. The Opposi- tion may rest assured that the money now being spent will be wisely and judiciously dis- bursed, and that every farthing will be faithfully accounted for. Brief as was the statement of -the PREMIER on Tuesday, and containing as it no doubt did all that could safely be said, we may say we should have been better pleased had it indicated in any way the manner in which our views are accepted by the other Powers. Is France to have any share for the future in the internal affairs of Egypt, or has she .by her vacillating policy for ever shut herself out from Egyptian Councils? - England undertook the work of pacification single-handed, is she to be allowed to remain in occupation alone, or is there to be any surveillance by the other European Powers? Is the SULTAN, who has done nothing for Egypt, to have a vetoing power over the arrangements we may enter into with the Egyptian Government ?, These are questions which we should have been glad to find answered; but we have no doubt that a sufficient answer will be forthcoming , at the proper time. A Government which has carried us through so many difficulties may well be trusted to see that the negotia- tions now pending shall terminate, not in the aggrandisement of England, but in the amelioration of the Egyptians, who must henceforth enjoy all the advantages of a self- governing people. The statement of the PRIME MINISTER seems to have at least dis- armed opposition. Mr. BOURKE has with- drawn a notice of motion relating to Egypt which he had on the notice-paper; and though Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE has not withdrawn his, he has done that which is almost equivalent—abandoned the idea of pressing it upon the attention of the House. This perhaps is the greatest compliment which could be paid to the policy which the Government are now pursuing.

The other Sunday I attended Divine service at Run- corn Parish Church, and on the whole was well pleased with it. Some persons may condemn the procession of the choristers as savoraing of Ritualism, and advocate the stoppage of the custom. Perhaps it would be as well to dis- continue it, if it wears the same aspect on all occasions as it did when I viewed it. I failed to see anything particularly edifying in watch- ing a number of men and boys attired in sur- plices which had long lost their virgin whiteness and which hang in ungraceful folds about their legs, parade the centre aisle of the church. Cleanliness is: generally credited with occupying second place only to godliness, and I was considerably surprised to find that it did not on the occasion to which I refer. Possibly times are hard and soap is dear, but churches and chapels have one unfailing resource in time of need a collection, and the surplices ought by all means to be scrupulously clean, and it is for this reason that I call attention to the matter.

The Marquis of Queensberry has unintentionally succeeded in making Mr. Tennyson's new play, "The Promise of May," famous. From all accounts it seems that the piece, which is now being produced at the Globe Theatre, is a complete failure ; but an interest has now been awakened in the drama which it could not otherwise have produced. The noble Marquis went to see the performance on Tuesday. He happens to be a Freethinker, and he appears to have become so enraged at the character of Edgar, who is Mr. Tennyson's typical Freethinker, that during the progress of the performance he stood up in his stall and said, " Tiiese are the sentiments that a professing Christian (meaning Mr. Tennyson) has put into the mouth of his imaginory Freethinker, and it is not the truth." When the curtain fell the Marquis,' in response to calls, endeavoured to explain the reason of his interruption, and in doing so he bccame so excited that he had to be "forcibly but kindly removed" from the theatre. In a letter to the newspapers the noble Marquis, who rather glories in the fact that he is a secularist, protests against Mr. Tennyson's "abominable caricature." I think Mr. Tennyson has reason to thank the Marquis for the singular lift which he has thus given to the drama, for curiosity to witness it is doubtless now more keen than ever it would have been without this episode. We are promised another Bradlaugh debate, and high time it is, I think, that this matter were settled. In the House of Commons, on Monday, the Speaker read a letter which be had received from the hon. member for Northampton, requesting to be heard at the bar of the House in order that he may state the grounds of law on which he claims to be entitled to fulfil the law and take his seat. Mr. Bradlaugh, who has been extremely patient, was impelled to take this course because the High Court of Justice had refused to hear a friendly suit—exactly as the suit of Miller v. Salomous—instituted against him by one of the electors of Northampton, to obtain a decision as to his legal rights and duties. The electors of Northamp- ton have thrice elected him as their representative, there is nothing to legally disqualify him from discharging the duties of that office, the law, in fact imposes certain obligations upon him; yet the House, of Commons—or rather a majority of the members thereof—the fountain of all law, will not allow him to discharge these obligations. 'I his amounts to a partial disfranchisement of the constituency, and it ought not to be tolerated. I have little hope that Mr. Labouchere's motion will be carried, or that indeed the majority will in any way be influenced by his rhetoric; but how long, I ehould like to kuow, is thia manifest injustice towards Mr. Bradlaugh and the constituency he represents to be perpetuated? Time it were that recalcitrant. Liberals were whipped up to the scratch, and in sufficient numbers to overthrow a bigotted Opposition. ThetO Are four political contests looming in the distance, and the result of each will be awaited with interest at the present juncture. By the resignation of the right hon. S. H. Walpole (Qouservative) a vacancy has arisen in the representation of Cambridge University, and for reasons beat known to himself, Mr. Raikes, one of the Conservative members for Preston, proposes to vacate his seat, and, if possible, step into Mr. Walpole's shoes. lam glad to find that Mr. Raikes, contrary, doubtless, to expectation, is not to have it all his own way, and that there is now a formidable opponent in the field in the person of Professor Stuart, who fills the chair of Mechanism and Applied Mechanics at Cambridge. Thp contest will be a keen one, and I should not be surprised to find at its close that Mr. Raikes is without a seat alto- gether. For the vacancy at Preston, which is a decidedly Conservative constituency, there is to be a fight between two Conservatives—Mr. Tomlinson and Mr. Hanbury. At the suggestion of Sir Stafford Northcote, Mr. Tomlinson gave way in favour of Mr. Raikes on the arcasion of the late Sir John Holker's elevation to the Bench, and it is scarcely fair that he should be opposed by another Conservativa now. However, dissension in the Tory camp is the oppor- tunity for the Liberals, and as the polling day approaches I hope a Liberal candidate will be rea ly, and that he will be run in. The approaching contest at Wigan may be expected to be a close oae. It is caused by the unseating of Mr. F. S. Powell (Con- servative). The Conservative candidate is the hon. Algernon Egerton, who was a member of the late administration, but, like others of the Ministerialists, was turned out at the late general elestion ; the Liberal candidate is Mr. Walter Wren, a vigorous writer an political topics. As the former is pledged to contest Sauth-East Lancashire at the next general election, he Can only, if elected for Wig in, represent that constituency during the present Parliament, it fact which ought to tell in favour of Mr. Wren, who, I trust, will be able to win back the conetituency to the Liberal party. The vacancy at Salisbury is created by the appointment of Mr. Grentell (Liberil, of course) to an office in the Royal Household In seek- ing re-election he will be opposed by Mr. Coleridge Kennard, but as Mr. Grenfell has already beaten Mr. Kennard by over 100 in the same constituency, which numbers under 2,000 electors, the seat may be con- sidered safe to the Government. Should Preston be contested by the Liberals, the Government will stand to lose one seat and gain three, and I shall be very much surprised if there is not a gain.
FLACCTTS.

FAILURE OF A WIDNES GROCER. —At Liverpool County Court, on Thursday, Mr. Beasley, solicitor, of Runcorn, filed a petition for the liquidation of the affairs of Thomas Whelan, grocer and coal dealer, 36, Wellington-street,Widnes. The liabilities are stated at £BOO.

ADDITIONAL GUARDIAN FOR WIDNES. The Local I Government Board have issued an order for an additlonal Guardian for Widnes. Two gentlemen—Mr. S. Sadler and Mr. J. Matthews—are mentioned as probable candidates, but as there is a general desire to avoid e contest, there is every likelihood that one of these gentlemen will be returned un- opposed. EXHIBITION AT RUNCORN.—We again call the attention of our readers to the exhibition of gas appliances, which will take place in Bethesda Lecture-room, on Monday next, and five following days. It promises to be of an interesting and extensive description, and will well repay. a visit. One of the novelties during the exhibition will be a large Bray's lamp of 1,000 candle power fixed at the higher end of Vicar-street, facing High-street. ACCIDENT AT 1 WIDN'E3 CHEMICAL WORKS.—AR accident, which is expected to terminate tally, occurred at Messrs. Hutchinson's chemical works on Wednesday after- noon. It appeared that whilst a train was passing aleng a siding, a man named Moses Edwards, of 10, West Bank, attempted to pass between the moving train and a row of stationary wagons. The space was too narrow to admit his body, and he was crushed in a frightful manner. He was at once removed to the Accident Hospital, where he was surgically attended. His injuries are of a most serious character, several of his ribs being frectured, and one aboulder dislocated.
ST. PATRICK'S INBA.NT SCHOOL, WI DI:MI.—The fol-

lowing is a copy of the report issued by Her Majesty's Inspector, Mr. Scott Coward, for St. Patrick's Infant School, Widnes, which reflects the greatest credit on its energetic and painstaking teacher, Miss Flanagan :—" The discipline and instruction here are of the very highest kind and character. I know no school where all the children are so uniformly bright, intelligent, and advanced. Every child passed with credit, and the knowledge of geography acquired by the six-year-old class was con- siderably above the average reached in the second stan- dard. The school is a remarkable example of how sure a basis of instruction through discipline is."

MAURIAGE OF Mr. F. H. GOSSAGE, OF WIDNES.—The marriage of Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., of Widnes, to Amy, daughter of Mr. E. H. Perrin, of Claughton, Birkenhead, I which was solemnised at St, John's Church, Notting Hill, London, on Thursday, was the occasion of some rejoicing at Widnes on that day. Mr. Gossage occupies a prominent position in the town, being a large employer of labour and chairman of the Local Board, and he is frequently brought in contact with the townspeople, by whom he is generally esteemed. This esteem found expression at the last meeting of the Local Board, when a cengratulatory address, which ,it is intended to illuminate, was passed unanimously for presentation. Flags and banners waved gaily in the breza on Thursday from various points of 111q8srs. W. Gossatte and Sons' \vorks, and the fiats lying in the canal exhibited similar tokens ef festivity.
