UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, RUNCORN.-TllO anniversary sermons in connection with this church, were preached by the Rev. E. Orme, on Sunday last. At each service the choir sang two anthems with good effect. Collections were made. LICENSM MATTERS AT RrniconN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before the Rev. E. A. P. Camp- bell and Captain Hazlehurst, Michael Murphy applied for " permission to sell " at the W'neatsheaf Inn, Bridge-street. Application granted.—Permission to sell at the Welsh Harp, Cooper-street, was granted to Peter Darbyshire.

RUNCORN BEURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.—The Rev. Canon Barclay presided over the meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, when there were present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. Thomas Rigby, Jos. Knowles, Thomas Andrews, Stokes, John Highfield, John Mclntyre, H. Linaker (clerk). There was no business of public interest.

REXCORN POLICE AND THEIR PEISONERS.—Before Mr. W. Bankes and Captain Hazlehurst, at Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, George Brookes, a boatman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in. High-street, at eleven p.m. on the previous night. P.C. Morris proved the case, and thejprisoner was fined 108. and costs, or, in default, 14 day& hard labour.—Henry Chisnall, a sailor, was charged with resisting P.C. Morris in the execution of his duty. It seemed that on the previous night, when P.C. Morris was conveying the last prisoner to the Police Station, Chisnall, thinking he was a fellow-seaman on the same boat, Asked Morris to let him go. Morris refused, and Chisrall then atteinpted to rescue the prisoner. He was then also taken into custody.—Prisoner \vas fined £1 and costs, or 14 days' bard labour.

ROBBERY FROM A -WIDNES Dnitrilli'S SHOP. On Monday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. John Brock and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, junr., a woman named Mary Mack was brought up in custody charged with stealing four singlets of the value of 103., the property of Mr. J. Birchall, draper, Waterloo-road. Sarah Jane Moorlands, assistant to the prosecutor, said the singlets were safe in the shop at half-past seven o'clock on Saturday night. About an hour afterwards she missed them, and subsequently gave informa- tion to the police. She knew the prisoner, but did not think she had been in the shop that night.—Mary Alice Newton said she assisted her father, who kept a pawnshop in Marsh- street, Widnes. On Saturday night the prisoner entered the shop and asked witness to lend ss. 9.1. upon them. She ad- vanced I,er the money upon them. The prisoner, who had been convicted on several previous occasions, was sentenced to one month's imprisonment with hard labour. MAINTENANCE 07 A SON AT WIDNEs.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Andrew Cavanagh, a chemical labourer, was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the support of his son, who is in an in- dustrial school.— Sir. Superintendent Barker said the defend- ant's son was sent from that court in October to St. George's Industrial School on the application of the School Board. He had received a communication from the Government Inspector .alking to inquire as te the amount the defendant would contfibute. He had made inquiries and found that the defendant was in receipt of £1 15s. per week, but heOnly offered to pay is. per week. The Government Inspector said unless Cavanaqh would contribute 2s. pet week he was to ask for an order to be made. He now asked for that order.— P.S. Strickland having given evidence, the Bench ordered the defendant to pay 2s. per week.

Fair- weather, Ardavick, Manchester, skirt manufacturer; J. Corbitt, Oldham, joiner; T. G. Bardsley, Eldon street, Old- ham, storekeeper; J. Willis, Scholes, Wigan, clogger ; A. W. L. M. RORBERY FROM A RUNCORN EATING HoUSE.—Ou Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, a woman named Martha Alice Jackson was charged with feloniously stealing one knife and one fork of the value of is., the property of John Bancroft. The prosecutor is the proprietor of an eating house in Church-street, Runcorn. On Saturday night, a little before nine o'clock, the prisoner went to the stop, where she had some refreshment. When she Ind afterwards departed, the knife and fork produced were missed. Information was given to the police, and Con- stable Finny went to the prisoner's house in Cooper-street. The prisoner was in, and he informed her that she was Inspected of stealing a knife and fork. She made no answer, hut in a cupboard in the house the constable found , the missing knife and fork. She was then taken into custody. She stated the articles had been given to her by a man whom she did not know. Prisoner now pleaded not guilty. She alleged that she went into the shop and a man peid for her two pennyworth of potato° pie. Some time after she came out the man passed her and said " Here, I will give you this," and placed the knife and fork in her baud. "Sire thought no more abeat 'it," hot took them home and placed thorn in the cupboard.—The Chairman said there was no doubt the prisoner had committed the offence, and she was fined ss. and costs El, or seven days. —Prisoner: I shall have to go, then. I cannot pey. LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE BAND OV HOPE UNION.— The annual business meeting in connection with this Union was held on Monday evening, at the Young Men's Christian Association, Peter-street, Manchester. Mr. Robert Whitworth, president of the Union, occupied the chair, and said that lee could congratulate them and all other friends on the very rapid strides which their cause had made during the last year or two. He had been a long time connected with temperance work, but he never remembered any period of its history upon which he could look with greater satisfac- tion than the present. They found every branch of the work making rapid progress, so rapid that a great number of their enemies thought it had no element of continuance. But he felt confident that, having as they had now the attention and sympathy of every religious body in the com- munity, their movement had every sign of permanence abeut it. (Hear. hear.) The Church of England Temper- ance Society bad made exceedingly rapid progress since the change of programme was made, and of the Alliance he might say that more had been done in the last two veers than in the preceding ten. ( Applause.) Their own Union had made satisfactory headway, and he congratulated the friends who had worked so earnestly in this cause on the success which they had attained during the last year. (Ap- plause.) The annual report was adopted by the meeting, which also passed votes of thanks to the Executive Com- mittee and other officials. The officers for the ensuing; year were appointed, and other formal business was trans- acted. A conference in connection with the Union was held on Tuesday, at the Young Men's Christian Associa- tion, Manchester, Mr. Abraham Altham (Burnley) in the chair. A paper was read by Mr. Martin Field (*Bradford) on "Baud of Hope work, past and present," and this formed the subject of discussion in the morning. In the afternoon, a women's conference was held, and in the even- ing the annual festival was celebrated in the Free Trade Hall, which was crowded.

A WIDNES PUBLICAN AND HIS CUSTOMEBS.-0/1 Wednes- day, at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Messrs. E. Gibbon, and Holbrook Gaskell, senr., Wm. Ince was summoned to answer a charge of permitting drunkenness to take place on his licensed premises.—Mr. Swift, junr., of St. Helens defended.—P.S. Strikland said at a quarter to ten o'clock on the 14th October, he visited the Stonemasons' Lrms beer house, which was kept by the defendant. In the bar he found. a man named Lennord, and a woman named Carney standing, and they were very drunk.—Mr. Swift said that defendant admitted the people were drunk.—The Sergeant continuing, said the landlady could see very well that the persons were drunk. On the counter were two half-pint glasses, one about half full of beer before Lennord, and one about three quarters full of porter. The landlady said she had not served the persons. Lennord said he had not been served, and drunk up his beer. Carney said "It is my beer. You are badly off for a case ?" The landlady alleged that the porter belonged to a man who had just gone out. Just then a man named Burgess came in through the back door and drunk the porter Which was before Carney, but the landlady said that was not the man she had mentioned. Witness then told the landlord, who then came in, that he would be repoited for pertnittingdrunkenness. He expressed his sorrow at the fact. Carney WAS taken home by her daughter, and on the 25th October, both Lennord and Carney were fined 103.. and costs at the court. P.C.'s Mur- dock and Nicholson gave confirmatory evidence.—Ml . Swift said it WAS a case undoubtedly full of suspicion, and unless the Bench believed there was room for considerable doubt in favour of the defendant, he should expect a conviction, hut after the evidence he should call before them he hoped they:would he of opinion that it was a case which there was substantial conflict of evidence between that of the police and that of the defendant, and would dismiss the case.—lle called the defendant and Mrs. Ince, who stated that Lennord entered the bar and asked for a pint of beer. She told him he had had beer enough and could not serve him._ A man named Giver then came in and asked the witness to fill Lennord ;; pint of beer, but she again refused. The man then gave the witness 21d., and she told Lennord he could have the beer at the opening time on Sunday. Witness then left the .bar, and when she returned he found the woman Carney and the police at the bar. She did not know anything whatever of Carney, and she had not served either her or Lennord .—Patrick tilyn corroborated this statement, and Janics Iraco a;so gave confirmatory evideoct.—lhe Bench said they coosideted the Case proved ; and tined the defend- and 40s. and cogs.
THE SECOND COMING or Crousr.—The third of a series of lectures on this subjecj was held in Runcorn Public Hall on Wednesday. There was only a moderate attendance.

THE FAUNWORTH READING Room.—The reading room in connection with the Farnworth Church of England Temperance Society, which was opened on Saturday last has been open each evening since, and gives every promise of having a successful existence. HOLY TRINITY DAY ScnooL.—The distribution of prizes to the successful scholars at this school will take place in Runcorn Public Hall. Mr. Clarke Aspinall will make the presentations, and a concert will be given by the children.

HALTON PARISH CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.-Mr. James Craig, 8.A., of Runcorn Collegiate School, gave a lecture to the members of this society on Tuesday. It was entitled " Reminisences of a tour through Germany, Holland, and France," and was of a very interest- ing description. Mr. Joseph Stokes presided.

PROPOSED NEW POLICE STATION FOR WIDNES.—A meeting of magistrates last week, at Prescot, we understand, decided in favour of erecting a new police station at Widnes, in the vicinity of Waterloo-road. The cell accommodation in the present one is stated to be insufficient. The matter will be brought before the next County Quarter Sessions.

GOOD THMPLARY AT WIDN2S. - The Star of Widnes lodge held its weekly meeting, on Wednesday, when about 30 persons sat doWn to tea. Subsequently an entertainment was given. Mr. David Houghton, president of the League of the Cross, Warrington, gave an address on temperance. Songs, recitations, &c., were also given by the members.

There was a large attendance of members of Bruns- wick Mutual Improvement Class, on Wednesday evening, when Mr. John Simpson delivered a lectbre on "A holiday in Switzerland." Mr. T. Simister, the president, occupied the chair. •

SRAKESPERIAN DRAMATIC COMPANY AT RUNCORN.—Mr. Lawrence Smythe's company made their first appearance in Runcorn Public Hall on Thursday evening, when " Othello " was performed. The representation was very creditably performed, but the audience was not a large one. The charcters of Othello and I>sdemona were ably sustained, and the audience frequently manifested their approbation. Last night "The Merchant of Venice " was given, and to- night (Saturday) " Hamlet" will be put on the hoards.

UNJUST WEIGHTS AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Charles Johnson was summoned for having in his possession far usa of trade two pairs of scales which were unjust.—Superintendent Williamson said on the 6th instant he visited the shop of Mr. Johnson, in Church-street, and 'found one pair of scales three drachms against the purchaser, and a second pair four drachms. The secand pair were slightly injured in a manner which might throw thcm out of balance.—The defendant said he had since replaced one pair with new ones.—He was fined ss. and costs Qs. 6d.

THEATRE ROYAL, RtiNCOßlZ.—To•night :(Saturday) this theatre will be opened under the management of Mr. Ott.ley, the lessee. The efforts Mr. Ottley is, making to provide suitable dramatic representations for the public, and the improvements he h:ts effected in the internal structures of the theatre, are deserving of success, which he will no doubt achieve. For several weeks workmen have been busily en- gaged in improvirg the interior, which has been greatly beautified, while new and expensive scenery has been added, so no doubt that the pieces will be effectively produced. We trust that the theatre will receive a greater share of patron- age than has been formerly the case, to encourage Mr. Ottley in his effort to hither the tone of dramatic at t in the town.

NVEsLEYAN SIINDVI SCIIOOL TEACHERS.—A meeting of Wesleyan. Sunday teachers of St. Helens and Prescot was field in the Wesleyan Chapel, Prescot, on Thursday evening. Tea was partaken of, and at the after proceedings the Rev. J. M. il'amsley presided. A model lesson on the catechism was given by Mr. T. Brown to a number of Sunday school scholars, the obildren showing great intelligence and under- standing in their answers to Mr. Brown's interrogatories. Some discussion then ensued as to the desirability of a sys- tematic te,ching of the catechism in the Sunday schoo's, most of the s')eakers being in favour of such a coarse. Mr. Brown afterwards read an exaellent paper on "Some of the dangers and wants of our Sunday schools," which gave rise to an animated discussion. The meeting was brought to a close by the usual votes of thanks. HALTON PAROCHIAL CLOTHING SOCIETY: Instituted May, 1834, by Sir Richard Brooke, Bart.—The annual distribution of clothing took place on Friday in the girls' school. The Vicar presided, and after singing and prayer, he addressed the members assembled. Lady Brooke as patroness and treasurer was also present, and made some excellent remarks respecting the society work. During the past year it ap- peared !our of the inernbrs had died. Two lost their bounty of five shillings each through irregular payments. There are fifteen supporters of the club, and the amount subscribed by the senior members during the past year was £llO 3s. 41. which with the bounty L'22 ss. showed a total of £132 Bs. 41. The children of the Sunday school had subscribed £3B is. 91. and recdved Bs.; total, £45 ss. 9d. Miss E. li. Ward mid Miss B. Short are the honorary secretaries, to whom the subscribers are indebted for their services. Hearty thanks were tendered to Sir Richard and Lady Brooke for their 'very liberal subscriptions, and to Lady Brooke in par- ticular, for her ladyship's great personal interest in the wel- fare of the society and its members.

ALI,EtIED EXTENSIVE RODBEFIY AT RUNCORN.—At Run- corn Police Court, on Thursday, George Radford was charged with stealing a coat, the property of Edward Imison, on the 31s: July, 1880; second, with stealing six pairs of stockings at the sime time, the property of Joseph Beasley, and thirdly with stealing a guernsey, the property of Samuel Williams. Mr. Superintendent Williamson said that at the time the two first-named offences 'ere com- mitted, the prisoner resided in Runcorn. Since then he had served two terms of imprisonment for other offences com- mitted about the same time. Mr. ‘Villiimsoo heard the other day that, the prisoner had again come to reside in the town, and he informed the inspector of that fact. Subse- rviently Inspector Hollingworth saw the prisoner in the street and apprehended him. He was wearing the guernsey (prcduced) which had been stolen from Mr. Williams' shop on Saturday night. His house was searched, and there was found a number of new articles, the proceeds of other robberies. Mr. Williamson asked for the prisoner to he remanded until Monday to give him time to get up the case properly—Prisoner remanded. ASTRONOMICAL FACTS AND EV aNTS.—Th is star of Beth- lehem appeared in 3997, 312 A.D., 627 A.D., 942 A.D., 1257 A.D., and 1572 A.D. Edwin Dunkin, F.R.S., F.R.A.S., speaks of the last appearance of this star, which suddenly burst forth with brilliancy greater than any other around it ; it was supposed to be a comet, but twinkled like an ordinary fixed star, increasing greatly in magnitude, till it surpassed Sirius and Jupiter, was observable at noonday, and, says .1. P. Nichol, L.L.D., it pierced through clouds which obscured all other stars, it continued one year and t! en became invisiblq ; this star will appear again in 1887 A.D, for the seventh time, after its usual interval of 315 years, when its brightness will surpass any before recorded, and this will be intensified by a concurrent total eclipse of the sun and the moon. Professor Grimmer says it will be seen at noon-day throughout the entire year, and it is sup- pased that the result of its next visit will be momentous, wars, famines, pestilences, and earthquakes taking p?ace un- usually in the meantime.—The great comet now rises at midnight, and souths at 5 a.m. FARNWORTII TOTAL AnstaNENCE Socmiy.—ln connection with this society, an entertainment was given in the boys' schoolroom, on Tuesday evening, when there was a crowded audience. Addresses were delivered by the Rev. Joseph Holden, who presided, and the Rev. G. Bond, vicar. The programme for the evening included two laughable sketches, entitled "Women's rights," and the Mysterious Stranger." The character of Tim Trotter in the hrst-named piece was taken by Mr. R. Rawlinson, while Mn, Trotter was ably representei by Miss Mary Fogg. The other characters were taken by Messrs. Stowe, T. Fogg, T. Knowles, and Miss B. Palmer. The piece was very creditably performed. The acting in the second sketch was also very meritorious, char- acters being taken by Messrs. F. Franklin, F. Whiteside, and R. Joynson. A temperance glee party sang several glees in good style, and an enjoyable evening's entertainment was contributed to by Clara Mercer, M. Houghton, Winifred Platt, Barbara Scott, Daniel Rathbone, John Hillyer, Maude Hunter, E. Toft, Alice Darwell, Jabez Smith, Wm. Hackey, and Joseph Hewitt. A number of persons signed the pledge at the conclusion of the entertainment.

NENTIOWN MISSION CHULCU, RITNCORN. The annual congregational tea party was held in Shaw-street Mission-room, on Thursday evening. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Miss Barclay, Mrs. Stringfellow, Mrs. Whitaker, Mrs. Nickson, Mrs. Lello, and Mrs. Robert Gorst. At the subsequent entertainment the room was packed. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and delivered an address. The Rev. J. J. Bryant, incumbent of Weston, conducted the proceedings of the evening, which consisted of a miscellaneous entertainment, which was very successful. Miss Wright sang the "Minstrel boy" and " Within a mile of Edinboro' town ;" Mr. T. Davies, We'vo swept the seas" and "Up with the lark in the morning," and he was encored on each occasion; Mr. J. Powell, "Old dreams" Mr. F. Davies, "The little news boy ;" Mr. Morris, "The village blacksmith." The choir also sang a number of glees in good style. Mr. Pownall presided at the piano. The JUN% T. M. Arinsma proposed a vote of thanks to the lay readers, the district visitors, Sunday school teachers, superintennent of the Sunday school, the ckoir, and Mr. Charles Pownall, the organist, which was carried. Mr. Lello and Mr. Suoimer field responded. A vote of thanks was also p,ssed to the ladies who had. pre- s;deLl at the tables, anl to the s.ubserib,'!rs, on the nlotion of the R c•A tv. R. Edwards. A similar npliment having been paid to the chairman, the meeting concluded.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

William Hollis, chemist, sentenced to death at the late Stafford Assizes for the murder of a woman, upon whom he performed an unlawful operation, has been reprieved. Yesterday afternoon their Royal Highnesee3 the Crown Princess of Germany and the, Duke and Duchess of Con- naught, who have been on a visit to the Quca, left the Castle for Buckingham Palace. An Exchange Company's telegram states that a magnetic storm is now affecting all the Continental lines of telegraph, rendering it almost impracticable to work through them. " Mr. Lalor, M.P. for Queen's County, has written to his constituents, stating that he cannot any longer fulfil his Parliamentary duties he must resign his seat. Last night's Gazette announces that the Queen has heels pleased to grant to Sir Beauchamp Seymour and Sir G. Wolsslev her license and authority that they may accept of the order of the Osmanieh conferred upon them by the Khedive.

Th,t Queen has been pleased to approve of the following officers being promoted to resume the appointments which they vacated on proceeding to Egypt on active service:— Col-Goodenough, Royal Artillery; the Hon. Paul Sanford Methuen, major Scots Guards;. Major and Brevet Lieut.. Colonel Herbert Stewart, 3rd Dragoon Guards; and Major James Alleyne, Royal Artillery.

, At a meeting yesterday of the Lord Provost's Committee of the Edinburgh Town Council, it was unanimously agreed to recommend the Council to confer the freedom of the c:ty on the Marquis of Salisbury, on the occasion of his visit ri..xt week. On Thursday evEn;ng the whola of the outbuildings and a great portion of the house of Talurn Farm, Pentrebychan, between Wrexham and Ruabon, were destroyed by fire, believed to have been originated by a tramp NI hose solicita tion for alms were not responded to. On Thursday, the first stag hunted by the county Down hounds after a short run jumped over a wall into a quarry, and falling a distance of sixty fect, was dashed to pieces. Two couples of hounds had narrow escapes. The number of applications under the Irish Arrears Act has now reached nearly 20,000. Since the beginning of the week the applications have gone in at the rate of about 1,000 per day, and a great increase is expected as the month draws to a close.

On Thursday night about eight o'clock Robert Wasking- ton, furniture dealer, aged over GO years, in the darkneSll walked into the canal at hlarple. His cries for help were soon heard, and he was got out and restoratives applied. Death, however, ensued consequent upon the shock received to his heart, he haring suffered from heart disease for some months.

The report that the British Government were negotia- ting the purchase of the domain lands from the Egyptian Government through the Rothschilds, is without founda- tion. It is, however, understood that the programme of reforms for Egypt now under consideration in Downing- street includes provisions for the removal of obaticles to the introduction of foreign capital for the improvement of these lanls. CAMBRIDGE UNIVERSITY ELECTION. .
The mrit for this election was served on the Vice- Chancellor. as returning officer, yesterday morning, at ten o'clock. The date for polling will be subsequently fixed.
THE PRESTON ELECTION.
- The writ arrived yesterday morning, and the Mayor has fixed next Tuesday for the nomination and Thursday for the polling. THE MAAMTRASNA MASSACRE.

At the Dublin Commission Court yesterday, Patrick Casey was found goilty of the murder of the Joyce family at Maamtrasna. Judge Barry sentenced the prisoner to be hanged on the 15th prox., the same day as Patrick Joyce. The prisoner, when asked had he anything to say against sentence of death, answered, "I had no hand in it." GREAT FIRE IN LONDON YESTERDAY MORNING. £lOO,OOO DAMAGE. Shortly before midnight on Thursday a destructive fire broke out on the premises of Mr. Whiteley, universal pro- vider, Westbourne-grove, London, in the upper part of the building, which presents an enormous street frontage. Several engines were promptly on the spot, followed by others, but the filmes raged for nearly five hours, and were with difficulty got under. although the wind was not high. The conflagration resulted in the partial destruction and the complete gutting of a block of buildings extending from 43 to 55, Westbourne-grove. The damage is roughly estimated at over £lOO,OOO. No lives, so far as is known, were lost. The origin of the fire is unknown. DISASTROUS FIRE IN MANCIinTER YESTERDAY. GREAT DESTRUCTION OF PROPERTY. Shortly before half-past one yesterday afternoon, a fire was discovered on the premises of Messrs. G. Hodgkinson and Co., makers-up and packers, 34, Princess-street, in that, city. The workmen were out at dinner at the time, the fire was not seen, therefore, until it assumed dimensions which caused the attention of persons outside to be attracted to it. The premises are situated at the corner of Faulkner-street, and are five storeys in height. Flames were first observed near the windows of the upper storey. Information of the outbreak: was at once sent to the chief fire station in Jackson's Row, but before the fire brigade arrived the flames had obtained complete mastery of the whole of the upper storey, and were rapidly spreading to the lower portion of the build- ing. Two steam fire engines were soon gol to work, but not- withstanding the great energy of the firemen the flames spread rapidly in the back part of the building, and before half-past two had in that part of the premises penetrated to the lower floor. The roof fell in at a very early stage. Among the persons occupying rooms in the building are Messrs. Clarence, Houghton, and Co., Staniar Bros. and Co., Hamel and Co., Cromopulo and Co., H. Varbctian and Co., and Wright, Cohen Bros., A. Bryce and Co., John Marsden, Funduklian Bros. and Co.

HOUSE OF COMMONS. CETEWAYO.--Mr. ASHLEY, replying to Dr. Cameron, said Cetewayo was not a prisoner at Oude Molen. He was stay- ing there in accordance with an arangement made by the Government. They were waiting for a despatch from Sir H. liver before any final determination was arrived at. THE DUBLIN POLICE —Mr. TREVELYAN, replying to Mr. Gray, said the Committee of Inquiry into the grievances of the Dublin police was still sitting. THE MINISTRY. Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Mr. Callan, said it was not intended for the future that thedual office of the First Lord of the Treasurr and Chancellor of the Exchequer was to be held by one person. The present arrangement occasioned decreased, not increased expendi- ture. He quite admitted that the preAnt arrangements were not satisfactory. It would not be long before a change took place. DIE DUAL CONTROL.—Mr. GIADSTONE, replying to Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, said the dual control had not yet been abolished, although the Egyptian Government was anxioas it should be. It was not on the advice of the British Government, but a spontaneous act of the Egyptian Government. Replying to other questions, he said he hoped next week to make a statement as regarded excess of ex- penditure over the vate of credit for military expense in Egypt. TILE PROCEDURE Rnms.—The adjourned debate on the procedure resolutions was resumed on 6th resolution "that in committee on a bill the preamble do stand postponed until after the consideration of the clauses without question put." —The resulution was agreed to.—The seventh resolution "that when the chairman of committee has been ordered to make a report to the House he should leave the chair without the question being put," was proposed.—After a short discussion the resolution was carried by 137 te 69. I —Resolution eight provided for relaxing to a certain ex- tent the half-past twelve o'clock rale.—Mr. GL ADSTOgE explained the alterations proposed, and said they would result in an improvement of the business, and they were in favour of freedom of speech. (Laughter.)—' e motion to- repeal the rule was rejected by 129 to 26.—Mr. Moms_ than moved an amendment that the rule should not apply to bills which had been read a second time.—After discus- . Bien the amendment was rejected by 76 to 21.

THE TRIENNIAL ELECTIONS QUESTION. . IttSULT OF THE POLL. The poll of the ratepayers of the Warrington Union has been taken this week on the question of triennial elections. The voting papers were delivered in the various townshias on Monday, and collected on Tuesday, the work of casting up the votes being commenced at the Workhouse on Wed- nesday. The returning officer (Mr. J. C. Sutton), with his assistants, completed the examination and record of votes last (Friday) evening. The return shows majorities in favour of the substiiution of triennial for annual elections of Guardians in Grappenhall, Great Sankey, Latchford, Newton' Poulton, Croft, Thelwall, Woolston, and Warring- ton : and against in Bartonwood, Cuerdley, Haydock, Houghton, Middleton, and Arbury, Peuketh, Elston, and Winwick. 'The total majority of votes for all the town- ships, except Warrington, Latchford, and Newton, in which contests have usually taken place, was in favour of continu- ing the annual elections. The two political parties having supported the change to triennial elections has favoured the poll in that direction in the three townships named. The totals, however, show considerable opposition thereto, even In those townships, a total of 1,969 having been given for annual, as against a total of 3.331 for triennial elections. The following list shows the number of votes for and against in each township of the Union, the gross totals being—ln favour of triennial elections, 4,209; against, 2,884; majority in faTour, 1,325. COUNCILLOR MACKIE AND ALDERMAN DAVIES. Sir,—l was extremely pleased, and no doubt moat of your readers were, to hear of the well-merited snubbing accorded to the irrepressible Councillor Mackie, at the Council meet- ing during the election of Mayor, last week. flow vain and tyrannical some people would be had they the power; and, in my opinion, Councillor Mackie exhibited extraordinary symptoms of bath these traits of character when he had the impudence. nay, the audacity, to think that he and his paltry clique could rule the intelligent opinion of the Council. I hope, however, for the welfare of the town, Dr. Mackie will, for the remainder of his term of office, " take a back seat" or betake himself to the editorial duties of the paper he extols with so much self-importance—that paper which is said to be "neutral in all things political and religious," but in my opinion the word " neutral " is like the glowing phrases found in quack doctors' advertisements, simply to attract public attention, for anyone with half an eye can see which way the paper in question leans. Alder- man Davies threw his shafts of scathing criticism with Unflinching aim, and the poor Doctor was fairly dumb- founded, nay, to use an expression I heard, "fairly flabber- gasted." That Dr. Mackie was justifiably snubbed I think all well-reasoning people will admit, especially when it is remembered that the Doctor, who strongly condemned cliqueism in the Council, goes and tries by the formation of an insignificant clique himself to direct the otherwise well-balanced opinion of the Council. That the right man, under the circumstances, was elected to occupy the civic chair, the favourable opinions expressed on all sides fully bear out the choice of the Council; but what the majority of ratepayers think of Dr. Mackie an d his followers trying to force a miserable sort of Closure upon the Council, I fail to conceive. It must be one of disgust. The view your able correspondent, "Attains," took of this " dog-in-a-manger clique" very much pleased me, as he seems to have found out the aspirations of the Doctor and his followers had their little scheme succeeded. Just think, dear reader, this clique attempting to rule the Council, so that, should the Man- chester canal proves successful and Royalty visiaWarring- ton, Dr. Mackie—mind that Dr. Mackie was to hold the proud position of Mayor. Imagine, if you can, the burly Doctor parading Royalty about the town. Wouldn't it be a sight for sore eyes? Imagine again, reader, as a result, the Doctor being knighted for entertaining Royalty. "Oh my sides." happily, however, the 'Best laid schemes o' mice and men Gang aft a gley." I must now close, for my risible faculties have been on the go so long that my sides are aching with laughing. The idea of Dr. Mackie being mayor, and dubbed a knight, is so irresistably funny, so outrageously comical, that, that— "Oh, my sides, my sides." PUZZLED.

div.head: HARE.
div.p: THE HARE.

Sir,—lt may be interesting to some of your readers to know that the hare belongs to that order of mammalia which is termed glires or rodentia "rodents," i e., animals which " gnaw " their food. They have none of the sharp teeth called "canine," but in the front of each jaw there are two long fiat teeth, slightly curved, and having a kind of chisel-edge. The constant labour which these teeth (called incisors from the Latin word ixeido,"l cut") undergo would rapidly wear them away, and therefore to counter- act this loss they are constantly growing and being pushed forwrd, so that as fast as the upper parts are worn away they are replenished from the root. So constant is this in- crease that cases have been known where an unfortunate hare or other rodent, haying lost one of its incisors, the oppo- site one, meeting nothing to stop its progress, has grown over the lip in a curve, and ultimately prevented the I wretched animal from eating. The family name of hares is that of leporidas, containing only two species, the com- monhare (lepus timidus), and the rabbit (lepus cunicalus). The word " " is from the old Greek xi9ropit,— (collat. form of Xay‘c,)—wbich is akin to the Sanserit "laugh," to leap, and thus it signifies the "leaping animal." Prom Plautus we find that it was used by the Romans,like the names of the quail and the sparrow (passer) as a term of endearment, as in Cas. I. 50, we have "Meus pullus passer, mea eolumba, mi lepus." The Eng- lish word hare ' is from the Anglo-Saxon "barn," which we find in various languages, for instance, the Dutch, the Swedish, and old German, and in various forms. Junius suggests that the Anglo-Saxon " hcer," the "hair," is the source of the word referring to the declaration of Pliny that I the "hare is the hairiest creature of all others." Another I etymologist refers it to the Anglo-Saxon " har," hoary, or I white ; while yet another will have it from the German I " har-en," to cry out. " Quod hiberno tempore acutissime clamat," i.e., because its cry is more shrill during winter. And yet again "one of the learned" suggests that the noun " hare" is not improbably of "the same origin as the old English verb 'to hare,' and that the name was given to the animal because of its terror when harri6d or pursued by barriers." Clarendon and Locke both use the verb "to bare" in the sense of frightening. Here, then, is a pretty wide choioe in the way of etymology for " Newtonian" and others to exercise his " shakefork "or their pens upon. The hare, again, is typical of cowardico. In Bishop Hall we I -find the line,— _
To rouse thine hare's heart from her cowardice.

The saying, "As mad as a March hare," is based on the fact that in this moneb, which is their first rutting season, hares are always on the riui live, frequently moving and shifting from their forms even in the open day, Jack hares especially, which latter from their constant exercise afford in March the best runs before harriers. Some naturalists have termed the hare family Dasypoda, which in the Greek signifies "hairy-footed," the hind feet being covered with hair, which gives the animal a firmer foothold, thus aiding the enormous power of propulsion existing in the long bind legs of the animal. Mr. Manley doubts the statement about the hare being able to "run faster up hill than down." Hares, again, are credited with having the curious fancy for lying within the sound of a dog's bark.—l am, sir, &c., Nevvington, London. ANG-LO-SCOTUS.

div.head: CHURCH PATRONAGE.
div.p: CHURCH PATRONAGE.

Sir,—lf the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton were a man blessed with a little modesty, and knew how to conduct and guide his tongue 'when speaking of others, he would possibly be all the better for it. There is scarcely an occasion upon which he has spoken during the past few years that he has let the opportunity slip of throwing out vile and slanderous charges against one or other of our public men. One would think Church patronage a subject upon which he could speak without dragging either Mr. Bradlaugh's or Mr. Spurgeon's reme to the front. The rev, gentleman seems to have a dread lest the loaves and fishes get into the hands of those needing them. It will be no question with the people as to whether the Methedists or the Churchmen are the worst when the day of deliverance conies. Cheap literature has made the people fully acquainted with the abominable way in which their future salvation is made to minister to the greed and selfishness of the black dragoons in this world. Witness the recent sales in Tokenhouse-yard, the public auctions for tithe rent. The Church ministry has, I know, gentlemen who are working hard, whose lives are devoted to the one great object, viz., introducing sunshine into the workingman's life, and for these I have nothing but thanks. They, although surrounded by superstition, are labouring honestly. May their eves be opened soon, and their hands set at liberty, BO that we may see good results. Let not your readers think I strike too hard in this matter; let them rather turn to the papers issued by the various parties in the Church, and they will see that no words of mine could possibly equal that which they use towards each other.. Mr. Carleton says, "Mr. Bright at present adminis- ters a large amount of Church patronage." Mr. Carleton only displays his ignorance when he makes such a statement. When Mr. Bright did dispense Church patronage he strove to do it honestly, and gave satis- ei. faction. Mr. Carleton charges Mr. Gladstone with coquet- ting with Mr. Spurgeon, and giving public support to Mr. Bradlaugh. Mr. Gladstone Mr. Editor, is a man who has the entire respect of the Secularists. For why ?; Because they see in him a man that does not allow his Christianity to trample underfoot his humanity ; who tries to do unto ' others as he would have them do to him. Mr. Gladstone's ethics are beyond the narrow comprehension of a bigoted -- churchman. Mr. Spurgeon is a man whose spiritual teach- - ings have none of my sympathies, but I recognise in him a I ' man who scorns to make others pay for what they do not receive ; who recognises the right of free thought and free speech. As such he commands the respect not only of Mr. Gladstone, but of all honest-minded men. sir, the man who is constantly sneering at better men than liimselt mug be neglecting his own work; nay, more, he is injuring ite party to whom he belongs. I ask is there an Atheist in this town likely to be won over to Mr. Carleton's party in conse- quence of his teachings and example ? Not one. For they utterly detest his uncharitable utterances. He is a fit repre- sentative of the priestcraft so ably sketched by Wm. Howitt, —the priest system that has kept Italy back, that steeped Spain in ignorance, that encouraged royalty to trample ON the French people, and who up to to-day have thought more of their Church, more of fat livings, more of social position, than of the poor. The Church was pleased to say bard words of Charles Darwin during his life; at his deaths solemn farce was gone through. Since then the publication of his

thoughts respecting the future has upset the Church not a little. Bo it has always been. Mr. Bradlaugh to-day fight- ing for freedom of speech, for freedom of action will make it possible for an Atheist to sit 113 Prime Minister in the House of Commons in the near future. Mrs. Besant, cruelly deprived of her two children by Christian laws, adds only another item to be counted upon when the day of reckoning comes; Mr. Foote being thrust into a felon's cell almost. These are things not to be forgot by those who do not respect untruths. - H. WHITHAM. Manchester-lane, Warrington.

DR. MACKIE AND YOUNG MEN. - Sir,—l was not present at the mayoral election the other day, but I read with great interest the very fall report of the proceeiings which appeared in your paper of Saturday last. I derived most pleasure, I must admit, from the dis- covery that in Alderman Davies a man has at last arisen who has the courage to call a spade a spade, and to protest in an unmistakeable manner against the meddlesome inter- ference of one "great" man in everything connected with the town, whether it concerns him or not. If Dr. Mackie had ever shown ability as a public man in Warrington, I for one should be only too glad to acknowledge it, for really useful public men are of great value and aught to be ap- preciated. But it seems to me that wherever he appears (and what does he ever leave alone?) lie somehow manages to introduce ill-feeling, temper, and general dissatisfaction, very largely by his overbearing way of forcing his opinions, often on subjects of which lie knows little or nothing, down people's throats, whether they will or no. To such a point has this been carried of late that it is now quite a cur- rent opinion that his advocacy of any scheme, however good, is almost certain to be its ruin. I hope to goodness the Ship Canal will net be allowed to suffer in this way— but with Alderman Davies to guard its interests in War- rington, perhaps we need have no fear. Dr. Mackie is death on "cliques, coteries, and caucuses" (how dearly he loves a bit of alliteration!) but it seems to me he tries very hard to be a clique all to himself; that is, what he urges must be instantly adopted or it is " infamous ! " Now I read the letter that seemed to have cut the Doctor so to the quick. It certainly rather floors him, but I must confess I saw nothing "infamous " in it, especially when we remember that he brought it all on himself by his own wild statements. But it is useless to discuss these things, and not my intention. My principal object in addressing you is to make the strongest possible protest against one expression in Dr. Mackie's speech at the Council, which is a serious reflection—a libel—on a large class of the community. After talking of cliques, &c, he asks "Is tLat the way to grow mayors ? Is that the way to encourage young men to give over wasting their lives in brandy, wine, and billiards ?" Another report has it " brandy and water and billiards." But whichever are the words really used, I say they are perfectly unjustifiable. Sensible young men, men of high principle, who un- doubtedly form the backbone of the rising generation, do not "waste their lives in brandy, wine, and billiards." They have their occasional game in their leisure hours, I admit, and probably now and then a glass of beer, or even whisky and water, and what harm? But to say they " waste their lives "—that is, spend most of their time in this sort of thing,—is outrageous. Surely, in making use of such an extravagant expression, Dr. Mackie must have been thinking of the time, now long past, if I am not mistaken, when he himself was a total abstainer. Ido not blame him for having ceased to be a teetotaller; I am glad of it, for it shows that he can, under some aspects, at last, take a broader view of this sub- ject than formerly. But as long as he sees no harm per- sonally in a glass of wine, or even of brandy and water, it is certainly too bad to bring a wholesale charge of hopeless debauchery against others who follow his example, simply because they happen to be his- juniors by a few years. Either Dr. Mackie cannot seriously have meant what he seemed to imply, or his experience of young men has been particularly unfortunate. I doubt not, however, that if he went to his club in Academy-street now and then in the evening, he would very soon feel that he ought to retract this charge, if he did not even get a few of the budding politicians and future mayors of our good old town to teach him how to handle a cue and score off the spot.—Ycurs truly, A YOUNG MAN.
