when Queen and Court graced Westminster Hall with their presence, you may imagine that the orator displayed his shining gifts. We leave it on the best authority—that of rare Ben Jonson—that in public discourse he had few rivals. Bacon sat in the Parliaments of 1586 and 1583 without dis- tinguishing himself particularly ; but when the Queen's necessities, arising out of the Spanish quarrel, led to the summoning of her faithful Commons, he spoke effectively about the need of Law lieform. His success emboldened him to criticise the royal demand for subsidies. This seems to have been the most spirited and patriotic, but at the same time the most unfortunate of Bacon's speeches. The Queen let him know how vexed she was. The promotion of Coke to the Attorney-Generalship created a vacancy in the office of Solicitor-General, but it is needless to say that Bacon did not get it. Burghley gave hint but cold comfort, though he humbled himself most abjectly. Ah ! Could he only have made a right noble resolve henceforth to "reverence his conscience as his King," but the glittering prize seemed to grow in value as it withdrew from his grasp. He could not re- sign his hopes of winning it ; surely it might yet be his; perhaps the royal tigress might sheathe her claws and smile upon him at the bidding of a favourite. So he plied his friend Essex with argument and entreaty. The spirited young noble dared much to redeem the pledges Bacon had wrung from him. Failing to get him the appointment, he presented him with a nice estate at Twickenham. Hereupon the disappointed suitor turned to the consolations of philo- sophy, and gave to the world the incomparable "Essays" in 1597. After showing that the age was every way a pro- pitious one for such a fresh and vigorous thinker as Bacon, the lecturer said: The " Essays " struck a deep and long re- sounding note in the higher life of the time. They were only ten in number at first, and we have them in a re- vised and extended form; but they must have made their mark early. They spread the fame of their author far and wide, as a literary artist and observer of manners. The condensation of thought in these fragmentary papers on "Truth," "Friendship," "Custom," "Judicature," and sundry other topics, is conjoined with a remarkable fulness and aptitude of illustration—they are at once terse and elegant. I should say that Thomas Carlyle, that master of forcible and picturesque English, must have been an early student of Bacon's essays. There is a grave majesty about the style, which never slides into pedantry. Bacon himself spoke of these weighty and wisdom-laden chapters as nothing more than "recreations," though he says "writings of this kind would; with less pains and assiduity, perhaps yield more lustre and reputation than others I have in hand." He might have worked this vein longer and more cheaply than the deeper one, no doubt; and we must give him credit foi• a genuine love of truth and progress at this time, inasmuch as the impecuniosity which seems to have been the bane of his life, tempted him to supply the market with saleable wares. All teachers of mankind have had to face this übiquitous Satan of vulgar seed. Would that he had always got it beneath his heel! Now the veil must be lifted, alas, from one of the darkest transactions in any great man's history. Not getting a bride, and what he wanted more, a wealthy dower, he fell into the hands of his creditors, but was there- upon helped by his hitherto reluctant kinsmen, and soon after began to get a more lucrative practice. Perhaps this was his happiest time. He distinguished himself bsth in Par- , Bement and at the bar. He published Law Treatises, which' added greatly to his reputation. The Queen began to take notice of him again. But the unfortunate and erring Essex was now going down hill to his ruin. Bacon stuck to him as long as he thought there was any chance of his becoming the favourite once more—advised submission to the Queen's whims, and sought to turn that most awkward of sovereign's thoughts .about her old love into a safe and profitable chan- nel. After the release of Essex from prison, he saw that he was headstrong, and quietly left him to his fate. When the abortive insurrection had taken place, and the unhappy traitor lay in the Tower, Bacon threw himself heartily into the impeachment. Stung by the reproaches of conscience and many observers, Bacon now defended his conduct vigorously in a pamphlet, which really maligns him more than any unfriendly criticism can ever do. We must leave charges and apologies alike, and note the steady advance of Bacon to eminence during the remainder of Elizabeth's and the early part of James the First's reign. That most "high and mighty prince" was, as we all know on the irrefragable testimony of the preface to the Bible, endowed with singular virtures and wisdom. On the setting of that "bright occidental star" of v:rginity, the " sun " of Protestant pedantry rose in his strength. Bacon basked in the shining thereof. He toadied the royal wiseacre by letter; he professed his desire to " sacriice himself a burnt-offering," or holocaust to his dred Majesty's service. He had set his heart upon knight- hood, as the preliminary to State advancement. He got it by purchase, like many more in those early Jacobite days, and forthwith wedded a wealthy alderman's daughter. He would have teken a more prominent part in Raleigh's trial had his still powerful rival, Sir E. Coke, permitted him to do so. He sat in Parliament for Ipswich, and ingratiated himself with the public again by hard work and talented speeches. His Helps to the Intellectual Powers appeared about this time. But it was not till 1607 that the death of the Chief Justice led to his peoinotion to the Solicitor- Generalship, for which he had so long striven. This made his private practice more valuable, and soon brought the Attorney-Generalship to his ambitious grasp. Carr, the King's Scotch minion, had been made Earl of Somerset, and Bacon courted him assiduously. He also employed his learning and eloquence to reconcile the Commons to the arbitrary " benevolences " which the King's extravagance called for. The condemnation and torture of Peacham, the poor old Somersetshire parson, who wrote some remarks in a sermon against tyranny but never preached it, is a still blacker spot on Bacon's moral escutcheon. On the 7th March, 1617, he attained the summit of earthly greatness as he conceitted it; the Great Seal was handed to him by the King at White- hall, and my Lord Keeper verified the royal prophecy of his childish days. The year 1618 finds him Lord High Chan- cellor of England with the title of Baron Verulain—a title exchanged soon after for the more imposing one of Viscount St. Albans. Adverting to the work this great man was doing and the fame he was achieving in those high walks of philosophy he was more than all else fitted to tread, the rev, gentleman said: It is not easy to guaee the value of eritinge so various in matter and manner, of gifts so versa- tile that, to quote the scripture eulogy on Solomon, he treated of all things "from the hyssop in the wall to the cedars of Lebauon." The keynote of his philosophy was "induction," says everybody, as a matter of course. Now what is induction " ? Not the logical exercise bearing that name surely. Aristotle knew that, and often practised it; yet Bacon was an avowed foe of the Aristotlean method. It seems clear, however, that the dethronement of the great medirevel idol left the greatness of the Greek Sage un- dimmed. Bacon has not superseded him, but taken his place in a vacant niche that awaited him in the same glorious pantheon. Aristotle himself praises Socrates as the inventor of inductive enquiry, but even this stops short of the primary fact, for, as Professor Blackie observes," beth induction and deduction exist in a state of constant action and reaction in every normally developed human mind." The abuse of the dialectical powers is not confined to the schoolinen who swore by Aris- totle either; it may be witnessed any day in police courts, at boards of guardians, town council meetings, debates on Irish affairs in Parliament, and (whisper it gently) even in scientific coteries. Bacon's English treatise on "The ad- vancement of learning" was the herald of his magnum opus, and it clears the way for a survey of the various fields of know • ledge, pointing out the gaps and imperfections therein. The De Augment is Scientiarunt embodies and adds to its sub- stance, forming the first instalment of that histazaratio Magna which he never compassed in its entirety—which the fertiie brain and untiring industry of a Comte has still left a desideratum. But the Novum Organum, which forms the second part of Bacon's comprehensive plan, is the book upon which his fame secure:y reposes. This new instrument of discovery turns out to be a development and further application of the good old method of questioning nature, and making her replies the stepping stones to additional knowledge. It is the rule of that "common sense" which uncommon men and women have displayed all through the ages. Our great philosopher presses it home in every variety of phrase, and applies it to every subject. He is for testing everything in physics, as Socrates tested all characters, viz., by experi- ment. Yentnring his private cavil against Bacon's scientific claim, the4ecturer said: Open the " Sylva Sylvarutn," or the " Hietoria Vita et Mortis," and you iney find ample cause to modify your worship of the experimentalist, though You will still admire the brilliant play of fancy, the literary art and grace, the sublime audacity which have fascinated so many minds and haply turned them towards physical research. It is not simply that he retained and promulgated afresh many errors and superstitions, but that he sophisceted himself and his readers by false analogies, unwarrantable assumptions, fruitless conjectures, which respect for the scientific workers of his time would have suppressed. His conceit and thirst for fame blinded him here, as elsewhere, to right method. In concluding his sketch, Mr. Perris said : The larger treatises about which I have been lately speaking, were composed for the most part in the closing year which followed Bacon's disgrace, the quiet, and we would fain hope, re- pentant Years when the cares and ambitions of State had fallen from his burdened shoulders. He had written in one of his essays (" Great Place ") " Men in great place are thrice servants: servants of the Sovereign of State; servants of fame; and servants of business ; so as they have no freedom, neither in their persons, nor in their actions, nor in their times. It is a strange desire to seek power ad lose • liberly, or to seek power over others, and lose power over a man's self ? " Prophetic words! too exactly suitable to his own case to be a tandom reflection. He was now to be pre- cipitated into the gulf which he had dug for his enemy Coke—to have ample time to meditate on the" vanity of human greatness" about which be had discoursed with the wisdom of a modern Ecclesiastes. He has managed to get reinstated in the royal favour, or at least to make himself i almost indispensable to the arbitrary monarch and his court.' He is Viscount St. Albans, resides at York House, his early ' home • gives dinners to the judges and ambassa- dors ;' helps to bring Raleigh to the block ; works the Star Chamber machinery admirably in support of the royal prerogative, while retaining much popular repute as a prodigy of learning and brilliancy. His villa at Kew was the resort of the fashionable great; and when he was at Court he was without a rival for magnifi- cence. All went well with him—save the inner man of the heart. The crush was sudden—the ruin was irremediable as unexpected. Sir Ed. Coke had become leader of the Parlia- mentary opposition, and in that capacity he moved for a conference with the Upper House on the subject of mono- plies and grievance, coupling liith it certain allusions to.

div.head: WARRINGTON LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.
PAPER ON "FRANCIS BACON."

The opening meeting of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society was held in the Lecture-room, at the Museum, on Thursday evening; when the Rev. H. Woods Perris, of Norwich (formerly of Cairo-street Chapel, War- rington), read a paper on "Francis Bacon." The President (Mr. C. Broadbent) occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance. The Crientawe briefly introduced The LECTURER, who said: Biography is all the rage just now. "Lives of great artists," of English authors, of dis- tinguished statesmen, of all sorts and conditions not of men only but of women and children, pour forth from the Press continually. Twenty lines or so in an encyclopedia will not content the readers of this generation. Portrait galleries such as our fathers placed upon their tables, and sometimes read, are not to the modern taste. Every celebrated poet and man of letters must haie a volume all to himself—an "introduction" to the study of Dante, or Pascal, or Hume, or Byron' turns out to be a vivid portraiture, a critical esti- mate, and a gossiping guide-book to a literary shrine, com- pressed into one dainty cover. Already the bookshelves of modest Englishmen groan beneath the weight of volumes clad in red, green, and blue, each having a single name upon its front ; and the librarians must be asking themselves where this sort of thing is going to end. Soon it will be possible to talk glibly enough of the cam- paigns of Cassar without ever having construed a line of the Commentaries, and to discourse feelingly about the mocking spirit of Montaigne on the strength of a newspaper critique. In fact such possibilities have already becoine actual pheno- mena in this year of grace new current. We are threatened with a pletkora of biographical criticism which may take the edge still further from the appetite for original knowledge. The levelling tendency of publishing schemes is also to be rather dreaded. Let us hope that the wider diffusion of facts tested in the fierce light of modern criticism, and the interest awakened in many minds by this sparkling flow of narrative, wherein prismatic bubbles of quotation float so easily, may, to some extent, counteract the tendency to slipshod habits of mental acquisition, which these spicy abridgements have been known to engender. They are only a larger sort of lecture, and like the lecture, only fulfil their proper func- tion when they entice or provoke the mind to deeper re- search. Francis Bacon has been a name to conjure with any time the last 250 years. Where is one to begin the recital of his life? Every schoolboy has heard of his fame and shame. He is known far and wide as the "first of modern philosophers," whatever that may mean, —as the statesman who was also -a creative thinker; the historian who was a polite essayist, a pungent critic, an ethical teacher, and a speculative enquirer as well. His writings have been published over and over again; all kinds of studies and commentaries upon them abound; no great man has been more perseveringly written about, always excepting the dii majores like Homer, Shakespeare, and a few more. Bacon is, indeed,!one of the Titans, though not one of the Gods. As such he has been, and will ever be, a figure of commanding genius and pro- portions. I find that the list of his works in their several editions—beginning with the "Essaies and religious medi- tations' published by Windet, of London, in 1597, and including successive reprints and biographies, fills nearly five pages in Lowndes' Bibliographer's Manual (BAn'e version). As for his literary admirers and detractors, their name is legion. Mr. Basil Montague brought out his colossal work-17 vols. of Bacon literature and commentary —between 1825 and 1835. Straightway Macaulay over- hailed it in the "Edinburgh." That brilliant criticism gave a mortal blow to the idolatry which had been with many the substitute for an intelligent appreciation sof Bacoa's philosophical merit. Mr. Spedding and Mr. Hep- worth Dixon have tried hard to get the verdict reversed, but no special pleading can alter or conceal the realistic portrait which Macaulay drew in colours that have something of the Titian fadelessness about them. In strong and nervous prose, as in undying stanzas, the character of this English Balaam, who saw truth so clearly, and sounded the depths of baseness se fully, stands discovered to all the reading world. As well talk of rehabilitating the character of Judas,!as of persuading the nineteenth century mind that Bacon was "indifferent honest" when justice could bring a good price in the market. Who would not wish, if so it might righteously be, that the Laureate's estimate of the philosopher might suffice' and Pope's dictum concerning the man be for- gotten? Alas! they jointly describe Bacon as he was amongst his contemporaries, as he is for evermore in our thought, an archangel ruined but still sublime. We see him him ideally and intellectually the peer of the noblest that ever Greece could boaet— .' Ana through the topmost oriel's coloured flame, Two god-ilke faces gazed below. Nato the wise, and la,-go browed Verulam, The first of those who know " We alga see him the venal courtier, the over-clever architect of his transient earthly greatness, the treacherous ally whose friendship was a curse to those who trusted in it— in one pregnant sentence, Francis Bacon, baron and vis- count, was

"The wisest, brightest, meanest of mankind." The materials for a brief study of this man's life and contri- bution to human thought are, as I have already hinted, of the amplest kind. In addition to those just mentioned I have open before me the admirable chapters of G. H. Lewes in the Biographical History of Philosophy, the more recent and detailed sketch in Campbell's "Lives of the Chancellors," and the excellent discourse of Henry Hallam in the "In- troduction to European Literature," not to mention sundry other authors who had found Bacon and his times a con- genial theme. Where the ground has been so thoroughly surveyed, and has become so familiar to every student, originality is unattainable. I shall be happy if I can deepen your interest in so instructive a career, and in works of such unperishable value and significance in the onward movement of the human mind. Francis Bacon was the son of Sir Nicholas Bacon, one of the sturdy school of Tudor statesmen who very happily combined (as Macaulay has pointed out) the practical knowledge of affairs with the habits of study which they brought with them from Cam- ' bridge, and practised in manor-houses and city mansions during that post-feudal period of intellectual vivacity and national tranquility. He seems to have been a worthy soul, who rose by sheer merit from the inferior courts to the wool- sack, being knighted in the early days of Elizabeth's reign, ' and getting the seals with the title of Lord Keeper, 1558. The virgin queen evidently set some store by his counsel in certain weighty matters of royal title. He was a very big man, described by Camden as a man "of gross body but subtle wit; of high eloquence, retentive memory, and sound judgment." According to his famous son's account, Old Sir Nicholas was "a plain man, direct and constant, with- out any finesse or doubleness,"—surely an exAmple that were well worth following in those days of courtly intrigue. Sir Nicholas was twice wedded; the second time to the daughter of an old tuter of King Edward VI. Sir Anthony Cooke. Francis was the second eon, and was born at York House, in the Strand, on the 22nd January, 1561. He was of the less robust order, and spent more time at home with his mother than abroad. The lady Anne was clearly a woman of sound judgment and quite exceptional attiinments. She translate Ochino's sermons on" Fate and free will "from the Italian.; did a like service for Bishop Jewel, whose " Apology " was said by Archbishop Parker to have been rendered out of the Latin original into English quite perfectly, and regularly exchanged epistles with the worthy author on points of Greek Testament criticism. So you see the grapes of philosophy did not grow on thorns, nor the figs of science on thistles. The child early developed the seeds of thought which were planted in his nature from the first, and assiduously tended from day to day. We hear of very early indications that the sickly boy was destined to cut a remarkable figure in the Intellectual world. His curiosity was unappeasable. Other boys were puzzled and amused by some clever "card tricks" which were played off by an amateur juggler; he never rested till he found out the law. An echo in St. James's fields drew him away from merry companions, and set him upon the quest for its cause. Of course he had fine opportunities for conversing with learned and travelled men, and he used them to the utmost. Grave in demeanour, but both wise and witty in speech, he soon drew the Queen's gaze upon him—too soon, perhaps, for his last- ing peace. The favour of raneen Bess was apt to scorch those upon whom it lighted. Asked" how old he wee." he replied, "Exactly two years younger than your Majesty's happy reign." No wonder Elizabeth patted her precocious courtier on the head, and styled him her "little Lord Keeper." After a brief reference to Bacon's academic career, the lecturer said: He turned his back on Cambridge and its paper distinctions with a sigh of relief. Three years spent in France gave scope and depth to his thinking. He passed from province to province, mingled with various grades of intelligence, from ambassadors to peasants. He took his first literary flight in a volume of "Notes on the state of Europe," learnt to write in cipher, and dreamed of diplo- matic fame. His father's death brought him to London again in March, 1579, and theslender estate he found himself possessed of—less in proportion than that which his four brothers had, owing to an unfortunate delay on his father's part to execute a deed in his behalf—forced him to sue for the courtly interest of Burgh] ev,Elizabeth's trusted Minister. Burghley had a pet son, Robert Cecil by name, whose ad- vancement was threatened by Bacon's superior ability, and the statesman, alas! quelled the whispers of chivalry and kindly feeling which, if heard and honoured, m;ght have made later and graver sins unnecessary. Thus do we pro- ject the giant shadows of our lower selves into the future which will mould the lives of those who shall come after- wards—making a moral tradition which shall trail ors like a , hereditary disease, subtracting from the sum total of human happiness for many a day. Bacon suffered in mind and in fortune from the "ancient prejudice industriously propaga- ted by dunces" arid selfish monopolists all the world over —(I quote Home's pungent words)—" that a man of genius is unfit for business." He was driven to Gray's Inn to qualify for legal practice, which to a mind of his order could only be drudgery. However, he applied himself to the study of jurisprudence in the widest sense, and soon became a master of the common law of England. In 1586 he was called to the outer bar, and in due time became a Bencher. As Lent Reader he had an opportunity to air his learning and eloquence, and was appointed "counsel extraordinary" for State prosecutions. It was an honorary post, unfortunately. Stray briefs and trifling fees making his heart sadly sick with hope deferred, be tried again to melt Burghley's obdurate heart. His appeal resulted in the promise of a reversionary registrarship, which was worth £1,600 per annum, but as the occupant declined to make decease and so vacate for Bacon's benefit, he had the morti- fication of waiting 20 years for the place. Meanwhile, when any cause celebre called forth his powers, and especially

the abuses for the legal courts, sanctioned and upheld by, the Lord Chancellor. The ship of State was in the breakers evidently, the fickle winds had begun to blow from the wrong quarter, and with ie vengeance too. The captain and steersman, that is to say James and Buckingham, soon came to the conclusion that Bacon was the Jonah who had brought this danger upon them. They stood not upon the order of their high procedure, but flung him over at once. In a short three days the public expose, of the Lord High Chancellor's corruption began. Twenty-seven different charges of bribery were established against him. The Great Seal for which he had so longed, toiled, and sinned, was taken from him. He was fined £40,000, imprisoned in the Tower, and though shortly allowed to retire to Gorliambury, could only describe himself as "old, weak, ruined, in want, and a very subject of pity." His fall was great and moving, as his rise had been the admiration of men. Bacon did hope again, and by-and-by he recovered a certain amount of the wealth and digniey he 'had lost. But the man was crushed—only the ingenious literary artist, and the graceful propounder of hard sen- tences remained. He lived on into Charles's reign—dying (as the elder Pliny did) from the effects of exposure while experimenting. He walked out to Highgate one wintry day, bought a recently-killed fowl, and stuffed it with snow, to see whether it could be preserved in that way from putre- faction. He chilled himself, and took, refuge in the house of the Earl of Arindel, where he parted from the world on Easter Sundiy, April 9th, 1626, in his 66th year. No hand of gentle affection smoothed his careworn forehead, his wife "for just and great causes" having been banished his house and deprived -of the reversion of his Kigali estate. His own verdict on his life but a little while before had been, " The talent which God has given me I have mis-spent in things for which I was least fit;" and again to Sir Thomas Bodley he freely acknowledges his many errors, "and this great one that led all the rest, that knowing myself by inward calling to be fitter to hold a book than play a part I have led my life in civil causes, for which I was not very fit by nature, and more unfit by pre-occuna- tion of mind." It is not for us to condemn him harshly, but to read in his history the blame of our own unfaithful- ness to the ideals we have got glimpses of in our nobler hours. As we think of the prodigious capacity, the flowing wit and wisdom, the encyclopedic fulness and the eloquent discourse of this famous man—of the phenomenal influence he has exerted, the splendid place accorded him in the popular fancy, the stimulus which he has unquestionably given (when allowance has been made for all drawbacks and inconsistencies) to inductive reasoning and research, we can only breathe softly, and wonder at the old, old mystery of man, the crowned king of this unintelligible world. 'What a piece of work! Ho ,r infinite in faculty! What a mixture of divinity and devilry ! The glory and shame of tine!
A brief discussion followed, and the proceedings con- cluded with the usual compliment to the lecturer and chairman.

div.head: LIBERAL MEE I'ING AT LYNN. MR. G. W. LATHAM ON THE CLOSURE.
div.p: LIBERAL MEE I'ING AT LYNN. MR. G. W. LATHAM ON THE CLOSURE.

A well-attended meeting of Liberals was held in the Assembly Room, at the Plough Hotel, Lymm, on Monday evening. Mr. G. W. Latham occupied the chair, and was supported by Professor Hopkinson, barrister-at-law, Messrs. W. Long, D. Boyd, A. E. Paterson, and others. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the meeting, said as a rule he hoped that he very strictly abided by the great principle that a chairman's duty was to listen and not t • speak, that he ought merely to regulate a meeting and keep order; and if he was, as the Speaker of the House of Commons must sometimes be, considerably bared by thc.se who talked— I (laughter)—he ought to remember that he would have his revenge some day, and the privilege of boring people in return. But on this occasion he was not only told that he might talk, but be was also told that he must talk, and al- though talk was against his grain—for he quite agreed with Carlyle, that speech was silvern but silence was golden— he supposed he must obey orders. He would say a few words to them before Professor Hopkinson made a longer speech—(hear, hear); but he hoped when Professor Hopkinson had spoken that would not be the end of it all. They particularly wanted all through Mid-Cheshire to clear up difficulties and to'give enlightenment, and they proposed that they should, by questions and by arguments, some- what help in settling a quantity of very difficult questions that were now arising in the political world. (Hear, hear.) He thought that perhaps one of the most difficult questions at the present moment to understand was why the Conser- vatives opposed the Closure, and it was worth their while to consider that question, because a great deal, it seemed to him, of their future conduct depended upon it. As a matter of fact, he did not think country gentlemen, as a rule, liked long long speeches. He thought, as a rule, Conservative principles rather tended to the stoppage of talk than to its promotion. (Hear, hear.) He thought, too, they found that, as far as freedom of debate went, the Liberal party had ever been the more anxious to allow debate and freedom of speech than the Conservative party had been; and yet, cer- tainly on this Occasion, with the exception of that arch- democrat, Mr. Cowen, who seemed to him hardly to know what he spoke about, and to answer arguments that had neverdeeen advanced, the Liberal party had been in favour of opening the floodgates of speech. (Hear, hear.) Now, he took it the first was this: that the Conservative party would be very willing to close debate only, as a condition precedent, Mr. Gladstone must not be Prime Minister when that was done. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) They believed that Mr. Gladstone was the arrow head; they believed that he had the whole vigour and power of the Ministry; and they were afraid that when this power of closing debate was obtained; the measures which Mr. Gladstone would bring fortyaid would be dangerous, as they believed, to the safety of the country. For his part, he believed that the very contrary was the case. (Hear, hear.) His belief was that Mr. Gladstone, first of all, was, excepting in matters where he saw a grave injustice, a most arrant Conservative; and, secondly, that if Mr. Glad- , stone was not Prime Minister the Liberal party would not be satisfied without very much stronger Liberal measures then they would be s ttisEed with if Mr. Glad- stone produced them. Mr. Gladstone was in his opinion, as it were the Conservative wheel in the Ministry that pre- vented the Ministry going at a very great pace of reform, for if my Lord Hartington were Premier the Liberals who. were real Liberals would put pressure upon him, because they would say that a man of rather Whig tendencies, and of a Whig family must have pressure put upon him to make him go fast enough; and if Mr. Chamberlain were Prime Minister they would not be satisfied unless he carried out all the promises of his previous life, and gave them thoroughly democratic measures. But in Mr. Gladstone's case thty had all such thorough trust in hime althsough a measure might have somewhat of a Conservative taint he it, yet he thought the Liberal party would be perfectly satisfied with it. Therefore, he believed that the first reason why Conserva- tives, in his opinion, opposed the Closure was a perfectly mistaken reason. He thought the second reason Conserva- tives opposed the Closure was this : that they had got to such a pitch obreform that now they see that all legislation that could-be promoted in Parliament mast hit them hard in the matter of privilege. (Applause.) It was privilege that the Conservative party ratted upon—(applause)—the privilege of a hereditary House of Lords to legislate. the privilege of an Established Church to set up our religion, the privilege of country gentlemen not elected by the people to spend the money of the ratepeyers—(applause)— and so on through a mass of other matters ia an attack upon which they see an attack upon their own privileges as a class, and they could see no legislation that did not bear upon themselves He believed himself that they had a very just opinion of what would be the legislation of the future; and in that seemed to him to be the weakness of that article that had appeared in the last moath's Fortnightly 4 and which had excited considerable attention, written by two Conservatives, in which they said Sir Stafford Northcote's management of the party and Lord Salisbury's management of the party was defective because they did not appeal to the people as a people on popular grounds to resist the advances of Liberalism. All he could say was this, that if any Conservative appealed to the people on popular grounds and proposed popular ineasures, he would :not find 20 men on the Conservative benches to believe with him. (Applause.) If they remembered, Lord Beaconsfield's game was as far as they ever could make out, to establish a despotism, that was, that the despots were to be elected by the people, and then were to rule without consulting the people again. But he found that that was no good, and consequently his plan was to rule England pretty neatly as he liked while he fascinated the public mind with a tremendous lot of fireworks let off all about foreign countries—(hear, hear)— and in that he was fairly successful until he was found out, and he was perfectly satisfied that no second men could ever play the same game that Lord Beacons- field played at that time. The Conservative workingman might have existed ; but fortunately Board Schools exist too ' —(applause), and as people got educated, as people got sober, as people got enlightened, they wauld hear very much less of Conservative workingmen and workingmen's poli- tics. (Applause.) Well, he took it that at all events, in the course of the next week or two the Governihent would have the power of bringing in bills with a hope of seeing them passed in a reasonable time. Mr. Lebouchere made the other night what perhaps might be called a brutal speech, in the sense of brutal that it had a great deal of uureason- ing force in it, but at the same time a speech in which he could not help thinking there was a considerable amount of force. He said, "What on earth is the good of making speeches in the House of Commons? The time is coming when all these matters will have to be settled by the votes of the people outside the House, and all we shall have to do in the House of Commons will be to pass bills accoraing to the votes of the people." (Applause.) He (Mr, Latham) believed that to be perfectly true of general principles. He believed that education, the circulation of newspapers, and the advancement of the enlightenment of the people would make the electors understand politics just as well as the elected, and consequently that the mem- bers of Parliament would rather have to fashion the will of the people in the statutes than to decide among themselves what was the very beet thing to do. He believed, too, that the formation of these grand committees, when it was carried, would be a very great help in that way, because having got first principles it seemed to him utterly absurd for a contentious assembly to set to work to haggle over clauses, the result of which was that judges had to decide what words, which had been quarrelled over, and settled by the contentious parties, meant. If he wanted an instance of that, he thought he could not give them a better one than the difficulties there were now to ascertain what a hanging-gale meant. Of the two parties in the House of Commons, one wished to give as much as they could to the itiah tenant, and the other to take it say; and so they

left the words in such an uncertain manner that they had to go to the Irish court to decide what the quarrels of these people might happen to mean. He believed it after the will of the people had been pretty plainly expressed, and after these first principles had been carried in the House of Commons a measure was then sent to the grand committee, who should be answerable for carrying out the resolutions of the Hoese of Commons, we then might hope to see in our statute book some Acts that would not puzzle every lawyer that came to examine them. Hehoped, the Closure now having come intt. operation, they might see some Liberal legislation, and the first resolution that he wanted to see—because he believed it to be most important in this country—was some resolution as between landlord and tenant. Lymm was a centre, a great agricultural centre. He thought he hth spoken there before on the broad topic of legislation as between landlord and tenant, but there was one point which he specially wanted to impress upon them as one which required speedy legislation. An Act was passed last session, brought in by the late Lord Chancellor, Lord Cairns, and supported by the present Chancellor, Lord Sel borne, which was described the other day by Mr. George Hastings, president of the Local Science Congress, as effecting a revolution. He could not imagine the feelings of either of those noble lords, if anybody was to tell them in sober earnest that they had been guilty of effecting a revolution. The most either of those lords would wish would be a mild reform, and the milder the reform the better it would please both Liberals and Conservatives. There was no doubt they did not effect a revolution, because it die not alter the law of entail in the slightest degree. But it did do this : it gave very large facilities for owners of entailed estates to dispose of these estates and invest the money ire other ways; and he believed it was probable, as soon as this Act came into operation, encumbered oWners—they under- stood what he meant, owners of property with heavy mort- gages upon them—would in a great many instances sell a part of their estate in order to pay the encumbrances of the other parts. Now the danger was that the landlord would not only sell what was his own, but being needy he would be under a horrible temptation to sell what belonged to his telant—(applause)—and consequently, unlessthey got some Act passed by which, at all events, unexhausted improve- ments were preserved to them,they would see more instances of injustice done in the next few months than had been done in a long aeries of years before. A man, for instance, wanted to get his estate clear. He wanted to get hie estate clear by the sacrifice of as few acres as he possibly could. The tenant had laid out a certain sum of money in the cultivation of that land, in the manuring of that land, and in the draining of that lend. He had no claiise in his agreement by which he could claim for improvements. The land was sold to the pur- chaser without:a word being said. The purchaser, of course, when he had bought, wanted to get as good interest on his money as he could, and he raised the rent for the man's own improvements. Now don't think that was uncommon, because the best landlords, many of whom they would con- sider the last to do suck things, were guilty of it. The other day the Crown bought a very large estate in the county of Bedfordshire. They bought the estate as Govern- ment servants, and the Woods and Forests Department felt it their duty to get the best interest on the outlay they could. They raised the rents over all that estate and broke the hearts of the tenants. Mr. Howard asked several ques- tions about it in Parliament during the last session, and he told hien the other day in. one case, shocking as it was to say, the tenant was so utterly heartbroken by this unfair raising of his, rent that he committed suicide. Of course all men could understand when a land- lord sold a farm, the purchaser knew nothing of who made those improvements, and he thought himself jus- tified in getting what he considered a fair rent. But if we had a proper law, so that every farthing a man spent he should certainly be paid back, such things could not legally happen, and the sooner we got that law the safer the tenant farmers would be. But it was not 'the tenant farmers' question only. It was a question for the consumers as well. It was their interest and his that the land should be made to produce as much as- it could, that there should be as much milk upon it, as much produce at all events grown on it of that sort which could not cone from, foreign eountries. Therefore the carrying of such a Bill was as necessary to the :consumer as it was to the producer. (Hear, hear.) He believed that up to this' time, taking them as a whole, the landlords had acted fairly to their tenants. It they had not done so, the laws under which they could have acted were so utterly iniquitous that they must have pressed hard, and the land laws must have been swept away long ago. There was hardly any iniquity in the world that our present land laws would not countenance, only- the landlords had, been wise and not put those iniquities into force. lie trusted the moment they had got their way clear to do it, the first measure Mr. Gladstone would bring in would be a bill to regulate the tenure of land, and a bill also to regulate the local government of the counties. (Applause.) The two things, ran very much together. If they got the farmers' property secure they would put him in such a posi- tion that he must be independent and able to speak his own mind, and not be the tool or sycophant of his landlord ; and therefore he would be able to take a fair and good part in county government. At present, from his observation, county government, as far as regarded the quarter sessione,quarterly business, was absolutely in the hands of the landlords— (hear, hear)--ae far as regarded the poor-law business and highway business, it was nominally in the hands of the tenant farmers, but practically in the hands of the landlords, who dictated to them what they should do. They wanted the tenant farmer made not only secure but independent, and they wanted hiiri to learn how to govern, and he could only learn how to govern properly by feeling perfectly safe, and that no man could injure him. (Applause.) They might depend upon it that the best way to elevate the third class, that was the labourer, was to lift up the farmer, and the labourer would rise, as it were, in the vacuum to take his place—(applause); and so they would have the three classes —landlord, farmer, and agricultural labourer—each in his right place. At present the squire, as they called him, the owner of the land, seemed to him to occupy the place of the two first classes; and by his weight, and by his undue pre- ponderance, he was able to trample on the third of these classes. Give but the tenant farmer a stand between the two, give him the opportunity to move, and ills very elas- ticity would prevent the landowner trampling upon him, and would give room to the labourer to rise a step higher in society. (Applause.) As they all knew, in the future the agricultural labourer was to have a vote—(hear, hear,)—and as it was their duty to try, before he had that vote, to put him in a position to exercise it rightly, the sooner they could elevate him in society the better it would be for the peace of the country. (Applause.) He would say one word of advice- to the landowners. If he might, it would Be wise in time, and settle your matters about your land with your tenant as quickly as you can, for fear something worse shall come." There were to his mind symptoms that if this question were postponed the people might take it into their heads that very much larger measures were necessary than they would now be content with. There was a book just published in a cheap form, " Progress and Poverty," by Mr. Henry George, of which he understood some 32,000 copies had been circulated at 6d each among the people, and the teachings of which, should they ba adopted by our future Legislature, might hit the landlords very hard. He was not going to say whether he agreed with that book or whether he did not. It was written with marvellous power, and perhaps it offended somewhat against the political economy at present in vogue; but he could not help thinking it would be a wonderfully attractive book to the uneducated mass of readers, and that the proposition that land belonged to the people and was for the people's use instead of being the private property of a few individuals, would be a doctrine that, until our electors were very highly educated, might be seized upon at any moment. Therefore, would it not be wise for the landowners of this country at all events to satisfy those who held their land, and to get them on their side in a possible struggle than to have them joining with those who agreed with the doctrines of Mr. Homy George ? (Ap- plause.) His belief was it was the wisest and safest policy of tha landowners at once to settle those burning questions, ' and so be able to present a broad front to the cerniug culties. Of course, if those propositions were true, if they stood the comments of philosophers, and the praotical work- ing of time, it might be that after all those propositions might be carried into effect ; but at all events, in their care the landowners of England would feel that they had only yielded to common sense and justice, and that they had not precipitated their fall by obstinacy and folly of their own. (Loud applause.) Mr. RICITLRD Selene then rose and asked if discussion would be permitted, and the Chairman replied in the affirmative.

Professor HorKiNsort, who was cordially received, sub- mitted a few reasons why he was induced to attach himself to the Liberal party, and contrasted the general policy with that of the Conservatives. In the first place he considered that a Liberal Government's administration of the nation's affairs at home and abroad was better than that of the Con- servatives. On thie point he held up to special commendation the present Government's action in reference to Egypt, remarking that lb had thereby prevented the outbreak of pos4bly a great IVlahometan rising in the East, secured the highway to India, and raised the prestige of England in Europe to a height which it had never attained since the year 1816. -lin the second place, the Liberal party, in his opinion, were much stronger in matters of finance than their opponents. In the third place, he argued that the, Liberal party had in the past promoted the best legislation and promised to do so in the future. With regard to future legislation, he urged the desirableness of simplifying the law relating to the transfer of land, the codification of laws, the reform of the criminal law, and the passing of a good Bankruptcy Act. Mr.. RICHARD SMITH then came forward and spoke at length from a Conservative point of view. As examples of beneficent legislation passed by a Conservative Government, he instanced the Prisons' Act and the Artisans' Dwellings Act. The former had done much for the economical manage- ment of prisons, and the latter had given comfortable and happy homes to thousands in London, Birmingham, and Glasgow.

On the motion of Mr. SWANWICK, seconded by Mr. BOYD, the following resolution was passed :—"That this meeting having observed the progress made so far in the passing of the resolution as to the procedure of the House of Com- mons, trusts that there is now a sure prospect that the measures promised at the last general election, and hitherto delayed by unscrupulous and systematic obstruction, will be brought forward and passed into law before the dissolu, tion of the present Parliament."

Mr, K B.REWTN&LL, in moving a vote of thanks to Pro- fessor Hopkinson, said the Prisons' Act, instead of promoting oconomy had done tho very reverse, and the Artisans' Pwalliogs Act, though tt had caused hundreds of houses to

be pulled down, had not came any to be-built, but hs placed the working classes in several large cities in a worse position than they were before. Mr. SMITH seconded the motion, which was PPorted bY Mr. BICBLEY, and carried with acciamation.

This too was There would always be work for the Sunday school teacher; the "one thing needful," if the religious life in the indivi- there would always be plenty of children outside the pale of dual soul was to be full and flourishing, and its experience the church, rich and deep. The faith which not only believed, but Singing and prayer followed. could tell what it believed—this was what brought not only intellectual stability, but the profoundest calm of peace, the most ecstatic joys and the richest growth of all the graces in the individual heart. In one word, if the Church at large was to realise all that her divine Head and Lord had designed for her of power and peace and saving usefulness —if she was to receive such a revival as they all implored that day, there must been her part, amongst other requisites, a revival 9f intelligence, irgnisitive, and eager pursuit of truth, and a more assiduous cultivation and consecration of the intellectual powers on the part of every member. Might they not name as a second defeat in the Christian lila of the day a serious and palpable lowness of spiritual tone? The church was probably never so wealthy as now in members of pure morality, high honour and outwardly consistent life, but still there was great rea- son to fear that the general tone of the Church's piety as distinguished from morality was decidedly low—that Chris- tian men were as a whole less devout, less spiritually minded, less given to prayer and meditation, less devo- tional in the general tenour of their life and speech, more worldly and given to amusements, less redolent of the savour of Godliness, and less ready to converse one with another on the blessed experiences of the divine life with- in them, than the early Methodists. What else was meant by the impatience and neglect of the class meetings that had sprung up in recent years? It was not uncharitable to say that it meant a lower experience and an emasculated spiritual life. Speaking of the expressed fear that Methodism would dwindle into a *thing of schedules, committees, s:atistics, and sub-committees lists, and so lose her higher mission, Mr. Mees said they need not fear, for the higher the life the more perfect the organisation; and that smaller the amount of organisation, the lower the order of life. What the Church required to keep up amidst her manifold machinery, a high degree of spiritual efficiency, was a deep penetrating all persuasive Godliness in the breast of- every member. Bat it Metbodism came to rely on her machinery as a substitute for spiritual power, and was not supremely careful that the one should be informed and dominated by the other, then, indeed, they might confidently predict her downfall ; her glory would depart, and her candlestick be removed from its place. Piety, deep ea/ritual and intense, was the Church's great want in the present day. The only other defect in present day Chris- tianity, which they ventured to mention, was the too common failure of religious professors to engage in direct personal service in the cause of Christ. Referring, under this head, to the neglect of attendance at public worship in the largest towns, as shown by the statistics published a short time age, Mr. Mees said on the testimony of Mr. liolyoake himself infidelity had not spread as extensively as they were prone to think. "The masses were found neither listening to secular lectures nor reading scientific books; they were found lounging in our streets, swarming in our gin palaces. The curse of the lower orders is not in- fidelity, but ungodliness." It was not so much the advance of scepticism as the neglect of private Christians which accounted for the prevalent neglect of public worship. The masses were not won because Christian people did not suffi- ciently go after them. The ministry, however devoted and untiring, could never alone overtake the needs of the population. But when the entire Church betook itself to the work of saeking the lost, and showed them that they thought them worth caring for, they would not fail to be found. Sunken and debased as many of them were, they would yet respond to sympathy. What they all needed was spontaneousAvork—intense conviction of duty—ardent love to God, and yearning pity for souls ; not cut and dried carry- ing out of formal routine because it was appointed and must be done ; but free, glad-loving service for' God and ,their brethren. And when this ideal became the actual, they might confidently rest assured that the "time to favour Zion ; yea the set time is come." May God speed the day ! At the conclusion of the meeting a free tea party was held in Brunswick school. Mr. John Simpson was the donor. There were many people present. Subsequently a meeting was held in St. Paul's Chapel, which conta. mineed es,amleassrgres audience. The Rev. George Hock presided, and amongst those present were the Revs. E. J. Robinson, s John Simpson, T. Norman, R. Norman, B. Kniveton, T. Bimister, Spearing. Mr. George S. Hazlehurst presided at the harmonium. div.head: MR- PIERPOINT'S CONCERT AT RUNCORN,
div.p: MR- PIERPOINT'S CONCERT AT RUNCORN,

Mr. Bantock Pierpeint's third annual concert took place in Runcorn Public Hall on Monday evening. From every point of view it was a great success, and fully sustained the reputation Mr. Pierpoint has gained as a caterer for the musical tastes of the public. The dress circle was completely filled, and the other parts of the ball were scarcely less crowded. The artistes were—Vocalists: Miss Clara Samuell, Miss Emilie Lloyd (by special desire), Mr. George Barton, Mr. Bantock Pierpoint ; violin solo: Mr. Frank Arnold (who is a Professor of the Royal Academy of Music). Mr. NV. I Argent performed the duties of accompanist. The following is the programme :

Miss Lk yd, Mr. Barton, Mr. Pierpoint It would be tedious and unprofitable to particularise each song; suffice it to say that we have nothing but praise for the manner in which each artiste acquitted him or herself, and so demonstrative were the audience in expressing their approval, that Mr. Argent, in fear that the performance would be inordinately prolonged, requested the audience not to encore during the first part of the programme. They acceded to the request, but during the second part of the concert each performance was loudly encored. If we may institute a comparison Miss Clara Samuell perhaps carried away the palm of the evening. To a cultivated soprano voice of great power and expression, she adds a manner which at once favourably impressed the audience, and she was most successful in each song. Her interpretation of that ever-popular song " She wore a wreath of roses," which is so seldom heard at pubic concerts, was very fine and she was enthusiastically recalled. Of Miss Emilie Lloyd we can scarcely speak in less terms of praise. Her mellow con- tralto voice was heard to great advantage in the songs she had chosen, especially in the gavotte from the opera Mignon," and" On the banks of Allan water." She was several times encored. Miss Samuel' and Miss Lloyd sang, 'in conjunction, a number of duets with grand effect, the " Venetian boat song "being especially pleasing. Mr. Geo. Barton is so well known to Runcorn audiences that hia reception was well assured. He was in good voice, and in the second part of the programme sang, "Draw the sword, Scotland." His rendering of the soul-inspiring song was impressive and effective without being, if the term is allowed, "showy," and in response to a most hearty encore he gave in an equally felicitous manner, "Remember me." 't The hidden land," a new song given for the first time, was sung by Mr. Pierpoint. Its reception by the audience was certainly not very flattering, although Mr. Pierpoint rendered Lt with considerable taste and feeling. He was most successful in the song, "Simon the cellarer," for his rendition of which he was encored, and favoured the company with an admir- able interpretation of " Tke midship-mite," a song for which his voice is well suited. We must not forget to mention I /11c. Frank Arnold's performances on the violin, which I showed that that gentleman had a wonderful command over his instrument. They were indeed one of the chief feature 3 of the evening; and the audience accorded to him a warm reception.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOTEMBER 18, 1881
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOTEMBER 18, 1881
WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The usual monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Board-room, Alforde Chambers, Market-square, Widnes, on Taesday afternoon, when there were present Messrs. Carey (in the chair), Kershaw, Sadler, Shuttleworth, Webster, Johnson, Manley, Midwood, Wright, Handley, Pankhurst, Foster, Dr. Booth, and Mr. Allen (clerk).

div.head: -THB ATTDITOR'S REPORT.
div.p: -THB ATTDITOR'S REPORT.

The Auditor's (Mr. Ilaslehurst) report was read as fol- lows: "In pursuance of the provisions of the Public Health Act, 1865, I have to report that I have completed the audit of the accounts of your Board for the year ended at Lady Day last. I have felt it my duty to disallow certain pay- ments charged in the accounts, amounting in the whole to £236 173 101, particulars of which I have entered in your ledger, and I have also stated my reascns for making the disallowance. I have also had to disallow the sum of £338 18s 2d charged in your treasurer's account without sufficient authority. This latter amount, although charged in the accounts of your Board as the salary of the treasurer, is, in fact, a.charge for interest on the overdrawn accounts of the Board with Parr's Banking Co. After making allowance for

loans paid off, and not re-borrowed, out of the 'current accounts, the net amount of overdraft appear to be £5,471 or thereabouts. This, as the Board must be aware, is a very serious state of things, and I would strongly urge upon the Board the necessity of taking the question into considera- tion, with a view of placing their finances on a more satis- factory basis. I have had a long conversation with your clerk respecting several sums appearing as assets in your balance sheet, but which ought to be charged to the general district rate, and profit and loss accounts respectively, inas- much as in some instances the amount expended has been in excess of the borrowing powers of the Boaid, and in others no powers have been acquired. and he has undertaken to amend the accounts in the current financial year. Several minor alterations in the forms of accounts, and the method of keeping the same, have been suggested to your clerk in order to comply more strictly with the accounts order of the Local Government Beard, and I have every reason to believe they will be carried into effect in the future."—Mr. WEBSTER asked if they had managed to make a payment over receipts of £ls,ooo.—The CLERK said that the sum of £14,000 had been renewed as a mortgage. They had s mply been carrying out the instructions of the Local Government Board in making out the returns as they had done.—Mr. HANDLEY said that at the end of the financial year, termina- ting in March last, over £40,000 of leans were falling daa, and these had either to be renewed or the sums borrowed elsewhere. On the 23th of March some of these loans were not renewed, but in a day or two after fresh loans were obtained, which made up the excess of expenditure shown on the statement. The CHAIRMAN (to Mr. Webster) : Do you understand that, Mr. Webster.—Mr. WEBSTER : No, I do not under- stand how we can be that amount in arrears.—The CHAIR- MAN said the money was not in the arrears, although it looked as if the money had been spent, but in the ordinary course of book-keeping it ought to have been placed on the other side.—Mr. WEBSTER : That is not satisfactory to the town.—Mr. HANDLBY asked if it were likely the Board would pay .£35,900 in one year. It was easily explainable —on the 25th March over £4,000 of loans were falling due, and the clerk had either to renew these loans or raise money elsewhere. The money did not all come in on the 25th March, some came in on the 27th.—The matter then dropped, and the auditor's return was referred to the Finance Committtee.

div.head: COMPLAINT.
div.p: A COMPLAINT.

Mr. Perexnunsr moved, and Mr. HANDLEY seconded a motion for the confirmation of the gas and water commit- tee's minutes.—Mr. MIDWOOD said he had a complaint to make against that committee, and wanted to know from the Chairman when would be his right time to bring it forward, as it was nothing which appeared in the minutes.—The CHAIRMAN thought it was the custom to discuss anything with regard to any particular department when the work of that department was before the Board. Was it an important subject ?—Mr. MIDWOOD : It is a very important subject. —The CHAIRMAN: I don't know whether the Chairman of the Gas and Water Committee will be ready to discuss it on the spur of the moment.—Mr. KERSHAW (to Mr. Mid- wood) : You had better name a day.—Mr. MIDWOOD : I will nante a day if the Board will decide to consider it.— The CHAIRMAN said that if Mr. Midwood would say what the subject was, then the Board would Ix in a position to say whether they could go into the question then or not.— Mr. MIDWOOD said what he referred to had regard to a cer- tain action which the Gas and Water Committee had taken upon themselves to do in last September. If that action was altos; ed to go on it would affect the whole of the property owners in Widnes very seriously indeed. What be wanted to know was whether or not was it legal for the committee to do what they had done, and, under the circumstances, would they allow him to go into the matter.—The Cnaitt- MAN : I think it would be better to go into it at once.—Mr. Mu:moon then said that he had built some houses in Win- dermere-street some time early in January or February, and these houses were connected with the mains of that Board. Everything was satisfactory, no complaints were made, and the water supply went on until about September, when the Gas Committee, for some reason which he knew nothing about, thought fit to send their men to take the whole of his drains up and put fresh ones down, charging him with the , expenses, which were just over £6. He wanted to know whether the committee had the legal right to go and do that; if they had it was worse than highway robbery.—Mr. MARTLEY also called attention to the deficient illuminating power of the gas which had recently been-supplied, and one or two other members also said they had heard camplaints with respect to the gas.—Mr. PANEHURST, in answer to Mr. Midwood, said it was strange that he had not brought that matter forward before, and as far as he (Mr. Pankhurst) was concerned he must say that he had never heard of it before, nor did he think it had ever been before the committee.— The WATER ENGINEER also said he had.neyer heard of that matter before, and he had never done any work of that kind without previously giving notice to the owner.—Mr. PANS- HURST : We will enqaire into it and report to you, Mr. Midwood.—Mr. MrDwooD said he did not want to have the matter shirked like that—surely the man who made the bill out would be able to tell them what it was for.—Dr. BOOTH: Is it paid P—Mr. MIDWOOD : It is not, and never will be as far as I am concerned. (Laughter.)—lt Was ultimately agreed that the matter should be enquired into and a further report made upon it.—With regard to the gas, the WATER ENGINEER said it was as good as they could make it with the present coal, and in order to improve it they would have to qhange the coal.—The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee were then passed.

div.head: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE'S MINTrTES.
div.p: THE HIGHWAY COMMITTEE'S MINTrTES.

Mr. KERSHAW moved, and Mr. SHUTTLEWORTH seconded, the confirmation of these minutes, which stated with regard to Waterloo-road level crossing, that Messrs. Shaw and Worthington attended as a deputation on behalf of the rail- way company, and after discussion and explanation they undertook to prepare plans of suggested alterations and sub- mit them to the Board for approval.—Mr. WEBSTER asked if that improvement was to go on, because if it had, what with it and other improvements they might expect a heavy rate next year. He should like to know the cost before they proceeded with it.—Mr. MARTLEY also asked a question with regard to the Mersey-road ferry approach.—Mr. KERSHIW, in reply to Mr. Webster, said it was not the intention of the committee to proceed with the Waterloo-road improvement without first submitting an estimate of the cost to the Board. As to Mr. Martley's suggestion about the ferry approach the committee had certainly asked the London and North- Western Railway Company if they were willing to contri- bute a portion of the expenses, but .they seemed at present to deny their liability, and it was not for him to say there whether or not they were liable. The committee had in- structed the clerk to reply to the company's letter, and it was not for him to go into the matter until they got a reply. —The minutes were then confirmed. MR. SUTCLIFFE'S CYLINDER.

The Hospital Committee's minutes contained the follow- ing: "The clerk was instructed to give Mr. Sutcliffe notice that if the cylinder is not tested and fixed, in accordance with the contract, within thres days, that the order must be considered cancelled."—Mr. Mmwoon said he understood that Mr. Sutcliffe had complied with the Board's requisition, even before it was sent out. Mr. Sutcliffe had given the clerk a guarantee from the makers that the cylinder would stand fifty pounds.--Mr. SADDLER said he had nothing to say in answer to Mr. Midwood, except to deny in tot) whit he bad .said.—The CHAIRMAN understood that Mr,*Sutcliffe _

was willing to fix the cylinder if the Board-w-a-s-w-illisn-g-tO accept the maker's guarantee.—Mr. SADDLER: Yes, and the maker's guArantee was not satisfactory. The CHAIRMAN said it was evident Mr. Sutcliffe did not himself think the cylinder would stand fifty pounds, and he was bound to make it equal to fifty pounds by the arrangement the Board made with hi m.--The minutes were then confirmed.. THE SEWERAGE COMMITTEE'S MINUTES.

These minutes contained a report from the resident engineer, stating that the progress with sewerage works had been satisfactory during rhe past month. The minutes also contained the following with reference to the Victoria-road drainage :—" Memorial read, dated 28th September, from Mr. S. B. Stringer and others, asking for a remedy to the present nuisance from drainage into cellars.—The Clerk was instructed to reply that the sewerage scheme provides fir the drainage of Victoria-road by a branch going up Whitt- road from Moor-lane, and that the surveyor is instructed to report as to the possibility and cost of connecting Victoria- road sewer and Hutchinson-street sewer, if not connected, or otherwise dealing with the nuisances complained of." It was also recommended that Mr. Henty Linaker, of Run- corn, should be appointed arbiter on behalf of the Board in the wayleave dispute as to Ditton-road. Mr. KEnsHAw moved the confirmation of these minutes. it would require, he said, a special resolution of the Board to appoint Mr. Linaker, and he would include that in his motion.—Mr. WEBSTER said, with regard to the resident engineer, he did not think be was a resident engineer at all, and the town should object till he did become resident.— Mr. MrDwoon did not think such a reply as that proposed in the above minutes should be given to the memorial as to the Victoria-road nuisance. They said that Victoria-road was provided for in the present scheme, but he said again it was not provided for, and, besides, the matter had not been brought before the Government inspector.—Mr. KERSHAW said, with regard to what 'IND.. Midwood bad said, that he did not care about taking up the time of the Board with that matter, but he must say he was astonished at the last Board meeting to see Mr. Matthews at the head of the deputation. _

A gentleman who had sat on that Board some three years, and promoted the sewerage.scheme, ought to have ken con - verdant with every route that had been taken. He (Mr. Kershaw) could say that, as a ratepayer, he attended the Local Government Board enquiry, and the drainage of Victoria-road was pointed out to the inspector, although Mr. Midwood said it was not, and Mr. Harrison took great pains

with it, and investigated the matter to the very bottom. He oven went down to the site to investigate it, and compli- mented the Board, and especially their engineer, on the way the plans and drawings had been got out. He certainly thought Mr. Midwood ought to have brought that grievance, as to the answer to the memorialists, forward in committee, and suggested a better reply by moving an amendment.— Mr. MIDWOOD, in replying to Mr. Kershaw, said he thought the answer they proposed to give was a misleading one but ultimately the minutes were confirmed—Mr. liidwood, Mr. Hartley, and Mr. Wright dissenting.
HEALTH- COMMITTEE'S MINUTES.

The Medical Officer's report contained in these minutes stated that during October the births numbered BS, or 43.2 per 1,000; the deaths 33, or 15 84 per 1,000. These included eight children under one year, and a like number between one and five years. There had been six deaths from scarlet fever, and one each from typhoid, measles, and dysentry. Five new cases of scarlet fever and three of diphtheria had been reported during the month.
FINANCE COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this committee contained the following: I —" Legal expenses—Mr. Beasley's account. The Clerk reported having been served with a writ by Mr. Riley for payment of £l6O and interest upon an order given to him by Mr. Beasley, and that the chairman of the committee and he called upon Mr. Beasley's trustee, and after consultation, instructed Messrs. Collins, Robinson, and Co. to defend the action, and to take the necessary steps to enable the Board to pay the money into court, or ether satisfactory arrange- ment. Recommended, that the instruction given as above to Messrs. Collins, Robinson, and Co. be approved. Recom- mended, that the following increase of salaries be made: J. H. Wilson, from £B5 to £95; J. Heyes, from £7O to £75; A. Dennett, from £45 to £52; and J. Sankey, from £39 to £so."—Some conversation took place with regard to the recommendation on the increase of salaries, and it was pro- posed as an amendment by Mr. KERSHAW, and seconded by Mr. WEBSTER, that the discussion of the proposal should be left over and considered "together with the salaries of the Board's officials all round."—Dr. BOOTH did not think the proposed salaries too much considering the work that was to be done for them. Certainly workingmen were better off than the officials downstairs, who were expected to keep up an appearance of respecta- bility. They would not like to see any of them dressed in fustian, yet they gave them only about £4o'. He thought as Mr. Midwood was a very economical gentleman, it would be better if he would try to reduce the legal expenses. By doing that he might save more in (me year than he would do by keeping the salaries down in ten.—Ultimately the minutee were confirmed with the exception of that part re- lating to the increase of salaries which was referred back.

div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

The Geneial Purposes Committee recommended as follows :—" Ship Canaljto Mauchester :—The Chairman of this Board having received a circular letter and other papers forwarded them to the Clerk to be placed before this com- mittee. It was recommended that this Board express its ap; proval of the project, and pledges itself to support the scheme, provided that the application to Parliament core tains such provisions as will secure to this township and i inhabitants all the advantages to wh'oh, in the opinion of this Board, it is entitled."—This recommendation was agreed to nein. con.

div.head: THB CHAIRMAN'S MARRIAGB.
div.p: THB CHAIRMAN'S MARRIAGB.
Mr. KERSHAW moved that the following address be suit- ably engrossed and presented to Mr. Gossage, chairman of the board :

Dear Sir.—We beg to offer you our sincere congratulations on your approaching marriage, and to take this opportunity of. expressing our appreciation of your many services to our town, of your enterprise as a manufacturer, and of your generosity In helping objects of publ:o interest in Widnes. We earnestly hope that you and your bride will enjoy a long and happy life. We are, sir. yours with much respect. [Here follow the Lames of the members.] To F. H. Gossage. Esq.. J. 13., Chairman of the Widnes Local Board, Nov. 14th, 1,:82. _ .

Mr. PetexurusT observed that, as one of the oldest mem- bers of the board, he had great pleasure in seconding the proposition.—The CHAIRMAN was gratified to have the opportunity of supporting the resolution. They had all known Mr. Gossage for a great lefigth of time and ackno w- his many good qualities, which were far more in number than those mentioned in the memorial.—The resolution was carried unanimously,after which the proceedings terminated.

Cronshaw, described as an infant, to recover from the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Com- pany, compensation to the amount of £l2O for personal injury sustained by the plaintiff to his left hand (which injury resulted in three fingers and part of his left hand having to be amputated, and tho permanent injury of the fourth finger), whilst engaged as an apprentice at a circular saw at the defendant's works, at Weston on the 24th July last.—Mr. T. Shepherhittle, barrister-at-law, instructed by Mr. Burton, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Pickford, barrister-at-law, instructed by Messrs.
