—William Cronshaw, the plaintiff, was then called. He said he was 16 years of age, and lived in Bold-street, Run- corn. He entered the employ of the defendants, at Weston Works, in April, 1831. On the sth July of the same year be was apprenticed as cooper. In June, 1882, he was put by John Ward, the foreman cooper, to work at the circular saw, which had been previously worked by John Cooper, an apprentice. Cooper had been cut by the saw. At the time he (witness) was set to work at the saw, there was a guage attached to it which remained whilst he worked the saw. On the morning of the 24th July, when he went to work, he asked Ward, the foreman, for a sharp saw, as the one he was working was dull. Ward replied that "The saw was sharp enough." Witness said "These are are all the fingers I have, and if these get cut off I shall get no more." Ward said he (witness) was frightened, and then went away. He had noticed that the saw was very dull when he commenced working, which made him say this. That day they were sawing staves, and in one of them was a knot, which raised the saw. The staff was thrown up, and his left hand came in contact with the saw in some way he could not describe. He was so much injured that he had to have three fingers amputated. (Wit- ness here described the manner in which he worked). When in the laboratory at the works, he told Mr. Kirkham how the accident had occurred. His fingers wer mputated at rir the Royal Infirmary, Liverpool. He was abse from his em- ployment eight weeks and three days. He aso told Ward how the accident occurred. Ward said the thing was done and could not be undone. Three weeks after that conversa- tion, he met ward in Church-street, and he shouted out to him "Coma here and let me look at your pig's foot." (Laughter.) During the time he was away from his work he received no wages.—By Mr. Pickford: When he told Ward that the saw was dull he was quite sure that Ward did not test it. The saw had not been worked for nine days. He was not talking to any boy in the shop at the time the accident occurred. When the saw was sharp it would cut through five staves at once; when it was dull, as in the present instance, be could only push one through. Witness was cross-examined at some length as to how his band had been cut in the peculiar way it had. He said it was done all in a moment, and he could not tell how it happened.— Mr. R. H. Mouri:z, surgeon, said he examined the plaintiff on the 24th July. He told him that it would be necessary to remove three of his fingers, and that his fourth finger might be saved. Plaintiff went to Liverpool, and in his opinion the amputation had been skilfulry per- formed. Mrs. Margaret Cronshaw, mother of the plaintiff, said that on the evening of the day on which the accident occurred, Ward went to her house, and in the course of conversation admitted that the saw was null, and said he would take care that there was never another dull saw to cause another accident.—Miss Sarah Frances Cronshaw, plaintiff's sister, gave confirma- tory evidence. She heard her mother tell Ward he had no right to put her son to saw on account of his age. Ward replied that he was surprised to learn that the plaintiff was only 16 years old, he was "so big for his age."—By Mr. Pickford : Ward did not say that he knew her brother had said the saw was a dull one.—Thomas Jones, a circular sawyer, of 27 years' experience, living at 0 house, 43 court, Liverpool, said in cutting staves for casks such as those being cut by the plaintiff at the time of the accident, the saw should be sharpened at least four or five times a day. Some spruce staves would take the saw kindly enough, while others were rough, and the effect of a dull saw would be that the timber would have to be forced through, and great exertions and force was required on the part of the workman. From experience, he did not think that Cron- shaw was at all a proper age to work the saw. He was too young. By the appearance of a saw he (witness) could tell wh3ther it was sharp or not.—Adam Gerrard, Kensington, Liverpool, who said he was a sawyer of 30 years' experience, corroborated the evident() of last witness. He stated that a boy 16 years of age should not be permitted to go near a circular saw.—Wm. Williams, 3, Vine-street, Wid- nes, and Daniel Loury,also of Widnes, gave similar evidence. —Walter Brown, of 5, Princes-street, Runcorn, said he had worked at the circular saw, and had met with an accident. The saw by which he was injured was somewhat dull.— John Dutton, /I, Plinces-street, having given evidence, the case for the plaintiff concluded. Mr. Pickford stated that the saw was not defective within the meaning of the Act, and even supposing the saw was dull the accident had not happened in consequence of that dullness.—John Ward de- posed that he had been the foreman cooper at these works for two years. He remembered the plaintiff being put to the circular saw, but he did not tell him to hold' the timber or staves in the manner he had described in the court that morning. If he had seen him hold the staves•in that way he should have told him to adopt a safer method, which witness demonstrated to the court. The plaintiff went to him on the morning of the accident and told him the saw was dull. He took no -notice of him because he thought it was nothing but laziness that was the matter with him. He told him the saw was quite good enough but did not say that he wanted a saw every day: It was true that he had the superintendence of Cronshaw, but it was not his place to see that the saw was properly sharp.— Geo. Kilcross, foreman lawyer, of 20 years' experience, said it was his business to see that the saws were in proper order. He did not receive any complaint from either Ward or , Cronshaw on the day of the accident. After the accident he went to the saw, and found two staves partly sawn through. He finished them, toss's whether there was, any- thing wrong with the saw. He found it was all right.— Charles Kirkham, manager of the works,• having been ex- amined, Charles Webster, saw-mill proprietor, Bootle, said he had had 16 year,' experieeee in a Raw mill. A saw used for cutting staves such as were used at the Runcorn Soap Works would only require sharpening once every three or four days. He thought it would be quite safe to use a saw' after it had been standing idle for five or six days.—'ln cross-examination by Mr. Little, witness acknowledged that he was not a practical sawyer. He had only occasionally sawn a little for his own amusement.—Mr. Pickford again, raised the question as to how the accident could ha ve occurred in the peculiar way described by the plaintiff.— Witness said he had never seen an accident occur in that way.—His Honour said he must tell Mr. Pickford he could, quite understand, how the accident could occur in the way , and exactly as described by the plaintiff. He thought it was quite possible.—The hour having become so late—half- past five—his Honour adjourned the case, and said he would hear Mr. Pickfora's address for the defence at Birkenhead I, County Court, on Tuesday next.—The court then rose.

A very common cause of explosion in houses wae that in the rooms were chandeliers, which were lowered down When lighted, and when the people of the house went to bed, they turned the gas out, but forgot to push the chandeliers up. In these chandeliers were three tubes. The outer tube contains water, another tube brings gas up above the water, and a third slides down into the water. If that outer tube becomes dry, which might be caused by the heat of the room evapourating the water, there was a passage for the gas, which would escape into the room unperceived, perhaps. During the night the gas was filling the room, and in the morning when a light was taken into the room, as was freqwently the case, there was an explosion, simply because the gas was mixed with air.. Pure coal gas would not support combustion, and if a light were plunged into the gas, it would be instantly put out. (This was demonstrated.) His advice was "Always push up your chandeliers before you go to bed at night." (Applause.) Mr. Frith then produced a gas jet which made a singing noise when placed in a tube, and another which was so sensitive to sound that when a bundle of keys were rattled at the far end of the room, or the hands clapped,it was violently agitated, much to the amusement of the audience. Before he closed he said be had there a substance which, although not gas, would yet show in another way bow in- candescence produced light just the same as the incan- descence of the lime, or that carbon of the gas produced light. This was the Swan electric light, to which he would apply heat not by the union of oxogen and hydrogen, but by electricity. What electricity was he supposed was not known, and therefore they could not expect him to tell them. (Laughter.) But be knew that it gave light, not perhaps of the best description. (Lagghter.) It gave a rather uncertain light, but it was a very brilliant one. He had never had any faith in it. Mr. Frith then lit the lamp, and expressed his obligation to .the audience for their attendance and attention that evening. (Applause.) Mr. ROBERT SHAW, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Frith for his interesting lecture, said he felt satisfied they might share in Mr. Frith's views, that the day of gas was not passed. In Runcorn they might rest satisfied with that fact, simply because the gas people new were not resting upon their oars, but were quite alive that they had got an important rival in the field. The unanimous impres- sion was that supposing the gas companies were to rest where they had been, the day of the gas was doomed; but he believed that there was yet a great future for gas, although there was no doubt the electric light would force its way before the public, and within the next 20 or 30 years great changes would take place. Up to the present there had been nothing to give an impetus to gas companies; their business had been profitable, and in a measure satis- factory ; but he thought that now they would have very great changes.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.

The Committee held their monthly meeting in the Com- missioners' Board-room, on Tuesday. The Rev.. Canon Bar- clay, chairman presided. There were also present Dr. Mc Dougall, Dr. chairman, Messrs. Jim. Simpson, F. Briscoe, T. Riley, W. Handley, W. Brookes (clerk), and J. D. Jones (librarian). The librarian reported that there had been 1,673 books borrowed from the library during the month of October. They were classified as follows : Theology 46, philosophy 14, history, travels, and biography 298, science and art 81, poetry 34. fiction 1,085, miscellaneous 115; 163 books had been presented to the library during the month, and the Committee, on the motion of Dr. McDougall, seconded by Mr. Peter Briscoe, instructed the clerk to con- vey their thanks to the donors. The librarian also presented a report with regard to the hiring of books from Messrs. Smith and Son's subscription library. He described the manner in which the system would be worked if the Com- mittee decided to hire books from the library. Dr. Mc Dougall moved, and Dir. Steele seconded, a motion that the Committee take no action in the natter for the present.— Carried.—The Chairman said he had received a letter from Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst, in, which he said it was with more re- gret than he was able to express that he left his place on the Library Committee..& discussion arose as to whether Mr Hazlehurst's resignation to the Board of Commissioners not haying been yet accepted; he had vacated his position on the Library Committee, and eventually it was decided that Mr. Hazlehurst's letter be referred to the next meeting of the Library Committee inasmuch as there was some doubt as to whether Mr. Ha;lehurst was still a member of the Committee.—The Librarian said. he had no room for the new ; books, and he asked for additional shelves to be erected. It was intimated that Mr. Barker, the surveyor, had the matter in hand.—This-was the whole of the business.

div.head: DI,TRICT NEWS.
div.p: DI,TRICT NEWS.
FRODSHAM.

REVIVAL SERTIC ES AT TRINITY CHAPEL, FEODSHAM.— Special services have been held during the week in the Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, and have been conducted by the Rev. J. M. Bamford (Frodsham), Rev. Alfred Johnson (of New Brighton), and Revs. E. 21 Robinson and George Hack (of Runcorn). THEATRICALS AT THE TOWN, HAMM, FRODSHAM.—Mr. Frank Hill's talented dramatic company have occupied the Town Hall during the past week. The "Colleen Bawn " was given oh Thursday evening under distinguished patronage, and the dresses, drc., in the various plays have been good and effective. In the entertainments which Mr. Hill provides for the public, there does not appear to be anything which the most fastidious person could object to. VOLUNTEER SUPPER AND DISTRIB:;TION OE PRIZES AT FRODSHAH.—On Saturday evening the officers of the 2nd ;1,.R.V. gave a substantial supper to the Company, in the Town Hall, Frodsham. The officers present were :—Cap- ,tain Robert Ashton and Lieutenants R. G. Henry and H. IHarrison. There were also present—Major Duncan, and IMessrs. R. Holden, D. Ashton, G. Ashton, F. Hilditch, J. B. Holland, Albert Harrison, E. Ferris, and J. Arrowsmith. After full justice had been done to the good things provided, Captain Robert Ashton took the chair, and proposed The health of Her Majesty the Queen," and also "The health of '•the Prince and Pricess of \Vales and other members of the Royal Family." These toasts were received in a loyel I manner and were drunk with musical honours.—Mr. Flank Hilditch said he had much pleasure in proposing "The I health of Captain Robert Ashton," which was received in an enthWsiastic manner, the band proclaiming loudly that he was a jolly good fellow.—Captain Ashton, in the course of his reply, expressed the pleasure it gave him to be with them that evening, and-to hold his present command, which he might say had been his ambition some 10 or 15 years ago. He had now been in command for about four years, and nothieg gave hirn greater pleasure than to have them on parade. He had said at the commencement of the season that if they were successful in winning the battalion cup he would give them a jolly good feed, but with regard to the supper on the occasion of the prize distribution, he had decided that it would not do to let a good rule drop through. (Applause.) He hoped that he might long be spared his health to retain the command of the Company, and trusted they would have more efficient& next year.—Song, "The British Lion," Bugler W. Jones.— Tth Chairmen in proposing "the Army Navy and Reserve Forces" coupled with it the names of Major Duncan, and Private Frederick Foster.—Major Duncan said that before he ventured to respond for ths reserve forces he should like to hear the gallant Marine, wile, he understood had been in the Egyptian campaign,and he would be glad to follow him on behalf of the reserve forces. They all knew the gallant stand which the Marines had made, and the good service which they had done for their country.—Private Foster gave an interesting account of his experience in the late Egyptian war, while serving on the Minataur flag ship of the Channel Fleet.—The Chairman said he was very, proud that one of the members of the volunteer corps had, passed through the late campaign. In his opinion it showed that the volunteer corps was the starting point for the regular arnty, and that they could find as good blood in Frodsham. as any in England.—Major Duncan.said, he was pleased to be present, and.as he was well acquainted with the Chester corps of the battalion he was glad to extend his acquaintance to the Frodsham corps, and hoped that it would last long. The more they knew one another they more they would like each other. He considered that this country. owed much to the very gallant force of which he had the honour to be a member. Private Foster had given a modest aecount of the experience of the Royal Marines in the late war, and he always felt that there was no company. which had borne such a splendid character during the whole course of its existence as the Royal Marines, as it had never known dis- grace; but they did not appear to have had that meed of praise in higher circles as they deserved. He concluded by thanking the company for the kindness and cordiality associated with the toast of the Reserve Forces.—Song, "The old arm chair," Ed. Turner,—" The health of Lieu- tenants Henry and Harrison" having been drunk, the task of distributing the prizes was then proceeded with. The first prize, a silver medal and cap, was won. by Corporal R. Lloyd, with 31 points. The dlowing is a list of competi- tors and number of points gained by each :—Corporal Lloyd, 31 points; J. Hazlehurst, 28; W. Beard, 28; J. Holland, 27; Sergeant T. Davies, 26; Corporal J. Atherton, 26; C. Hitchen, 23;; Corporal G. Edge, 23 • Sergeant J. Midge, 23; W. Grady, 23; Bugler W. Jones, 2; J. Davies, 21; J. Caldwell, 20; W. Henshaw, 20; S. Charlesworth, 19; W. Chesters, 19; J. Smith, 19.; J. Worrell, 17; Sergeant T. Earlam, 15; A. Hayes, 15; E. Sutton, 15; Sergeant W. Watson, 14; J. Garner, 14; J. Massey, 14; J. Gould, 13.; P. Walker, 13; W. Hughes, 10; E. Turner, 8; H. Bell, 7; H. Frankish, 6; G.Regers, 6; J. Ryder, 4; W. Wharton, 2. Each competitor received one prize at least. The distance was 200 and 300 yards, with five rounds at each dietance, but the weather was very unfavourable. CULCHETH.

NIGHT PoAcw,NG.—On Wednesday, at the Liverpool Assizes, Albert Smith, aged 34, labourer, and George Harri- son, aged 33, labourer, were indicted for lyving at Culcheth, near Leigh, on the 19th September, trespassed on the farm of Wm. Monks in pursuit of game while armed with offen- sive weapons. Mr. Heywood prosecuted, and Mr. Cottinghana defended. The prisoners were found guilty, and each was zontenoed to six months' imprisonment with bard labour.

Incorporated uader the Companies' Acts, 1882 to 1880, whereby the liability of SharehAders is limited to the amount of their Shares. Capital £150,000. First issue £lOl,OOO, in Shares of £1 each, payable as follows :-2s 6d per Share on application, 2s 6d on allotment, and the balance as may be required; but further calls shall not exceed 23 ad per ahare, nor be made at inter- vals of less than 3 months. DIRECTORS —Joseph Hubback, Esq. J.P , Liverpool, Chair- man; G. E. Mountain, Eq. Manchester; Fredk. Parke, Esq, Chorley; R. W. B. Sanderson, Esq, Rersal, Mar,chester; Frederick Thompson Esq, Manchester. BANKERS.—Manchester and Liverpool District Bank, Liver- pool, and Branches. BOLICITORS.—Messrs. H. W, Collins, Robinson, and Ce., 3, Union-court, Castle-street, Liverpool. SURVEYOII.—John Blenkarn, Esq. Manchester. AUDITOR.—Mr. Alfred Williams, 21, Harrington-street, Liverpool. SECRETARY (pro tem).—Mr. Thomas Ingham. TEMPORARY OPFICES.-21, Harrington-street. Liverpool. This Company has been formed for the purpose of purchasing and developing a valuable Freehold Estate in Lancashire, ad- joining the Gateacre Station on the Cheshire Lines Railway. comprising the Lee Hall Mansion, Throstle Nest, and various other residences on the property, including in all. about 150 acres. A contract, for the purchase of which, for £95,000, has been secured. £BO,OOO will remain on -mortgage for a term of rears at 4 per cent. The pra sent proprietor of the property is the vendor, and he undertakes to pay all preliminary expenses incurred in or about the formation of the Company up to the time of allotment. Tee Estate is about six miles from Liver- pool. The following report from Mr. John Blenkarn, Surveyor, Manchester, who has been, more or less, connected with Land Companies for fifteen years, gives very fully his views of the property : Dear Sirs, Manchester, Oct. 25th, 1882. LEE HALL FISTATE. I have walked over and cairefully examined The Lee Hall Estate, at Gateacre reported to me to contain from 240 to 250 acres. The Estate is within the Local Board District of Little Wootton, and is well situated for sewe age and drainage. The public roads intersecting the property are in very goad condition, and the Liver pool Corporation have already laid down pipes in the road for we' er supply. There is excel- lent sand on: the Estate; good clay in a detached posi; ion, and the well-knewn Woolton stone quarries are within a short distance. In my opinion, the Estate may be developed for building sites with very great advantage considering its proximity to Liverpool. Gateacre Station stands immediately adja- cent to the property; and there is a good train service— about twenty minutes to the Central Station, Ranelagh- street, Liverpool, and about the same to the Midland Station at the North-end of Liverpool, at Bootle—the fares being moderate. Looking at the rapid growth of the population of Liver- pool, and the universal desire et the growing classes, connected with the shipping and manufacturing interests, to provide salubrious and comfortable homes for their families, the Lee Hall Estate offers advantages scarcely to be surpassed in the neighbourhood of Liverpool. I do vast hesitate to st:te from my long experience in the development of similar estates in the neighbourhood of London and other large centres of population, that, if judiciously laid out, the property in qu-s,ion would, with- in the next ten years (after paying all out-going expenses), realise a net profit of not lrys than £95,000. I would suggest, in the event of the land being purchased for building. that peculiar advantages should be offered to the industrial and saving classes, of securing at a very moderate cost small plots of freehold which would be appreciated by them. Every facility should be given to the Building Societies with the object of covering the property.—l remain, Sir, your obedient servant, JOHN BLENICARN. Joseph Hubback, Esq„ J.P., Liverpool. The features of the property are greatly varied offering suit- able sites for almost all classes ot domestic buildings. In issuing this Prospectus, the Directors need hardly draw atten- tion to the fact that, as the property of the Company is Free- hold, with the exception of a small portion of Copyhold (which will be converted into Freehold), purchased oa advantageous terms, the security which its shares willy afford will not be of a speculative character, and there is every probability that tha developement of the Estate will yield a satisfactory return to the Shareholders. A plan of the Estate accompanies this Pro pectas. Boarders are received in the Head Master's house, which has recently been fitted for the purpo,e, and their comfort and will-being secured under the care of the Head Master and his wife. The climate is identical with that of Buxton; education sound and thorough in preparation, either for the Universities. the various Local and Preliminary Examinations, or for Mer- cantile life. Separate beds; food abundant and wholesome. Board and education £4O a year inclusive. Cricket field. Governing Body includes Ven Archdeacon Ralston, D.D., late Head Master of Eton, Lord Scarsdale, the 'Vicar of Tideswell, and others, under the New Scheme sanctioned by the Queen In Council. Apply to Rev. A. C. Fix. Tideswell, Sheffield. BOTELEX GRAMMAR SCHOOL WAR EtINGTON. FOUNDRY.) A.D. 1526. Head Master: The Rev. B. J. WILLCOCKS, M.A.. Late Scholar of St. Catharine's College, Cambridge. Second Master: The Rev. H. G. SMITH, M.A., Schuler of St. John's College, Cambridge; And five Assistant Masters. The Eisthool contains two divisions. The work of the Lower Division comprises a regular course of instruction in English, French, the rudiments of Latin, elementary Mathematics and Science, with Reading, Writing, Arithmetic, Drawing, Drill, and Vocal Music, and all other elements of a sound modern education. In the Upper Division, the choice is offered of a thorough mercantile or high classical course; Gorman aid *reek being optional subjects. Eight Free Scholarships. Two Exhibitions to Oxford and Cambridge. The year is divided into three Terms. Capitation fees, everything included, £1 and £8 per term Is the Upper and Lower Divisions respectively. Entrance Fee, £l. For furtheepartioulars apply to the Head Master.
